in writing. ‒ harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicps) are designed to measure inflation in a harmonised way and are of fundamental importance as they are used to assess national competitiveness. they are also essential instruments for achieving the objective of price stability. the current iacp rules date from 1995 and are not adapted to new realities, taking into account recent developments in consumer price statistics. this resolution provides for a control on the impact of fiscal changes in inflation by a separately calculated price index, as well as the establishment of price indices for housing and in particular for owner-occupied housing. this is an important step towards improving the relevance and comparability of hicps and would also allow for the identification of real estate bubbles at an early stage. the report also provides the legal framework for the implementation of rapid hicp estimates, which are essential for monetary policy in the euro area. moreover, it advocates the launch of pilot studies to strengthen the progressive harmonisation of consumer price indices by assessing the feasibility of using additional basic information or applying new approaches, which is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the european system of central banks (escb) is one of the main drivers of our economy, without which the value system could not function. thus, its use of harmonised indices of consumer prices helps to harmonise inflation in the member states of the european union. the introduction of harmonised indices of consumer prices at a constant value of tax rates (hicp-ct) will improve the european economic system by creating a better possibility of analysis and control. i encourage member states to contribute to the start of pilot studies, the verification of current information and the design of new methodological approaches, in order to achieve a progressive strengthening of consumer price indices. they also support the idea of improving europe's economy by implementing ecoicop (european classification of individual consumption according to purpose) and thus gaining a broader view of current and future problems, statistics, visions, possibilities and ambitions. the proposed new system will establish a uniform legal framework for the development, production and dissemination of data on harmonised indices. member states will thus commit themselves to submit monthly provisional information on inflation and estimates of these indices.
in writing. ‒ this regulation establishes a uniform legal framework for the development, production and dissemination of data on harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicps) and house prices (hicps) at union, national and sub-national level. the hicp is a measure of inflation used, inter alia, as a valuable input on the deflation of economic values such as wages, rents, interest rates and therefore forms the basis for economic and monetary policy decisions. it is therefore essential that those statistics are objective, unbiased and allow comparisons between all member states and all product categories. harmonised indices of consumer prices are an important tool for analysing the causes of inflation and for forecasting the impact of future fiscal changes on inflation.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the inclusion of our main achievement, which is to ensure sufficient implementation power for the commission to make the statistical methodology evolve on hicp (the council sought to strengthen the national level during the trilogue negotiations) and to better integrate into hicp indices both owner-occupied housing indices and house-price indices, which are crucial in addressing macroeconomic imbalances in the eu. flawed statistics were partly responsible for the financial crisis in 2008. this new legislation improves the quality of indices of consumer prices which are important to correct macroeconomic imbalances in the eu.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it improves the quality of indices of consumer prices which are very important in the rectification of macroeconomic imbalances.
in writing. ‒ this report presents a uniform legal framework for the development, production and dissemination of data on harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicp) and of housing prices (hpi) at union, national and sub-national level. the hicp measures consumer price inflation in the euro area. i voted for this report that will bring a revision of the above-mentioned framework in order to ensure maximum compatibility for the main users of the hicp. i consider it worth mentioning that the hicp is also used in assessing whether a country is ready to join the euro area.
in writing. ‒ the objective of this regulation is to establish a common framework for the development, production and dissemination of the harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicps) and the house price index (hpi) at union and national level. high-quality and comparable price statistics are essential for union policy-makers, researchers and all european citizens. the commission and the european central bank (ecb) use the dissemination of the harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicps) to assess price stability in the member states. by 31 december 2018, the commission will have to prepare a report addressing the appropriateness of the ooh price index (owner-occupied housing price index) for inclusion in the hicp coverage. depending on the results of the report, the commission shall, if appropriate, within a reasonable timeframe, submit a proposal to amend this regulation as regards the integration of the ooh price index into the hicp coverage.
in writing. ‒ at national, sub-national, and eu levels, the commission’s proposal for a regulation establishes a uniform legal framework for the development and dissemination of data on harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicp) and of housing prices (hpi). the hicp provides a measure of inflation used as valuable data for deflating economic values and shapes the basis for economic and monetary policy. therefore, it is important that statistics are objectively comparable across all product areas and member states. for the power of the commission to alter elements with delegated acts, two issues are excluded and decided directly in the regulation. first is the determination of the sub-indices of the hicp, secondly the selection of sub-indices. furthermore, since early conditional information on inflation is crucial for the conduct of monetary policy, euro member states must provide hicp flash estimates monthly. the breakdown of the estimates of the hicp, owner-occupied housing (ooh) price index and the hpi must also be adopted by means of implementing acts. lastly, with the influential pilot studies, the commission shall appropriately contribute to their financing and report to the european parliament and the council assessing the main findings of the studies. for these reasons, i have voted for this regulation.
in writing. the variation in prices for the various products and services on the european market is an element of uncertainty for consumers in the member states. the existence of significant differences, both between different countries and between different regions, contributes to the maintenance of important disparities at european level, creating the conditions for unfair discrimination between consumers. to counter these problems, the commission has developed a single statistical methodology, which can now be embodied in the harmonised indices of consumer prices (hicps). these indicators aim at establishing uniform treatment of similar product groups in the member states in order to reduce the possibility of interpretation or infringement of the rules, which contributed to the 2008 crisis. the treatment also concerns the real estate index field, which represents a significant part of the european economy, but does not concern areas of public interest such as education, health etc. i believe that supporting this document and applying it as soon as possible will help to reduce the development gaps that exist at union level. that is why i support its adoption in its present form.
in writing. ‒ the protection of the union's financial interests must be a central element of the eu's political agenda. both the european union and the member states must protect financial interests against crimes that cause significant financial damage. unfortunately, corruption affects all member states and costs the eu economy around €120 billion. the effects of corruption are also felt in the diminished trust of citizens in european institutions and democratic processes. i welcome the commission's implementation of a new anti-fraud policy, in line with the principle of sound financial management and with the aim of ensuring adequate protection of the eu's financial interests, which is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ public spending and the protection of the eu's financial interests must be key elements of the eu's policy of increasing citizens' confidence by ensuring the fair, efficient and effective use of their money. corruption affects all member states and costs the eu economy around €120 billion a year. i voted for the european executive to take full responsibility for recovering unduly paid funds from the eu budget, as well as for improving the collection of own resources and establishing uniform reporting principles in all member states to collect adequate, comparable and accurate data. increasing irregularities have been detected through the commission's ex-ante and ex-post controls and therefore it is necessary to further promote such controls. the competent authorities in the member states must also improve controls and use all available information to avoid errors and irregular payments related to the use of eu funds.
in writing. ‒ concerning the annual report 2014 on the protection of the eu’s financial interests, i believe that the methodology for calculating error rates must be harmonised at eu and member state level and that the european public prosecutor’s office (eppo) regulation should be adopted swiftly. moreover, i would like to welcome the commission’s commitment to publish an eu anti-corruption report biannually. i support the call on the commission to swiftly promote legislation on the minimum level of protection for whistle-blowers in the eu, and i urge the commission to maintain its strict policy on interruption and suspension of payments in accordance with the relevant legal basis. i believe that, through this report, the goal of expressing a clearer and fair picture of the main challenges in the protection of the financial interests in the eu was accomplished.
in writing. ‒ the report is very important if we think about the level of fraud and the effects of fraud on citizens. fraud leads to corruption and corruption leads to polarization of society. i appreciate that the report also states that many of the errors found by olaf are not fraudulent and therefore i believe that there is a need for prevention, simplification and transparency in the spending of money. i voted for the report even though i do not believe that the creation of new institutions solves the problem, just as i do not agree that for the mistakes of national institutions or legal entities, citizens should be sanctioned by suspending or interrupting payments to european funds. i appreciate that the report makes reference to simplification of procedures, but the commission must also check over-regulation at national level.
in writing. ‒ there are several points that should be highlighted. fraud and errors are two different things; both must be fought and not confused. the methods for calculating error rates at the european and member state level should be harmonised. prevention is important and should involve constant training and support for staff responsible.
in writing. ‒ the european anti-fraud office (olaf) has the responsibility of protecting the european union’s financial interests by investigating fraud, corruption and any other illegal activities. i voted for this annual report that emphasises olaf’s role and presents the areas that need improving.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report, which i also supervised as a shadow rapporteur, because i believe that the problem of fraud and corruption affects all eu member states, not just romania. it is clear that fighting fraud and ensuring a transparent environment ensures that organised crime is reduced and citizens' trust in public institutions is increased, while protecting the eu's financial interests by increasing its competitiveness on the world market. in this respect, as the document suggests, the european commission, together with olaf and the member states, must improve controls at customs level, but also at the level of public institutions empowered to obtain and spend european funds in the member states. also, budgeting on the basis of performance rather than on the basis of a formalistic evaluation of programmes will allow and create a favourable framework for the economic development of each member state.
in writing. the fight against fraud involving european money has become one of the european union's priorities in recent years. in this way, the efforts of taxpayers in each member state are protected and it is ensured that funds reach the areas that really need them and not the pockets of people who are only looking to get rich easily with public money. the commission's annual report on budgetary control for 2014 shows a total of eur 3,24 billion affected by irregularities. in total, the amount of fraud increased by 36% compared to 2013, while the number of irregularities increased by 48%, thus significantly. the main sector affected is rural development, which is precisely where the need for funding is greatest. the european parliament supports the commission's initiative to publish a biannual report on the fight against corruption at eu level and the activities of civil society in this regard, as well as the suspension of payments where deemed necessary. however, this latter measure should not affect the actual development of those sectors. the eu's european anti-fraud office (olaf) should also not have immunity from scrutiny by national structures, in order to avoid systemic flaws. i support the adoption of this report.
in writing. ‒ the report on the financial protection of the european union highlights that financial irregularities reported in 2014 increased by 36% compared to 2013, and that corruption affects all member states. each year, the european union economy suffers costs of around €120 billion caused by corruption. moreover, corruption is a phenomenon with extremely negative effects, damaging the image of institutions and participating in the financing of organised crime or terrorist actions in europe. in this regard, further strengthening of the role of the european anti-fraud office is needed, as well as other actions such as the establishment of uniform principles for reporting fraudulent or non-fraudulent irregularities at member state level, in order to have a real picture of the situation in the european union, but also to be able to find solutions to these problems. i also believe that there is a need for more transparency in the management of european funds. i appreciate that the report i voted for stresses the need to strengthen the role of the commission by introducing control and monitoring activities, through action plans and warning letters, and by providing technical assistance to member states by the commission.
in writing. i voted for the own-initiative report on the 2014 annual report on the protection of the eu's financial interests combating fraud, which also introduces the suggestions of the international trade commission (inta). the inta suggestions focus on anti-fraud measures that should be introduced into eu trade policy. the commission notes that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the application of the exemption from the anti-dumping duty on imports of certain footwear with uppers of leather originating in the people's republic of china. in the same text, inta also welcomes the key role played by the eu's macro-financial assistance programme in promoting reforms in the countries that are the eu's closest trading partners, one of its aims being to fight corruption and fraud in the beneficiary countries.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the report on the mainstreaming of the gender perspective in the work of the european parliament. i'm against favoring one gender over another. qualification, not gender, should be the deciding factor in an individual's profession. i also oppose the idea of a permanent gender mainstreaming rapporteur who examines the work of all committees. this would be an additional element that would add to the administrative burden without any effect. on the other hand, they advocate maintaining the practice of gender mainstreaming, which has been shown to have beneficial effects. gender equality should be guaranteed through equal opportunities. we could achieve our goal of achieving gender equality through other avenues, for example, by promoting education for both women and men and by eradicating gender discrimination. i want to stress that i support gender equality, but i do not think that this report is a step forward in this regard.
in writing. ‒ gender mainstreaming is essential in the preparation, design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of policies, regulatory measures and spending programmes with the aim of promoting equality between women and men and combating discrimination. this includes both mainstreaming a gender perspective in the content of the different policies and addressing the issue of the representation of women and men in those policies. balanced representation of women and men and the existence of gender-sensitive content should be taken into account at all stages of the policy-making process. even though laws treat women and men equally, women still do not have equal access to and control over resources and goods, and gender mainstreaming is an essential element of an appropriate gender equality strategy.
in writing. ‒ i totally support this resolution, which stresses for the need for gender mainstreaming amendments, gender impact assessment and gender budgeting in order to integrate a gender perspective in all policy areas. it is fundamental that we call on the commission to make gender impact assessments on new legislative or policy proposals in order to guarantee that the eu is upholding women’s rights. as female representation in key decision-making positions at political and administrative level – including political groups in parliament – remains low, i support the proposals to increase gender equality at staff level. on 8 march, i therefore support the call on parliament, its institutional partners and ngos to closely work together with a view to making gender mainstreaming a continuous process, and integrate gender equality at all levels, in all areas and into all stages of policy-making.
in writing. ‒ the european union must guarantee equal opportunities and treatment for men and women. the european parliament and its institutional partners should step up their efforts to mainstream gender equality at all levels, in all areas and at every stage of the policy-making process.
in writing. ‒ even though i support article 23 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union and article 8 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, i voted against this report for the sole reason that i have not found any gender discrimination in parliament, therefore i consider this report useless.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report that should integrate a gender perspective in the content of different policies, and should address the issue of representation of women and men in the given policy area. gender mainstreaming has been embraced internationally as a strategy towards achieving gender equality.
in writing. ‒ to this day, even though gender equality is recognised by the eu as a fundamental right, structural gender inequality persists to exist in our society. sadly, the report highlights that activities of bodies responsible for gender mainstreaming in the european parliament and with other institutions are not yet effectively coordinated or integrated and that 2009 gender balance targets at senior and middle management level have still not been met. i voted in favour of this report because integration of a gendered perspective is a necessary component of all areas of policy-making and a prerequisite for creating equal opportunities for women and men. the european parliament should therefore continue to work on embracing and implementing gender mainstreaming in all aspects of its work. the report is a necessary step in the right direction.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the mainstreaming of gender in the work of the european parliament, as the achievement of gender equality is essential for the protection of human rights, the functioning of democracy and social inclusion. at present, the presence of women in key decision-making positions at administrative and political level, as well as in political groups in the european parliament, remains low. within the european parliament, the committee on human rights and gender equality is the central body responsible for promoting and mainstreaming gender equality in the political and legislative processes of the european parliament. however, all committees should be actively involved in this process and, to this end, should adopt their own action plan. in this regard, the establishment of a permanent rapporteur on gender mainstreaming is particularly important for the achievement of gender mainstreaming objectives. moreover, the action should not be limited to the european parliament. in this respect, i believe that there should be a continuous dialogue with national parliaments to ensure an exchange of views and practices in order to promote the integration of the gender perspective into the - better coordinated - work of the european legislative forums.
in writing. ‒ the wave of refugees coming to europe is also creating problems for the situation of refugees and asylum seekers in the eu. it is indeed a difficult and at the same time problematic situation and their rights must be respected without any doubt. on the other hand, respect for the rights and freedoms of individuals, regardless of gender, is an essential condition of a state governed by the rule of law. to mention only women as benefiting from ill-treatment is discrimination. the preferential treatment discussed in this report concerns only refugee girls, but not refugee boys. in view of the recent incidents in the calais refugee camp where boys aged 14-16 were raped, i believe that boys should also have the right to equal protection. at the same time, the report provides facilities for the lgbti community, but does not propose facilities for christians persecuted by muslims in the camps. this fact needs to be foreseen. in view of the arguments mentioned above, and the fact that most of the measures mentioned in the report imply burdens for the camp volunteers and local leaders, i am against this report.
in writing. ‒ a reform of eu migration and asylum policies and procedures must include gender-sensitive measures to ensure the safety of women seeking asylum, many of whom travel with young children, and other dependants. this report highlights the particularly vulnerable situation of refugee women in the european union. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 26 to supplement this regulation by laying down detailed rules for the implementation of this regulation. member states should guarantee the right to require that interviewees and interpreters be women, to provide appropriate training to interviewees and interpreters in the field of sexual violence, trauma, to provide trauma counselling to women who have suffered gender-based violence, to provide information on asylum procedures and the specific rights of women seeking asylum, to provide childcare during asylum checks and interviews, to inform women about their right to lodge asylum applications independently of their partner and to have a legal status independent of their husbands.
in writing. ‒ in 2015, about 1 million people crossed the mediterranean. women and children account around 35% of refugees. in january 2016, women accounted for 55%. i strongly believe we need to highlight the exceptionally vulnerable situation of women asylum seekers and refugees in the european union. they have fled persecution in their home countries only to undertake a perilous journey in order to reach a place of safety. on arrival at reception centres these already vulnerable women, who may be victims of sexual violence, trafficking or other violent crimes, face additional barriers which further increases their already vulnerable positions. i therefore support the call for gender sensitive asylum procedure through a number of measures, such as gender-specific training for staff, gender-segregated sleeping and sanitation facilities, the right to request female interviewers and interpreters, access to gender-sensitive health services including prenatal and postnatal care.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report that calls for gender sensitive asylum procedures through a number of measures. the eu has played an important role in highlighting the issue of gender equality and placed it at the heart of the values on which european union is based. the report calls for support for vulnerable women refugees and asylum seekers who may be victims of sexual violence, trafficking or other violent crimes, or discrimination, and to ensure the women’s needs throughout the asylum process.
in writing. ‒ women refugees have shown great strength to risk everything and flee their war-torn home country, cross the seas in dreadful conditions facing physical assault, abuse and violence and look now for protection in the eu. during the asylum process, on european soil, they are still exposed to gender-based harm and remain a particularly vulnerable category. europe needs to stand together and give a humanitarian response, and as policy makers we need to address their basic social, medical and economic needs. it is the week we celebrate international women’s day; following our european values, i hereby support and respect the right of these women, who have been through enough already, to seek asylum in proper conditions.
in writing. ‒ half of the world's refugee population in 2014 were represented by women and girls. the european parliament was the first international body to acknowledge the need for a gender-sensitive interpretation of the refugee convention, in a resolution of 13 april 1984. i have voted for this report that reiterates the need to guarantee a consistent and gender-sensitive treatment for women seeking protection in europe.
in writing. ‒ in 2014, half of the world’s refugee population were women and girls. laws and policies, despite the establishment of the common european asylum system (ceas), differ significantly across member states. additionally, there continues to be a discernible gap in the protection of women seeking asylum in the eu. as a result, a new all-inclusive set of eu-wide gender guidelines should be adopted as part of wider reforms to migration and asylum policy. the acts making up the ceas have so far not assured consistent and gender-sensitive treatment for women seeking asylum. although there is currently legislation and policy designed in a gender-sensitive way, significant shortcomings persist. while some policies are gender-sensitive, this does not always ensure their effective implementation. this policy must be sensitive and responsive to women’s experiences at every stage. women asylum seekers and refugees must be given a greater voice for policy makers to comprehend how gendered relations of power yield forced displacement and specific gendered needs. unequal gender relations have intensified during this humanitarian crisis. however, this time also allows for the possibility to harmonise best practice in the treatment of women asylum seekers. for these reasons, i have voted in favour of the above proposal.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, let me start by saying that we discussed this issue – the situation in syria and our work to try and put an end to the war – on 19 january, so less than two months ago. many different things have happened since then so i would like to thank you for this debate and for the opportunity that this offers us all to check and double check the steps taken, the sense of direction and also the difficulties we still have ahead of us. first of all let me remind us all again what has happened in this one and a half months. first of all we had the london conference on syria. i start with this because this was not only a pledging conference where the european union and the member states represented two-thirds of the contributions to support syrians inside syria and in the neighbouring countries, but this was also a way of showing the unity of the international community and solidarity and a sense of hope for the syrians in their own country. we have pledged eur 3 billion in support for the refugees and the internally displaced people inside syria and for the humanitarian aid. i will go back to the role of the humanitarian aid in a moment from a political and also from a security point of view, but we also prepared two packages, two compacts as we call them, one for jordan and one for lebanon, which comprise not only financial support, but also some measures that can support these countries in the effort of integrating syrian refugees into the host communities, giving children education, giving young women and men job opportunities, and also making it sustainable for the communities in jordan and in lebanon to sustain this effort in the mid-term period. the second thing that has happened since 19 january is that the first round of talks among syrians took place in geneva – almost immediately suspended because of clear problems that were coming up in the first talks that staffan de mistura was holding at the time – and a subsequent meeting of the international support group in munich. here we met at length for many hours together with john kerry, lavrov and all the other foreign ministers represented there from some 20 countries, the european union and the arab league, all around the table, trying to check exactly whether the suspension of the talks in geneva was due to difficulties that were impossible to overcome – not only locally, internally, nationally, among the syrians but also in the bigger regional framework – or if it would be possible, through the international support group, to move forward and revitalise a process in which all of us have invested so much in the last months. out of this meeting in munich we established two task forces: one on the modalities of the cessation of hostilities, co-chaired by the us and russia, these being the two actors that needed to coordinate the most, especially in military coordination, to identify in concrete terms the maps, the groupings and the areas for the entry into force of the ceasefire or the cessation of hostilities. and a task force on humanitarian aid, because we identified very clearly the need to have a second round of talks in geneva, which staffan de mistura has now announced for tomorrow and the coming days, to make sure that these talks happen with a completely different, or very substantially different, atmosphere on the ground, rather than the one that we experienced on the previous occasion, meaning to try and reduce the gap between syrians talking in geneva about a very difficult political transition and process, while on the ground syrians are dying in besieged areas and cities with no access to humanitarian aid. so we know that delivering in an effective way humanitarian aid, food and medicines to the syrians inside syria would give credibility. it would create conditions for a credible process in geneva and would also open up some channels for political discussions among different parties. we then has, as you know, the task force on cessation of hostilities producing very advanced work – the humanitarian task force as well, i will come back with details in a moment – and the adoption of un security council resolution 2268 on cessation of hostilities that started on 29 february. since then, i have to say – not only myself but also the un special envoy staffan de mistura and the two co-chairs of the taskforce, the us and russia – that the cessation of hostilities, the ceasefire, is substantially holding even if we are seeing several breaches throughout syria, in different parts of syria. however, the overall assessment is that the ceasefire is holding and that the situation on the ground for this whole week has been significantly improved compared to all the previous weeks of the conflict. that is to say that this is probably the first time in five years of conflict that we see in many parts of syria no major armed intervention even if, as i said, breaches are happening continuously but with an intensity and a magnitude that is definitely on a different scale from in the past. on the humanitarian task force: we have managed in these weeks to deliver aid through 180 trucks to 150 000 syrians inside syria in different besieged areas and we are working – the eu in particular and together with the un – i will come back to that as i said, to reach areas further beyond the ones we have managed to reach so far. as i said, staffan de mistura has announced that talks will restart from tomorrow onwards. we do not expect this to be an easy process, on the contrary, but the fact that we managed to somehow recreate, or create rather, the conditions for the talks to be taking place is definitely good. i met riad hijab in paris a few days ago and we discussed at length not the conditions that anyone places on going back to geneva but how the international community, the regional actors and the participants to the talks managed to create the conditions for the talks to be significant and substantial. and let me say that one strong message that we, all of the european union, together with the rest of the international community but here i talk for the european union, are passing on united is to encourage all the parties, starting from the regime obviously but also the opposition, not only to go to geneva and take part in the talks but also to do this in a spirit of engagement and compromise. obviously we are also working as the european union to support the opposition in this very difficult task of entering these difficult negotiations. this is the first time after five years of war that we have this combination of cessation of hostilities holding overall, even if with significant breaches but holding overall, and humanitarian aid being delivered in besieged areas. so this is indeed not creating a rosy picture from one day to the next or from one week to the next, but there are some steps that are finally going in the right direction. one of these is the coordination that i mentioned before that the us and russia have developed, especially on the military-to-military level, a close coordination with regard to first the establishment and then the monitoring of the ceasefire, and the work to defuse tensions that could endanger this very fragile truce. this is why i believe that those who talk about a new cold war definitely need a reality check when it comes to this level of coordination and messaging. now, the role of the european union. the european union is part of both the task forces, with different roles. on the ceasefire, on the cessation of hostilities task force we have a presence, together with other countries or organisations that are part of the international support group. we have our military experts present there and we are also working out ways in which we can contribute to monitoring the cessation of hostilities, together with other friends. on the humanitarian assistance task force our role is definitely a much bigger, relevant one, not because we are the ones who are the good ones and not the ones that get implicated in military things, but simply because in specific terms, the role of the european union in syria has not been – this was a political decision and i think it was right – it has not been and it is not a military player on the ground in syria. some member states are, but nonetheless, the leading role here is for the two main countries that have a military presence and activity, knowledge and control of the military activities that can be done, leading to negotiations on the establishment of cessation of hostilities. this does not mean, as i said, that we are not part also of this very crucial work with our active presence there and that, as i said, might increase in future days. on humanitarian assistance: there is here a very strong link between humanitarian aid and the political process that needs to restart. the last time we met, i remember that many of you mentioned the need for a marshall plan for syria. if we consider the numbers, the money we are putting into this inside syria, in the neighbouring countries and elsewhere, i can say that the marshall plan has already started in a very significant way. the humanitarian task force in which, as i said, we have a leading role has already met four times and, as i said, has succeeded in delivering 180 trucks of aid to seven besieged areas and we reached out to more than 150 000 syrians in cities like madaya, mouadimiya, al-sham, kafr batna, foua, kafraya, zabadani and deir ezzor. this is not an exhaustive list. on the contrary, we are working on further cities all over syria that need to be reached – and could be reached – in terms of priorities in the coming days and weeks. the plan is to deliver assistance to more than 1.7 million syrians inside syria during the first quarter of this year, so in the next couple of months. to provide direct help for the humanitarian deliveries and work hand in hand with the un agencies on the ground we have reactivated our echo office in damascus. among international actors, let me say that the european union is probably the only one that is considered trustworthy by all sides – inside syria and in the region. somehow we have privileged access to many of the interlocutors that then have to work on the steps that are needed to allow humanitarian aid inside the difficult-to-reach areas. our major role on humanitarian aid gives us also a major political role to play and we are doing this. we are helping to create windows of trust between different parties in the conflict. our role is to open wide such windows for meaningful and comprehensive negotiations towards a political transition. we have to keep in mind, even with these positive steps that have taken place in recent weeks, that a new escalation might still happen anytime. the regional situation remains very tense. every day we see news that is extremely worrying – even this morning – and that the proxy war among regional and international powers could still turn into a direct war. this is something we must always keep in mind all through our work, keeping the hope that moves are going forwards on the diplomatic track, on humanitarian assistance and also on the work on the cessation of hostilities and the monitoring of the ceasefire; keeping in mind the risk that this could still degenerate and go backwards if we do not show consistency and if we do not encourage enough the players on the ground – the military groups, the political actors – to engage, the regime first and foremost, to engage in meaningful political process. we have had talks. i have had direct talks in recent days with all our partners, friends, interlocutors – not friends – both inside syria and outside syria in the region, to pass on the same message: to engage in the political process, to allow humanitarian access to improve and to work significantly to have the cessation of hostilities hold and improve day by day. just yesterday, we discussed this with our turkish partners and, if you look at the communiqué that came out of the council yesterday night, you will also find a reference to the need to work together – turkey and the european union – to improve humanitarian conditions in more and more areas inside syria. this is a common commitment we discussed with the turkish yesterday. everyone must do their best at this time. we have opened a window – a very small one – and we have to make sure that it does not close but that it opens further on the three levels – humanitarian, military ceasefire and the political one. let me take this opportunity here to thank staffan de mistura for the excellent coordination work that he is doing. we are in daily contact and the way in which we are working together with the united nations in all these three aspects is really, i think, an example for our work also in other fields. i think we have seen that diplomacy can work in recent experiences last year. we know that daesh can be defeated and that it can be defeated only through a process that puts an end to the war in syria and guarantees a transition in damascus. we know that the war inside syria can be over and forces can merge to fight terrorism – daesh and al-nusra – in the country. we have today the first steps in the right direction which are the result of the very determined – i would say stubborn – work we have done, coordinated with many others, starting with the usa. after five years of war diplomacy, including european diplomacy, is starting to bring some first results that, as i said, could turn back at any single moment if we do not have all the actors pushing in the same direction with the same stubbornness we have shown in recent months. we need to continue to build on this to try to have a new syria. most likely the one that has been destroyed in five years of war will not come back with all its beauties, but maybe we can allow the syrians to build their country again beyond ethnicity, religion or political creed, to be united, democratic, non—sectarian, not governed by the same men who presided over so many years of civil war, but with an inclusive governance guaranteeing all different syrians to be part of the same country, with no space in it for daesh and al-nusra which have nothing to do with the history of the country and will have nothing to do with its future if we manage to work well together as we have done in recent weeks.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, madam high representative, i am pleased to hear you stress that the conflict has already lasted five years. yes, during that long period, the syrians had little reason for hope. when they took to the streets five years ago, it wasn't what they expected. so that's why i think the ceasefire that came into effect on february 27 is a very important element, and it is - again, i agree with you - because it allows access to humanitarian aid that the syrian people desperately need. i remember we talked about this recently when you came before our committee. the ceasefire is also important because it is a beacon of hope which must be held fast in this political perspective. the ceasefire is not perfect, but it exists. it is generally respected, and it is up to us to seize this opportunity to turn it into a credible political transition. "credible political transition" does not mean, of course, "immediate elections" as al-assad or putin have suggested. this is unacceptable. we must concentrate our efforts on the peace process, and only when stability has been fully restored can elections be held.

in writing. the free provision of services and the posting of workers are fundamental principles for the freedom of movement and the european internal market. the last european directive on this subject was in 2014 and its entry into force will take place in a few months. surprisingly, however, the european commission came up with a revision of this directive before it could even analyse the results of the implementation of the previous rules on posting of workers. the reason is allegedly the discovery of shortcomings in cross-border services, worker protection and equal treatment in terms of remuneration provisions (equal pay for equivalent work under equal conditions). first, the commission does not take into account the position of several member states when it comes up with such a proposal. in addition, the commission must be a driver for stimulating the economy and competitiveness in the labour market, not a hindrance. last but not least, the commission must defend the rights of cross-border workers, the development of smes, and stimulate competitiveness and competition in the labour market based on productivity, expertise, innovation and cost-effectiveness. i believe that the commission's proposal is against the fundamental principle of the eu - free movement of labour.
in writing. the european commission proposes to amend framework directive 96/71/ec on the posting of workers by a company from one member state to carry out work in another member state. i believe that some of the proposed amendments to this directive will have a negative impact on labour mobility. the current directive thus clearly provides that a posted worker must be paid at least the minimum wage in the country where he is posted. it is a clear prediction, without any doubt of interpretation. another criterion, which is unclear and liable to be interpreted differently and therefore abused in its application, is proposed: the provision of 'the remuneration necessary for the protection of posted workers'. in addition to the fact that such a criterion is unclear, it also does not take into account the competitiveness of the companies that post workers. i am confident that in the european parliament we will be able to persuade the commission to abandon such amendments.
in writing. the freedom to provide services, a fundamental freedom of the european union's single market, gives businesses the right to provide services in another member state, where they can temporarily post their own workers to provide those services. in this regard, directive 96/71/ec sets out a number of conditions to ensure a minimum level of protection for posted workers, which has, for example, enabled the posting of around 1,9 million european workers to other member states in 2014. however, there is a proposal for a revision of this directive by the commission which is likely to constitute an obstacle to the freedom to provide services and labour mobility. the proposal provides that posted workers will benefit from the same rules governing working conditions and pay as local workers. in addition to the fact that these new provisions may constitute a breach of the principle of subsidiarity, moreover, they will most likely lead to a decrease in the number of romanian enterprises operating in the territory of other member states. this proposal could thus have negative effects on the competitiveness of the companies concerned, leading to a decrease in the number of service contracts and job losses.

in writing. ‒ this directive sets maximum sulphur permitted content of heavy fuel oil, diesel oil, marine fuel and marine diesel fuel used in the union. emissions from shipping from the combustion of marine fuels with high sulphur content contribute to air pollution with sulphur dioxide and particulate matter, which are harmful to human health and the environment and contribute to acid deposition. in the absence of the measures laid down in this directive, emissions from maritime transport would soon have been higher than emissions from all land-based sources. in order to facilitate the transition to new engine technologies with the potential to deliver further significant emission reductions in the maritime sector, the commission should also explore other possibilities to allow and encourage the use of gas-fuelled engines on board ships. in accordance with the existing guidelines on state aid for environmental protection, member states may grant state aid to operators affected by this directive, including aid for the modernisation of existing vessels, provided that such aid is considered compatible with the internal market.

in writing. ‒ this regulation aims to prevent the possibility of differentiated priced products being imported into the union. derogations are provided for in certain situations, provided that it is strictly ensured that the final destination of the products concerned is one of the countries listed in annex ii to this regulation. many of the poorest developing countries urgently need access to affordable essential medicines for the treatment of communicable diseases. those countries are heavily dependent on imports of medicines, as their local production is low. it is therefore necessary to set different prices in the markets of developed countries and in the markets of the poorest developing countries in order to ensure that the latter are supplied with essential pharmaceutical products at much reduced prices. therefore, these much reduced prices cannot be considered as a benchmark for the price to be paid for the same products on the markets of developed countries.

in writing. ‒ the european union and andorra signed an agreement on 12 february 2016 on the automatic exchange of financial account information with a view to enhancing tax cooperation and compliance at international level. the agreement will enter into force provisionally on 1 january 2017. the agreement is an important step in the ongoing efforts to combat tax fraud and evasion. under the new agreement, eu member states and andorra will automatically exchange information on financial accounts held in their territories by their respective residents. the purpose of this approach is to address situations where the taxpayer attempts to conceal capital representing income or assets for which no tax has been paid. the agreement also aims to ensure that andorra applies enhanced measures equivalent to those provided for in the eu legal framework and complies with the automatic exchange of financial account information. as a result of the new agreement, the tax authorities of the member states and andorra will be able to: correctly and unequivocally identify the taxpayers concerned; administer and enforce national tax laws in cross-border situations; assess the likelihood of tax evasion; and avoid unnecessary additional enquiries.
in writing. the european union has recently embarked on a broad process of combating tax evasion and tax fraud. to this end, the eu has concluded a number of agreements with third countries on cooperation in the exchange of information on bank accounts. the commission has also concluded that the measure is compatible with the internal market within the meaning of article 107 (3) (c) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the exchange of information will be extended, as of 2017, to accounts of residents of both parties, in order to avoid the concealment of capital for which the appropriate taxes have not been paid by taxpayers. the application of these measures by andorra will be equivalent to the application of european legislation in this field, in line with the global oecd standards. in these circumstances, i support the adoption of the present document as an important step in solving this problem.

mr president, i did not support this report for the following reason. i agree with the basic idea of a uniform procedural protection for children, but i do not agree with the way the directive is actually written. and that's for two basic reasons. firstly, the scope of the rights thus unified is too broad, for example the right to privacy is being unified, and i believe that this should remain the responsibility of the individual national states. for example, in the czech republic right now, there's a debate about whether or not the perpetrators of serious crime, children, should be anonymous. and the second reason is that i think it is too much protection for the european parliament to extend the category of children to the age of 21. it seems to me that this is too much protection and that we should stick to the original proposal that the commission was preparing, which was the age of 18.
mr president, the commission estimates that over one million children are subject to criminal proceedings each year. this is equivalent to 12% of all persons involved in criminal proceedings. that's a very large number! children's rights are not sufficiently guaranteed in reality, in practice, in the various criminal proceedings in many member states. the ecthr already has numerous judgments on specific situations in which children's rights have not been respected in the course of criminal proceedings by various authorities in the member states. that is why it is very important to have some minimum standards for respecting the procedural rights of children so that they can enjoy a fair trial: for example, legal aid, the right to a lawyer, the right to an interpreter if needed and so on. i voted for this report precisely because we need to guarantee a fair trial and common minimum standards for persons under the age of eighteen who are, for various reasons, accused or victims and therefore involved in criminal proceedings.
in writing. ‒ the right to a fair trial can only be ensured by establishing common minimum standards and by its effective and sufficiently homogeneous exercise at all stages of the procedure. moreover, in the case of persons under the age of eighteen, that right is linked to the objective of facilitating the mutual recognition of judgments and judicial decisions in criminal matters and ensuring the fair functioning of the european area of justice. i appreciate that the proposal aims at defining a limited but properly structured set of rights for children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings (or who are subject to a european arrest warrant procedure), through a set of minimum standards, interconnected and calibrated to the specific needs of children throughout the procedure. in conclusion, i support the eu agenda on the rights of the child and the effective implementation of justice in the best interests of the child by voting in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ every year, more than one million children in the member states of the european union are in situations of illegality. lack of education and the ease with which minors can be influenced to commit wrongdoing are just two of the reasons why legal systems need to be adapted to their particularities. whatever the offence or the reason for suspecting the minor, he or she must be treated in accordance with his or her intellectual capacity and understanding. it is also important that an assessment be made from the very beginning of the proceedings, taking into account the degree of maturity and the family, social and economic environment in which the minor has developed. particular attention should be paid to minors from vulnerable groups such as street children, minorities, immigrants or persons with disabilities. i believe that the european union and the member states must ensure procedural guarantees for children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings, respecting both their particularities and their dignified and non-discriminatory treatment.
in writing. ‒ i strongly support this report, which strengthens the initial commission proposal, as children are a specific category of vulnerable persons and strong minimum standards at eu level will help to properly protect child suspects safe in criminal proceedings across the union. i welcome the important gains obtained by my colleagues during the negotiations with the council, such as the provisions on assistance by a lawyer, the individual assessment and the medical examination. moreover, i welcome the fact that the text counteracts negative provisions introduced by the council in relation to audio-visual recording of interviews, the use of detention as a measure of last resort, the right to privacy, and possible costs implications. consistency with the previous adopted measures of the roadmap should be maintained; member states must fully respect fundamental rights and prevent violations giving rise to european court rulings.
in writing. ‒ i salute the proposal for a legislative report regarding a directive on procedural safeguards for children suspected or accused in criminal proceedings. this report strengthens the initial proposal – in particular with regard to provisions on assistance by a lawyer, individual assessment mechanisms and the medical examination.
in writing. ‒ this proposal for a directive is established in order to strengthen procedural rights of suspected or accused persons in criminal proceedings. i have voted for this report that has as its main provisions: the rules on questioning; the right to an individual assessment; the mandatory right to be assisted by a lawyer, in close connection with the right to free legal aid; the provision for the child to take part in the proceedings; compulsory special training for judges, law enforcement authorities and prison staff, lawyers and others who come into contact with children in their work; the provisions on detention, under which children should be held on remand only where there is no alternative, and in such cases, it must be ensured that the children are held separately from adults, except where it is in their best interests not to do so.
in writing. ‒ as there is at present no definition in the eu of what constitutes a ‘fair trial’ for children suspected or accused in criminal proceedings, this proposal is very timely. the continuous involvement of the european court of human rights in challenging member state court rulings against children, as well as the fact that only in some member states do children have the right to be assisted by a lawyer, testifies to the need for a more coherent and streamlined catalogue of rights to protect children throughout the eu. it is with this in mind that i voted in favour of this proposal.
in writing. the administration of justice within the eu member states has remained, for the most part, a strictly national responsibility. however, at a general level, the european institutions can issue recommendations and even directives on the procedures applied by the member states. one such area, which is quite sensitive, is procedural safeguards for children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings. children are, by their very position in society, the most vulnerable to criminal offences, and they generally lack the discernment to avoid certain criminal behaviour. in these circumstances, juvenile delinquency cases should benefit from special legal assistance from the office, alongside the medical and individual assistance that is required. the use of audio-visual recordings of hearings should also be limited as far as possible, alongside the right to privacy. another very important element is the use of custodial measures for juvenile offenders, which should be the last resort and only in extremely serious cases, involving mainly adolescents. this document is a first step towards regulating this rather complex area, but it is a necessary measure. therefore, i consider his adoption to be auspicious.
in writing. ‒ in the context of the refugee crisis, solidarity between member states is a highly debated topic at eu level. i believe that, as regards the aid granted by each state, account should be taken of the possibilities of each state to be able to contribute to the resolution of this crisis. one of the amendments to this report, amendment no 22, speaks of this solidarity shown by the member states. it states that it is unevenly distributed across the member states and asks the commission to come forward with a proposal on how the eu budget can encourage member states to take a more balanced approach in this respect. in other words, the european commission should sanction states that some people think have not shown solidarity in the refugee crisis. given that this amendment was voted on and therefore adopted, i cannot vote in favour of the report on the general guidelines for the preparation of the 2017 budget, section iii, because complying with amendment 22 would clearly be in breach of the treaty on the functioning of the european union.
in writing. ‒ the european union and its member states are facing various internal and external crises, which can have an impact at budgetary level. first, at the external level, the eu is facing emerging security threats (terrorism, extremism) as well as a migrant and refugee crisis. these external crises have a strong impact on internal crises. but the eu must remain an area of freedom, security and justice and strengthen crossborder operational cooperation to ensure decent conditions in line with human rights. at home, the european union and the member states must continue to promote the social values that underpin the union by bringing people closer together. to this end, the general budgetary guidelines should take into account: reducing unemployment, especially among young people; combating poverty, socioeconomic inequality, exploitation and social exclusion. these can be improved by promoting the convergence, integration and cohesion policies set out in the europe 2020 strategy.
in writing. ‒ i welcome this report, which sets the guidelines and the main political priorities for the european parliament for the 2017 eu budget, and provides a comprehensive overview of the current budgetary situation. i welcome the fact that flexibility regarding contributions to the eu budget from the member states under the stability and growth pact (sgp) has been included. however, i regret the fact that the idea of solidarity as an underlying principle of the eu budget, an idea that should also be respected in dealing with the refugee crisis, has not been included. finally, i believe we must be ready to mobilise all means available to address the current social and economic crises.
in writing. ‒ this report is about the main priorities for the european parliament for the eu budget 2017, and gives an overview of the current budgetary situation. this includes among others: refugee and migration crisis, efsi, economic growth, youth employment initiative, child guarantee (poverty), climate change, payment crisis, refugee facility for turkey. the european parliament is ready to mobilise all means available to address the existing crisis in europe.
in writing. ‒ the current geopolitical situation that europe faces will affect the 2017 budget through the evolving migration and refugee crisis and by the economical dependency on global developments of the eu. i have voted for this report that should lay down the road towards economic growth and job creation, in the current context of a fragile economic recovery that is jeopardised by the situation in emerging global markets and ongoing geopolitical tensions.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the establishment of the 2017 budget is a very important issue and must take into account the continuation of eu growth and job creation, in the context of a fragile economic recovery, jeopardised by the current geopolitical situation and tensions. in this respect, as the report proposes, i believe that the preparation of the budget must take into account the stimulation of public and private investment, but also the increase in the use of the structural funds in order to achieve the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. these policies must be the main tools for ensuring stable economic growth and strengthening cohesion within the eu, which is why i am glad that the european parliament has expressed its consensus on this issue.
in writing. the budget of the european union is the main instrument through which european structures can ensure the smooth running of the european project in practice. the general budgetary guidelines for 2017 indicate the main priorities of the union for the period ahead. these include the refugee and migration crisis, the european fund for strategic investments, economic growth, the youth employment initiative, the child guarantee (against poverty), climate change, late payments, the facility for refugees in turkey, etc. there are still a number of problems with the flexibility of member states' contributions to the eu budget and the respect of the principle of solidarity. unfortunately, solidarity between member states is being tested by the problems of the moment and has not been included in the current document. overall, however, the document reflects the main areas of union interest where consistent action is needed. the adoption of this document will allow a better response to the crises currently facing the eu, although greater commitment by member states is also needed to overcome the existing problems.
mr president, we have a rich, perhaps too rich, sometimes unclear legislation in the european union, because each or many of our colleagues comes with a personal agenda, and so our legislation is full of gift, and, or, moreover, especially, particularly, and that makes it like a christmas tree. that is why many european citizens do not understand what we mean by 'everything' and sometimes we run out of content. that is why i am very much in favour of this report. the laws must be simple, clear, precise, short. short, i insist we are here to legislate for european citizens and not to promote on the agenda each one a subject that we want to find in every law we pass. the commission, parliament and council must consult each other and also consult the citizens for whom we work. transparency and public consultation!
in writing. ‒ in order to ensure a well-informed, inclusive and transparent decision-making process and the correct application of legislation, with provisions protecting the prerogatives of legislators, interinstitutional negotiations were formally opened between the three main institutions of the union on 25 june 2015. during these meetings, a number of priorities were set, in particular as regards the quality of the drafting of the commission's legislative texts, multiannual and annual programming, strengthening the impact assessment of draft laws, equal treatment of the two arms of the legislative authority throughout the legislative process on access to information, appropriate interinstitutional consultations, the commission's response to parliament's proposals and recommendations and the provision of detailed justifications for each withdrawal envisaged. the three institutions consider that public and stakeholder consultation, ex-post evaluations of existing legislation and impact assessments of new initiatives will contribute to the achievement of the objective of better regulation. given that this agreement reflects the competences of the european parliament, the council and the commission, and the balance between these institutions, as provided for in the treaties, i voted in favour of this draft.
in writing. ‒ given the complexity of the european union's legislative process and the crisis of confidence we are currently facing, it is necessary to promote simplicity, clarity, coherence and transparency in the drafting of legislation, while maintaining the importance of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. in addition, for better law-making, it is appropriate that the three institutions take into account the impact of their legislative and non-legislative initiatives, public and stakeholder consultation through feedback tools, as well as ex-post evaluation of the legislation in force.

in writing. ‒ i stress the importance of the provisions in the new interinstitutional agreement on better law-making tools (impact assessments, consultation of the public and stakeholders, evaluations, etc.) for a well-informed, inclusive and transparent decision-making process and for the correct application of the law. i believe that impact assessments need to be comprehensive and balanced and should assess, inter alia, the costs borne by producers, consumers, workers and administrators and the environmental costs that are generated by the failure to adopt the necessary legislation. the impact assessment on smes should be included in the impact assessment reports and we ask the commission to provide further information on this practice. the three eu institutions agreed to cooperate on updating and simplifying legislation and to exchange views on this before the completion of the commission's work programme. the burden-reduction targets in specific sectors need to be carefully assessed on a case-by-case basis, in close cooperation between the institutions, with a focus on the quality of legislation and without undermining relevant union standards. this agreement will allow for better implementation of eu legislation, respecting agreements with the social partners and ensuring greater transparency.

in writing. codification of european legislation requires good cooperation between the main community institutions, the parliament, the council and the commission. even when disagreements arise between the three actors, there are mechanisms for dialogue to reach a mutually acceptable solution that takes into account the interests of the member states and of european citizens. the interinstitutional agreement provides the framework for the conduct of this dialogue within the appropriate parameters. the old agreement, adopted in 2003, was updated in december 2015 without major changes. however, additional protection of agreements with the social partners is required, as well as a change in impact studies to include the social, economic and environmental dimensions, alongside the regulation of areas that are not currently included in the european legislative pillar. in this respect, the european parliament must have a stronger say in the field of annual and multiannual programming and the council's legislative procedures must become more transparent. member states may apply directives in a manner as close as possible to existing national legislation, but the application of directives must be monitored by the commission. the current agreement is an important step forward and deserves to be supported.

the next item is the joint debate on– the report by françoise grossetête, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on veterinary medical products (com(2014)0558 – c8-0164/2014 – 2014/0257(cod)) (a8—0046/2016), and – the report by claudiu ciprian tănăsescu, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on authorisation and supervision of veterinary medicinal products (com(2014)0557 – c8-0142/2014 – 2014/0256(cod)) (a8-0035/2016).
the reporter. madam president, i would like to begin by saying that i welcome the commission's proposal to separate marketing authorisations for veterinary medicinal products from those for human medicinal products in order to take account of the specific needs of the veterinary sector. in addition to the new regulation on veterinary medicinal products, to which ms grossetête has just referred, the commission also had to amend regulation no 726/2004. however, as my report shows, there were a number of elements in the proposal that needed improvement. firstly, for the sake of clarity, since all the articles relating to the authorisation procedure for veterinary medicinal products are now moved to a new regulation, i have clarified in the text that the european medicines agency remains responsible, under the centralised authorisation procedure, for both human and veterinary medicinal products. the report shall also ensure that the revised regulation is in line with the new financial regulation. we now have a clear and updated picture of the principles applicable to the agency's budget, including a separation between the different sources of revenue that make up the budget of the european medicines agency. as a result of the broad support received within the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, parliament should be fully involved in the process of setting the agency's fees through the ordinary legislative procedure, as was recently done for the legislation on fees for pharmacovigilance. finally, the text voted in the envi committee recognises the role of the european medicines agency in increasing access to medicines. the report also contains a reference to the agency's cooperation with htabs, as currently in place, to further facilitate cooperation and the exchange of scientific information. ema should also be able to provide member states with a comparative assessment of medicinal products for human use. such an assessment could subsequently be used by member states, on a voluntary basis, during the national decision-making process on setting prices and reimbursement conditions, activities which, of course, remain within national competence. now, as the alternative rapporteur on the grossetête report, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and her colleagues on their good cooperation. we now have a very well-structured report which allows for considerable improvements in the field of veterinary medicinal products. the proposed measures include limiting and controlling the use of antibiotics in animal treatment, but also creating a favourable environment for investment in research and development of new medicines and more. the aim is to increase access to veterinary medicines and to make a much wider therapeutic arsenal available to veterinarians. in this respect, the requirements for medicinal products for narrow markets are also simplified. in addition, the movement of veterinary medicinal products between member states is facilitated by improved authorisation procedures and clear rules on modern retail forms. in this respect, we have reached an agreement allowing the retail sale of veterinary medicinal products on the internet, with the exception of antimicrobials, psychotropic products and biological immunological products. in a similar way to what happens for medicinal products for human use, the commission is invited to adopt guidelines to support member states in developing a harmonised system of digital prescriptions in the european union. it is regrettable that a large proportion of the antibiotics sold in the european union are given to animals. it's our duty to protect the effectiveness of antibiotics in health care facilities, but also on farms. this report provides clear measures for the correct and appropriate use of antibiotics on the farm and the prohibition of the routine preventive use of antimicrobials. this is complemented by stricter standards for the use of antimicrobial metaphylaxis. in order to combat antimicrobial resistance, everyone should be involved, including national authorities, patients, doctors, but also veterinarians, farmers and consumers.
member of the commission.– madam president, you have heard my explanation setting out the commission’s intentions and opinion on this proposed new regulation on veterinary medicines and i have listened to the views of this house with great interest. it is important to reach an agreement on these new rules in order to increase the availability of veterinary medicines and, even more urgently, to address the risks to public health arising from the use of antimicrobials in veterinary medicine. the commission welcomes further provisions addressing amr and considers most of them positive. i also welcome the amendment introducing precise conditions on prophylactics and methaphylactic use of antimicrobials, inter alia prophylactic use restricted to single animals and only when fully justified by a veterinarian, and methaphylactic use restricted to clinically ill animals and to single animals that are identified as being at high risk of contamination. i am sure that we will have very interesting discussions on this issue during the trilogue and you will be able to access those in detail. some members have mentioned very important issues relating to innovations. use of new innovative treatments is very important to all of us. innovations, access to veterinary medicines, the fight against amr and the protection of public health are not in contradiction. on the contrary, innovation is a main tool to guarantee public health. i am sure that we must also debate in detail many other issues;
