mr president, commissioner, the zika virus is an international health emergency, as the question to the commission also states. commissioner, you have presented the commission's view today, recognising the urgency of this matter. i am surprised because in most cases the commission's reaction is late. prevention and public information are known to save lives. the population must be well informed and timely, and the measures presented must be taken in a timely manner. i have a question for you: i don't know how you came to the figure of 10 million euros. why ten and eight or twenty? do you have a study that comes up with that amount? are there solutions to counteract the virus? what should the population do to protect themselves? i believe that the european institutions must be much more focused on health protection measures and do much more in common policies with the member states for information and prevention.
in writing. zika virus is known to be transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected aedes mosquito, especially aedes aegypti, which is found in tropical areas. the rapid geographical spread of this virus, particularly in south america, requires eu support measures for the health authorities in affected countries to implement control area strategies aimed at reducing aedes mosquito populations. at this point, the eu needs to invest in prevention measures, which translate into scientific research for the creation of vaccines. i am pleased to hear that this is the direction the commission is taking and i hope that it will keep parliament regularly informed of the state of play of its research. i am pleased to hear that the commission's approach to zika is based on measures against serious cross-border threats to health and that it will work with member states to this end. we need close cooperation because, in the context of summer in europe, the health of citizens may be threatened by the activation of the zika virus in mosquito populations on our continent. the objectives to be pursued are clear: prevention and treatment of the epidemic, and cooperation between member states will be the basis for these actions.
mr president, commissioner, the major problem we are facing in the banking union is the transfer of authority to the single supervisory mechanism. we have all seen what it means when, in tense situations, you cannot make decisions on internal matters and have to wait for a centralised decision from brussels. i would point out that each member state has a different banking market according to the standard of living and the behaviour of consumers. i consider it a priority at this stage of the report to clearly identify those instruments which will remain at the disposal of the member states in order to ensure independence and security in the event of crisis situations. the second problem is the economic disparity between member states. the banking union will not be possible as long as the european commission has not achieved its objectives of standardising living standards, and in the event of future crises, i believe it is necessary that the banking security of the member states be ensured exclusively and independently by the national banks, because they have historical experience, adapted to the internal problems of the respective countries.

in writing. ‒ following the terrorist attacks last year, the tunisian economy has been hit hard and the european union has reaffirmed its support, taking concrete action to support tunisia's economic development. the union will thus provide tunisia with a duty-free tariff quota available for a period of two years, until 31 december 2017, of 70 000 tonnes in total, for exports of olive oil from tunisia to the union, on a temporary basis, in the form of an autonomous trade measure, without increasing the overall volume of imports. the measure will bring important benefits to the olive oil sector, which indirectly employs over one million people in tunisia and represents one fifth of all agricultural jobs. by engaging concretely with the tunisians in supporting their economic development, the eu is also contributing to the promotion of democracy in tunisia.
in writing. ‒ i have voted according to the commission’s proposal to parliament and the council. the tunisian economy has been devastated following the terrorist attacks of 2015. it is crucial for the eu to support tunisia through exceptional measures in order to boost its economy, and i fully support the quotas set by the commission.
in writing. ‒ i support the adoption of emergency trade measures for tunisia. following last year’s terrorist attacks the tunisian economy is facing serious difficulties and is in dire need of further assistance. i welcome the council’s decision to agree with the additional safeguards introduced by the ep in its plenary vote of 25 february 2016 such as the mid-term impact assessment. in this way a trilogue will be avoided and the measures will enter into force quickly.
in writing. ‒ the tunisian economy, already facing serious difficulties, suffered after the terrorist attacks of 18 march and 26 june 2015. i have voted for this report that has as its aim the temporary offering of a zero-duty tariff for exports of olive oil from tunisia to the eu.
in writing. ‒ the terrorist attacks in tunisia and the resulting instability have prompted the eu's response to the need to continue to support tunisia in a concrete and specific way in its political and economic transition. the emergency trade measures are intended to improve the difficult economic situation facing tunisia following the terrorist attacks. it is important that those measures apply for a limited period of time and are without prejudice to the negotiations between the union and tunisia on the establishment of a deep and comprehensive free trade area. the european commission proposes to grant tunisia, unilaterally and temporarily, a tariff quota of 35 000 tonnes per year, from 1 january 2016 to 31 december 2017, for the duty-free export of olive oil from tunisia to the union. olive oil is the main agricultural product exported by tunisia. this quota will enter into force as soon as the current zero duty tariff quota of 56 700 tonnes provided for in the eu-tunisia association agreement is exhausted. i support the eu's engagement in supporting tunisia's economic development, which also contributes to the promotion of democracy in this country.
in writing. ‒ the livestock sector accounts for 41% of total investment in agriculture, with a total of over 12 million animals worth eur 142 billion. harmonisation of the conditions for veterinary prescriptions, their recognition at member state level and the authorisation of other qualified persons to issue certain prescriptions contribute significantly to reducing red tape and to the rational use of veterinary medicinal products. in addition, taking into account technological developments, the use of electronic prescriptions facilitates the work of farmers. we take into account that antimicrobial resistance is a major risk factor for animal health and welfare and its effects are directly felt in human health. the prohibition of the use of antibiotics in prophylactic treatments contributes significantly to reducing the volume of medicines administered to animals. i believe that prevention is often more effective and less costly, and that the amount of drugs used in preventive treatment is much lower than in metaphylactic treatment. the proposal for a regulation on veterinary medicinal products must be adapted to the realities on the ground, must aim to reduce administrative burdens, take account of the needs of farmers and respond to the requirements of consumers. i believe that the vote in the envi committee was the necessary guarantee for this report to enter into the interinstitutional negotiations.
in writing. ‒ the impact of veterinary medicines on both animal and human health is of great concern. the use of medicines is closely linked to antimicrobial resistance developed in animals and, through the consumption of dairy products or meat originating from those animals, resistance is also transferred to humans. the main cause is the prophylactic administration of antimicrobial medicines to animals, sometimes used to improve performance or compensate for poor development. the report aims to limit the prophylactic use of antibiotics to situations justified by the presence of clear clinical symptoms. combating antimicrobial resistance is a priority for the eu as it aims to improve patient safety, and ms grossetête's report underlines the role of the union in creating a single action plan to tackle antimicrobial resistance. on the other hand, this report aims to create a framework to stimulate and support innovation in veterinary medicines, so as not to reduce the therapeutic arsenal of veterinarians. the industry needs encouragement to create new medicines and to bring them to the market for veterinary medicines, as it is relatively small and fragmented.
in writing. ‒ this regulation aims to regulate the authorisation, manufacture, marketing, distribution and use of veterinary medicinal products throughout their life cycle, as well as the related pharmacovigilance process. this legislation is more ambitious in terms of provisions to combat antibiotic resistance, in particular it clearly defines the different forms of treatment (curative treatment, control treatment and preventive treatment) and prohibits the prophylactic use of antibacterial medicines. close consistency between the medicated feed regulation and the veterinary medicinal products regulation is therefore essential. the establishment of a list of important antibiotics reserved for human medicine that the commission wishes to achieve should only be done on the condition that it is based on sound scientific criteria. the sale of antibiotics (and, more generally, the sale of veterinary medicinal products requiring a prescription) on the internet should also be prohibited as it poses a serious risk to public health.
in writing. ‒ i would like to endorse the proposal and to welcome the alignment with the lisbon treaty. i support the decoupling of marketing authorisations for veterinary medicinal products from those for human medicinal products, to take account of the specific needs of the veterinary sector. it is important to harmonise the requirements for a veterinary prescription and recognition of prescriptions across member states; to stimulate innovation and the development of new veterinary medicines; and to harmonise the periods of protection (and potential prolongation) of new data packages related to antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products. i believe the regulation will provide better access to veterinary medicines, take measures to fight antimicrobial resistance, reduce the administrative burden, and promote innovation and competitiveness within the sector. finally i support action to reduce the use of antibiotics, which may not be sold via the internet.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report since there must be a regulation that sets more efficient and effective access to veterinary medicines. moreover, such a regulation will also promote competitiveness within the sector, while reducing the administrative burden.
in writing. ‒ the commission published its new draft regulation on veterinary medicinal products in september 2014. i have voted for this report that will improve the existing rules on medicinal products for veterinary use set out in directive 2001/82/ec and regulation ec 726/2004.
in writing. ‒ i welcome this report. the measures contained in it, especially those concerning prophylactic and metaphylactic use of antibiotics and restrictions on internet sales, should help in the struggle against antimicrobial resistance. at the same time, the distribution of essential veterinary medicines throughout the eu should be increased and the administrative burden reduced.
in writing. ‒ antimicrobial resistance in both humans and animals is a growing health problem in the european union and worldwide. it is essential for both humans and animals to have a clear picture of how antimicrobials are used in order to be able to significantly reduce their use and put an end to all abuses. the responsible use of antimicrobials in the treatment of diseases of bacterial origin contributes to the control of diseases affecting the livestock sector. their abusive and excessive use in animal farms stimulates resistance, which can spread to humans in a number of ways, including through food. diseases can be prevented by implementing good practices in biosecurity, nutrition, hygiene and animal comfort. under no circumstances should an antibacterial medicinal product be allowed to be prescribed without a clear diagnosis of disease. it is necessary to ensure that the package leaflet of antimicrobials for veterinary use contains appropriate warnings and instructions, in particular clear definitions of the different forms of treatment (curative treatment, control treatment and preventive treatment), and to prohibit the prophylactic use of antibacterial medicinal products.
in writing. ‒ the report on the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use aims at separating the marketing authorisations for medicinal products for human use from those for veterinary medicinal products, precisely to take account of the specific needs of the veterinary and human sectors. the initiative proposes that the new measures be targeted at the veterinary and human sectors and that the related fees be accessible to the veterinary industry, with the aim of promoting the development and availability of new types of medicines at european union level. i voted in favour of the report because i believe that the needs of the veterinary sector differ significantly from those of the human sector, which is why these two areas should be treated separately, depending on the specificities of the sectors. the market for veterinary medicinal products is fragmented, given the multitude of animal species; therefore, veterinary medicinal products need to be addressed separately from those for human use.
in writing. ‒ this proposal to amend regulation no 726/2004 is closely linked to the report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on veterinary medicinal products. the commission's evaluation studies in 2014 identified the need to bring together all the rules on veterinary medicinal products in a single regulation in order to meet the specific needs of this sector. the market and needs of the veterinary sector are fundamentally different from those of the human sector, as we are dealing in the first case with a multitude of animal species, which results in a fragmented market. it is important to underline the role of the european medicines agency (ema) in the authorisation and supervision of veterinary products through the centralised procedure, as its tasks should apply to both medicinal products for human use and veterinary medicinal products. the objectives of the two regulations adopted should therefore be interlinked so that the end result leads to the stimulation of competitiveness and innovation while aiming at reducing red tape and ultimately aiming at the availability of new veterinary medicinal products that combat the public health risks posed by antimicrobial resistance.
in writing. ‒ the veterinary medicines directive and the regulation laying down community procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use and establishing a european medicines agency constitute the european union's regulatory framework for the manufacture, authorisation and distribution of veterinary medicinal products. it is important to provide for the application of the quality, safety and efficacy criteria laid down in european legislation to medicinal products authorised by the union and for the possibility to assess the benefit-risk balance of all medicinal products when they are placed on the market at the time of renewal of the authorisation and at any other time the competent authority considers appropriate. the european medicines agency should also have access to other sources of funding to support its work on public health projects, such as the innovative medicines initiative.
in writing. ‒ this proposal accompanies the new regulation on veterinary medicine products that will repeal and replace directive 2001/82 /ec, and amend regulation (ec) no 726/2004 laying down community procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use and establishing a european medicines agency. it must be amended to take account of the fact that centralised marketing authorisation for human and veterinary products is being decoupled so that the new regulation on veterinary medicinal products (com(2014)0558) will cover all routes granting marketing authorisations for veterinary medicinal products in the union – both at centralised and national level. in addition, it seeks to align provisions to the lisbon treaty and to introduce implementing acts to set the fee provisions – previously set by co-decision. i voted in favour of the report, especially since i believe the european parliament must be involved as co-legislator in setting the structure and level of fees payable by the industry to the european medicines agency.
in writing. ‒ this regulation sets procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use. the european medicines agency (ema) is a long-needed institution. it is paramount that the european parliament, as co-legislator, takes part in establishing a structure and level of fees payable by the industry to the ema.
in writing. ‒ following an assessment of the functioning of the internal market in this sector, the commission published a proposal to bring together the rules on veterinary medicines under one regulation on veterinary medicinal products in september 2014. i voted for this report that will, among other things, align the regulation to the lisbon treaty.
in writing. ‒ the proposal from the commission intends to align the legislation with the lisbon treaty, which provides for improved democratic oversight and transparency through the increased role of the european parliament in the legislative process. i welcome this report, and especially the emphasis it places on parliamentary scrutiny of the structure and level of fees payable to the european medicines agency.

in writing. ‒ the data-driven economy has a number of benefits both economically and socially. the successful, data-driven economy can generate growth and boost employment through various economic incentives. the data economy is seen as a success story in the context of the high-volume data market's growth rate, which by 2017 will be six times faster than the global ict market, reaching a total global value of eur 50 billion. it is also seeing unprecedented growth, with 16 trillion gigabytes of data by 2020, indicating a 236% annual increase in data generation. at the same time, the benefits of a data-driven economy will drive an additional gdp growth of 1,9% by 2020. i voted in favour of this resolution because i believe that the data economy has the potential to boost competitiveness at union level and to accelerate europe's economic recovery, as well as to drive increased investment and innovation in various key sectors.
in writing. ‒ the development of big data is an integral part of a new digital market and should ensure the development of innovative and competitive business models, respecting the eu data protection framework. however, large volumes of data can entail significant risks and challenges, in particular for fundamental rights (including privacy and data protection). a strong service provider base is needed to promote the benefits and assets of the integrated use of data for the economy and society and to promote trust in big data technologies among smes. the widespread application of big data services needs to be supported in order to improve efficiency in different economic sectors and to support new service providers. it is also important to create a one-stop shop to help smes make better use of their own and public data, while adhering to eu data protection legislation.
in writing. ‒ i strongly support the data—driven economy, which will stimulate research and innovation on data while leading to more business opportunities and an increased availability of knowledge and capital, in particular for smes, across europe. the development of the digital world, beyond connectivity, needs common standards, interoperability, accessible platforms, high-speed networks and high—performance computing infrastructure. i therefore support the call on the commission to clarify its plan on how to support the development of broadband infrastructure, cloud computing, innovations in standards and a stable legal framework. i believe the commission must ensure that the framework for a data-driven economy is legally sound, respecting data protection standards, yet flexible enough to adapt to the changing environment of digital markets. finally, i would like to understand how the commission will encourage and support the member states in implementing training initiatives related to data handling and the development of the necessary skills.
in writing. i voted for the resolution 'towards a successful data-driven economy' because it is necessary to create, as soon as possible, a legislative framework for the digital single market, which will have a decisive impact on the future of smes. in the technology and innovation economy, smes will use big data to compete as global leaders in a data-driven economy. the eu urgently needs to prepare legislation on the value of data and how to use it to develop new investment models and to encourage economic growth. the european commission must accelerate the process of stimulating the emergence of new business and service models that can create many jobs in the coming years. in order to achieve this, the commission and the member states should implement the necessary regulations to guarantee increased investment in network infrastructure. without a strong network infrastructure that guarantees adequate data capacity and speeds, the digital economy will not be able to take off.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this motion for a resolution, which expects the benefits of a data-driven economy at national and european level to have an impact on society and on all types of enterprise in the value chain. at the core of the digital single market strategy is the creation of a data-driven economy.
in writing. ‒ the creation of a data-driven economy is at the heart of the digital single market strategy and has the potential to help europe regain competitiveness in advanced sectors and accelerate europe's economic recovery. the commission and the european data industry have committed to investing €2.5 billion in a ppp to strengthen the data sector and put europe at the forefront of the global data race by maximising the potential of the digital economy. access to open data portals and electronic research infrastructures is a possible way to reduce the disadvantages that researchers and smes in peripheral regions may face. we call on the commission to adopt policies that remove excessive barriers in innovative sectors and stimulate investment in research and development and european standardisation. we also call for the creation of a future-proof regulatory environment that reflects the changing nature of the market, is technology-neutral, stimulates the creation of new businesses and the entry of new operators, ensures a level playing field and fair competition, while avoiding the burden of excessive regulation and ensuring full compliance with data protection and privacy rules. we welcome the commission's intention to review the eprivacy directive.
in writing. ‒ the unprecedented development of new information technologies has led to a real revolution in the way we conceive of human society today. new devices have become part of our lives, as indispensable tools through which we communicate, work and spend our leisure time. at the same time, however, these technologies can also make a key contribution to the development of the economies of our countries and the european union as a whole. they can stimulate research and innovation, create new business opportunities, increase the availability of knowledge and capital, help in particular the development of smes and bring about the so-called 'data-driven economy of success'. the european commission created a new strategy on it databases in july 2014 to accelerate the transition to the information economy on the european continent. the resolution proposed by the european parliament on this issue highlights the persistent shortcomings in common standards, interoperability, high-speed networks, it infrastructure and consumer and data protection. this requires investment in broadband infrastructure, consumer protection, development of opportunities for smes, and effective innovation. the current resolution is a laudable initiative and deserves to be supported.
in writing. ‒ the situation in eritrea is characterised by serious violations of human rights and freedoms, amplified by an authoritarian regime based on fear of indefinite military mobilization, arbitrary detention, torture and other human rights violations. according to a un report on the human rights situation in eritrea, there are three issues that need to be addressed in order to ensure respect for fundamental rights and freedoms, namely: smuggling and trafficking, the increasing number of unaccompanied minors who are among the 5 000 persons leaving the country every month, and the exercise of economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to adequate housing. threats to the right to adequate housing have been manifested in forced evictions, which have intensified since the beginning of 2015. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the principles and values of the european union must be translated into joint action and efforts to respect human rights in the context of development cooperation. restoring the rule of law and promoting democratic governance in eritrea must be on the european agenda, given that the eu is founded on a firm commitment to the defence of human rights and democracy.
in writing. ‒ the deterioration of living conditions in eritrea through the curtailment of human rights and freedoms has caused the departure of over 9% of the population. every year, 5,000 people risk their lives trying to leave the country. the government's intentions to reduce legal and illegal immigration through shoot to kill policies and the diaspora tax are inhumane and contrary to freedom of movement. this is just one example, which indicates the extent and gravity of the violation of human rights and freedoms and the eritrean government's lack of concern for the well-being of its citizens. for this reason, i regret that the concerns expressed by the european parliament have not been taken into account by the commission, i denounce the resumption of the eur 200 million aid by signing the pin for eritrea and i ask the commission to monitor fully its implementation. i therefore strongly support the return of eritrea to a state of political normality, the establishment of a true separation of powers in the state, the development of democracy and the rule of law. i condemn the policies of european companies, which take advantage of the inequalities in the system, thus indirectly involving the use of forced labour. last but not least, i believe that respect for human rights and freedoms, access to education and the abolition of torture are essential elements of the healthy development of the state.
in writing. ‒ the european union decided to resume its development assistance to eritrea notably via a national indicative programme (nip) for eritrea of eur 200 million. scrutiny working group a of the committee on development of the european parliament, which i chair, called on the edf committee on 11 november 2015 not to adopt the draft nip pending further discussion. this is explained by the human rights situation in eritrea, that has long been deteriorating – civilians are regularly arbitrarily detained or arrested for a number of unjustifiable reasons – criticising or opposing the government, practising journalism, practising an unofficial religion, evading or deserting mandatory national service, trying to flee the country. eritreans fleeing the country now constitute the third largest group of refugees making the perilous journey to europe. however, our call upon the commission was not taken into consideration. i ask the european commission to review its scrutiny arrangements with the european parliament and to seriously consider how eu aid and resources can be best focused to address the situation and help bring about change.
in writing. ‒ the eritrean authorities have been lashing down hard on their citizens. this situation, where basic human rights are violated through harsh conditions imposed by the government, must stop. the use of the ‘diaspora tax’ is deplorable, as is the lack of freedom and the arbitrary arrests. as a matter of urgency, eritrea should ratify and enact the un convention against torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
in writing. ‒ the human rights situation in eritrea has forced many women, men and children to flee the country, risking further abuses in the hands of smugglers and human traffickers, in order to reach safer grounds. the ones who stayed behind face an oppressive regime and severe problems with indefinite conscription, food security, restrictions, abuses and repression of all basic freedoms. i therefore support this resolution and strongly hope that the international community will use all diplomatic tools available to intervene before this crisis becomes even worse.

in writing. ‒ the european union has become a champion of human rights protection internationally in recent years. in this regard, the european institutions have highlighted violations of fundamental rights in various parts of the world, encouraging the development of equitable democratic systems based on the sovereignty of citizens. the situation in eritrea has now become critical following the arbitrary measures of the authorities, who have sent a considerable number of people behind bars for criticizing the government, practicing independent journalism, practicing unofficial religions, not satisfying the mandatory military service or attempting to leave the country. a recent un report concluded that eritrea has one of the lowest human rights records in the world, with no immediate prospects for improvement. significantly, eritrean nationals are the third largest group of migrants heading to the european union countries in this period. in these circumstances, the union must act, with the resources at its disposal, to put an end to this situation, which is not favourable to the citizens of eritrea or to the member states. as representatives of the european citizens, it is our duty to support this resolution.

in writing. ‒ this is the first report by the european parliament on the banking union. it includes an assessment of the implementation of the fully operational single supervisory mechanism as of november 2014, the single resolution mechanism, tasked with resolution operations as of january 2016, as well as other challenges for the banking union, in particular the achievement of the third pillar through the creation of a european deposit guarantee scheme and further initiatives to reduce risks in the banking sector. the banking union is one of our key achievements since the start of the 2008 financial crisis, which can ensure safe and resilient financial and banking sectors, restore confidence among citizens and develop investment in the real economy. in the absence of these elements, the banking union cannot be considered as completed and therefore able to achieve its objectives and reduce risk.
in writing. ‒ banking union is one of our key achievements since the financial crisis in 2008 to ensure safe and resilient financial and banking sectors to restore confidence, investment in the real economy and a high level of protection for citizens from the failure of banks and financial firms. i have fully supported the first steps: the single supervisory mechanism (ssm), operational from november 2014, and the single resolution mechanism (srm), fully operational from the beginning of this year. the third pillar – a common deposit insurance scheme – is unfortunately still missing, and work on a common fiscal backstop to be available as a last resort to support the single resolution fund has not yet started. together with the ssm and the srm, the capacity to afford a uniform and high level of protection of deposits, irrespective of their location, should be ensured in an effective banking union. in the absence of these missing elements, the banking union cannot be considered as completed and therefore able to fulfil its ambition and reduce risk. it should be our priority for the coming year.
in writing. ‒ this is the first report by the european parliament on the banking union. the financial crisis in 2008 reminded us that the european project is far from complete. we need a deep reform of financial regulation and supervision to ensure sustainable and job-creating growth in the european union. the first steps have been taken: the single supervisory mechanism, which has been operational since november 2014, and the single resolution mechanism, fully operational since the beginning of this year. the third important pillar, a common deposit insurance system, is in a deadlock. at the moment we can say that the banking union is not completed. that should be our priority for next year.
in writing. ‒ as a response to the financial crisis that emerged in 2008, the european commission pursued a number of initiatives to create a safer and sounder financial sector for the single market. these initiatives, which include improved depositor protection and rules for managing failing banks and stronger prudential requirements for banks, form a set of rules for all financial actors in the 28 member states of the eu. this set of rules is the foundation on which the banking union sits. i voted for this report that calls, amongst other things, for the implementation of the banking structural reform which was conceived to reduce systemic risk.
in writing. ‒ the banking union plays a key role in financing investment and therefore in stimulating economic growth and job creation across the union. this european parliament report on the banking union includes an assessment of the implementation of the fully operational single supervisory mechanism (ssm) as of november 2014, the single resolution mechanism (srm) in charge of the january 2016 settlement operations, as well as other challenges for the banking union, in particular the achievement of the third pillar through a common deposit guarantee scheme and additional initiatives to reduce risks in the banking sector. the banking union is one of the key achievements following the 2008 financial crisis to ensure secure financial and banking sectors and to restore confidence, investment in the real economy and a high level of protection for citizens in the event of the failure of banks and financial firms.
in writing. – in line with the rapporteur and the econ committee, i welcome the introduction of the banking union and the establishment of the single supervisory mechanism and single resolution mechanism for the eurozone in the aftermath of the financial crisis of 2008. i voted in favour of this annual report, as oversight over the implementation and development of financial supervision at the eu level functions as an important safeguard mechanism.
in writing. ‒ the banking union is one of the main gains from the financial crisis that hit the european union in 2008. this action by member states and european institutions has led to the strengthening of the financial and banking sectors, ensuring their safety and resilience, and to the restoration of confidence in banks, alongside investment in the real economy and a high level of protection for citizens. the establishment of the single supervisory mechanism (ssm) in november 2014 and the single resolution mechanism (srm) represented the first steps towards the emergence of a new regulatory pillar for the financial and banking sector at european level. unfortunately, this pillar is not yet fully structured at present, in the absence of a common fiscal backstop to support the single resolution fund. in the coming years, the banking union needs to be developed in this direction by establishing a european deposit guarantee scheme (edgs). the current document is a first step in the right direction; therefore, i support its adoption.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the european pig sector is indeed in a very tense situation. the main reason is a significant increase in production over the last two years. the fall of russia as an export market has aggravated the situation, but it is not the only cause. the commission has responded to this situation by granting private storage aid for pigmeat under the common organization of the market, and in january this year 90 000 tonnes of pigmeat were stored with a budget of approximately eur 27.6 million. the purpose of this measure is to withdraw meat from the market at short notice during periods of low prices at the beginning of the year and to return it to the market after the seasonal price increase in early summer, when the barbecue season is in full swing. this explains why the commission can only use this market measure for a limited period of time. if the quantity stored is too large, the negative effects exceed the market effects of the removal of frozen products. the recent stocking has stopped the seasonal fall in prices in january and thus had a direct impact on agricultural incomes. so the safety net worked. let me also be very clear: the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, but it is still in the process of drawing up a proposal for a directive. however, they can support the necessary market adjustments. we're seeing clear signs of market reaction right now. in addition to the direct market support measures, the pig sector benefits from the solidarity pact adopted by the commission in september 2015. this includes the possibility of targeted measures in the livestock sector for a total volume of eur 420 million.as regards the sanitary restrictions on trade in fat, bacon and by-products imposed by russia, the commission already launched a wto procedure in 2014. although there is no official wto decision yet, all preliminary information from geneva indicates a confirmation of the eu position. this will undoubtedly strengthen the commission's negotiating position on market access. in conclusion, let me say that the commission is monitoring the market situation very closely and, as in the past, will take any necessary action in a timely manner.

member of the commission.– mr president, on behalf of the commission, i would like to thank the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and, in particular, the rapporteur ms van bossuyt for this report. we agree that the single market is a cornerstone of european integration. in recent decades it has delivered more jobs and contributed to higher growth. we need to address the whole policy cycle, so last year the commission presented two main initiatives designed to do that: the better regulation package and the single market strategy. last may we proposed a better regulation package, covering the entire policy cycle from consultations and impact assessments to the adoption, implementation and evaluation of eu legislation. the package will help us make sure that eu laws tackle the real problems of citizens and businesses. from now on, eu laws should be adopted according to better evidence and a more careful assessment of their impact on the real world. this will help us regain the trust of eu citizens. more recently a new interinstitutional agreement on better law—making was negotiated by parliament, the council and the commission. we now have a strong political framework and a renewed commitment from the institutions in support of better regulation. after formal adoption it will be up to parliament and the council to work with the commission to ensure its timely and effective implementation. we need to ensure that we deliver the benefits for citizens and businesses in practice rather than just in theory. let us take the regulatory fitness programme as an example – the one which we discussed a while ago. the commission’s regulatory fitness and performance programme will also play a central role in simplifying the body of existing legislation and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens, especially for microenterprises and small and medium enterprises, and we will do so without weakening any of our important social and environmental goals. the second major initiative that we took last year is the single market strategy adopted in october. it has three key aims: creating new opportunities for people and businesses, encouraging and enabling the modernisation and innovation that europe needs and, above all, ensuring practical delivery. in some areas we need to launch new initiatives, such as introducing a service passport for key sectors of the economy, adopting a legislative proposal to prevent discrimination against consumers based on nationality or residence, or revising the mutual recognition regulation. however, it is not enough just to come forward with new initiatives. we need to ensure the effective and efficient application of the existing legislation. we need to design legislation better and to evaluate and fix things which do not work as they should. we also need to make sure that existing rules are applied correctly by the member states and backed by a smart approach to enforcement and the development of a compliance culture. for example, we will promote an enhanced partnership with member states through implementation plans for new legislation and yearly compliance dialogues with each member state. we all have the same aims. we have the same broad vision of what we want to achieve: we all want improved single market legislation and better delivery. let us work together – the rapporteur.– mr president, currently, european citizens have limited knowledge about the eu and how its institutions work. according to a 2014 eurobarometer opinion poll, 71% of european union citizens feel that they are not very well informed about the eu and 44% feel that they have a limited understanding of how the eu works. even more worryingly, 52% of europeans believe that their voice does not count in the eu. under these circumstances it is little wonder that citizens feel distant to or even increasingly estranged from the european project, become even more eurosceptic, and perceive democratic deficits in the decision-making processes of the union. therefore, enhancing dialogue about the eu in our schools and other educational institutions is crucial in order to bridge the long-standing gap between the european union and its citizens and to restore their faith in the merits and necessity of the european integration process. this is even more important in the current context of the ongoing refugee crisis and of serious threats to fundamental human rights and democracy due to the recent terrorist attacks. the report ‘learning eu at school’ highlights that the main role of education is to train fully aware and active citizens in an increasingly complex, multicultural and integrated europe and should therefore equip all learners with solid knowledge about the eu and in-depth understanding of its functioning and concrete added-value. an eu dimension in education should also encourage learners to critically reflect on european matters and how these influence their country and their own activities. this will empower them to form well-informed and balanced opinions, exercise their democratic rights and responsibilities, value diversity, intercultural and interreligious dialogue and be active and responsible citizens. with this in mind, the report stresses that the eu should become more visible in teaching materials and extracurricular activities at all levels and in all forms of education, including non-formal and lifelong learning. teaching about the eu should reflect both the role of member states in the development of the eu and the influence of the eu on national developments. in this context i would like to stress the importance of a european approach to the teaching of history in developing a reflective awareness of the past and a critical ‘culture of remembering’ based on european values. another important aspect the report focuses on is the strengthening of citizenship education with the aim of enabling learners to acquire the competences they need to live and actively engage in pluralistic democratic societies and make their concerns heard. core elements to be taught include tolerance, awareness and understanding for other cultures as well as democratic values and human rights. until now, a majority of member states has progressively integrated an eu dimension into their curricula and into teacher training, but gaps and disparities between and within member states continue to exist. much more could be done, for example, with regard to curricula, teacher training, textbooks and teaching methods. therefore the report strongly encourages member states to review and update their education systems and all forms of eu-related curricula content, to support all possibilities of conveying more information about the eu to learners as well as to teachers and other educators through formal, non-formal and informal learning, and to fully exploit and complement eu financial instruments, programmes and initiatives in this regard. at the european level, existing possibilities offered by the eu programmes in the field of education and culture should be fully used to promote active citizenship, cultural awareness, intercultural understanding and other valuable key and transversal competences. in this regard, the report calls for adequate financial support for these programmes, a greater focus on their qualitative outcomes and wider access to mobility, paying special attention to teachers and other educators, young people with different socio-economic backgrounds and vulnerable and disadvantaged groups. in addition, platforms such as eu twinning, the school education gateway and epale for adult learning can be used for the development and exchange of teaching materials and projects related to the eu and its institutions, as well as citizenship education. the report calls on the commission to continue to support member states in their efforts to develop and promote an eu dimension in education while respecting their competence in the field, also by providing a common framework and guidelines for learning about the eu and by actively conveying information to key stakeholders and citizens. i want to thank, first of all, the committee and all the people that helped on this, and the shadow rapporteurs.
mr president, education is the basis of society and i congratulate the rapporteur on his approach to including the concept of the european dimension in school curricula and the exchange of good practice between educational institutions in the member states. as a member of the committee on agriculture, i would like to reinforce an idea expressed in this report, namely that the union must constantly keep pace with new societal and technological challenges and that member states must ensure the continuous harmonisation of vocational and technical education programmes in order to meet these challenges. the rural environment is the main driver of economic development and therefore agricultural education must be an important component of vocational and technical education programmes at european level.

member of the commission.– madam president, i welcome the european parliament’s own-initiative report on innovation and diversification of small-scale coastal fishing in fisheries-dependent regions, and i would like to thank rapporteur tomašić for the report. the european maritime and fisheries fund (emff), which as you know is the structural support tool for the common fisheries policy for the period 2014-2020, was the fruit of intense negotiations between the european parliament and the council. thanks to the fund, member states can and probably will implement most of what is requested or proposed in the report. the fund permits a higher intensity of aid – 80% – for all operations related to small-scale coastal fishing. some examples are: young fishermen starting out in the sector; health and safety; diversification; partnerships between scientists and fishermen for the purposes of training; lifelong learning; marketing and processing; and innovation. however, it is the responsibility of member states to decide, under the respective operational programmes approved in late 2015, how to translate their strategic preferences into concrete support to their small-scale coastal fishing fleet. the figures for small-scale coastal fishing fleets are telling. they account for only 8% of gross tonnage yet they represent nearly three quarters – almost 75% – of active fishing vessels. they account for only 12% of the value of landings and 16% of the gross value added, yet they represent 48% of the total number of jobs and 36% of the full-time equivalents, which means that a significant proportion of the jobs are part-time. this last element implies that fishing is not the only, or even the main, source of income for many small-scale coastal fishing fishermen and families. in any event, it is a fact that small-scale coastal fishing vessels are fundamental for the viability and resilience of coastal communities dependent on them, and i fully agree with that view. however, it is also a fact that industrial or large-scale fishing fleets are also based in coastal areas and that they represent most of the value of landings, gross value added and full-time equivalent jobs within the eu. thus, these are at least as fundamental for the viability and the resilience of coastal communities as small-scale coastal fishing fleets. furthermore, the simple fact that some 36 stocks in the atlantic are now operating at maximum sustainable yield shows that large-scale fleets can also fish in a sustainable way whilst producing a lot of added value and social benefits. in view of the above, we need to support all fishing fleets and avoid instituting an asymmetric fishing policy, even though we do recognise the equal importance of this small-scale coastal fishing. regarding control requirements, let me recall that small-scale coastal fishing can already benefit from preferential conditions of support from the emff for the installation of control equipment on board. as to the proposal to relax control requirements for the fund during the review of the control regulation, we have to be particularly careful in ensuring that this does not jeopardise fishing resources in the coastal band. the coastal band is a strip about 12 nautical miles wide where most small-scale coastal fishing occurs and where most member states grant preferential access rights to vessels. in particular, there is a serious risk that further relaxing regulatory requirements on small-scale coastal fishing could encourage fishing by additional vessels and worsen crowding in the coastal band, especially in areas where there is already a lot of pressure on regulated and unregulated stocks. i am convinced that such a further relaxation would backfire both in terms of economic viability and environmental protection. regarding the definition of small-scale coastal fleets, according to the emff regulation, article 3(14) covers fishing vessels of an overall length of less than 12 metres and not using towed fishing gear. it was subject to intense discussions during the trilogues on the emff regulations. many alternatives, including the criteria proposed on point one of the report, were proposed, analysed and discussed, but in the end it was not possible to come to an agreement on any new definition, and the existing one was proposed. a regionalised approach to the definition could have some merit but would also risk creating an uneven playing field. in conclusion, all fleets, including the small-scale coastal fishing fleet, are fundamental for the continued viability of coastal areas. a successful cfp is the best possible way to ensure the environmental, economic and social sustainability of eu fisheries and coastal areas. there is a lot of public support for that. finally, be aware that relaxing further control requirements and allowing over-capacity to develop or increase in the 12-nautical-mile zone would clearly threaten the resilience of these communities. i have no doubt that the co-legislators will get back to us on these issues as part of the planned revision of the control regulation. thank you for your valuable comments.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank my colleagues in the committee, and in particular the shadow rapporteurs, for the way in which we have collaborated in the preparation of this report, which i regard as a clear message of support for the european commission, while also underlining the priorities of our committee in relation to the negotiations on the new international agreement. as you know, almost 64% of the world's waters remain outside the scope of the convention on the law of the sea, so the protection of the environment, marine biodiversity and the sustainable exploitation of resources are not covered by this convention, which is over thirty-five years old, which applies the principle of freedom of the seas in a world where things have changed, where the economy is diversified, the need for food and resources of the population is very different. as such, this convention is to be subjected, we hope, in the near future, to amendments that will bring it into line with present reality. as regards subsequent agreements, the most important agreement to which we wish to refer is the one concerning fish stocks, concluded in 1995. this agreement specifically addresses highly migratory fish stocks and those outside national jurisdiction. the agreement is in force, it is a good agreement, there are certainly still matters that can be discussed in relation to the effects of this agreement, but our committee recommends that the provisions of this agreement be firmly upheld and maintained unchanged in the future legal instrument. in 2004, the un general assembly decided to begin the first forms of negotiation of this convention. subsequently, on 6 june 2015, the un general assembly decided to open discussions and negotiations in preliminary commissions. the committees will start work in 2016 and we hope to have a first report in 2017. the purpose of these committees will be to prepare the substantive negotiations on the development of an international legal instrument, subordinate to the convention on the law of the sea, which will fill the gaps and complement the agreements currently in force. i would like to stress in particular the important role played by the european commission, as one of the voices that took this initiative in relation to the working group, but in this context i would like you to know that there are states that want the exclusion from this agreement of certain types of activities that take place outside national jurisdiction and in particular fishing, which puts us in difficulty, the european commission and the parliament not agreeing with this exclusion. in short, the inclusion of fisheries in this new international, legal instrument is a priority for us for the reasons stated earlier, but with a very firm amendment that this will not lead to the renegotiation of the 1995 fish stocks agreement, but will ensure its inclusion in a new international framework. i also recommended the use, extension and enhancement of regional fisheries management organisations. they are part of the 1995 agreement, some of them have worked less well, but in general the work of these regional organisations is worthwhile. we suggest the united nations find a way to motivate the states less involved in this agreement. as regards marine protected areas, they cannot be successful unless there is coordination and collaboration between all areas of activity and unless they are set out in an overall logic of biodiversity protection. we hope that the new international instrument will include an institutional structure for such decision-making.
