vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, let me start by thanking parliament for keeping the situation in palestine and israel in the spotlight at the top of our political agenda. once again, i wonder if there is a specific reason why these strategic debates always take place in the night sessions. i hope this is not a political sign. we all know that the lack of progress towards peace, especially in the holy land, is always a prelude to a new escalation, and this is why we need to keep focusing on the two-state solution, even when israel and palestine do not make the headlines. this is a consistent, constant eu effort to work in that direction because we all know that, on the ground, the viability of a two—state solution is challenged on a daily basis and it is our key interest and also it is our political duty to keep it alive and possible in concrete terms. the expansion of settlements challenges the two-state solution. so does the growing trend of demolitions and confiscations of palestinian structures, including those funded by the european union and member states. the same goes for the worsening living conditions of palestinians in the west bank and gaza. let me be very clear from the outset. demolitions and israel’s settlement policy are not the only challenges to the two-state solution. unfortunately, we see many different challenges taking place on the ground. terrorist attacks and hate speech challenge the two states and the possibility of people living side by side. the lack of palestinian unity challenges the two states and their political perspective. a growing sense of disillusionment and despair on both sides among the people is a powerful enemy of peace. so we always need to keep in mind the bigger picture, even when we focus – as we do tonight, because this is the issue on which you decided to focus our debate tonight – on one specific element of this bigger picture that is not encouraging for many different reasons and on many different aspects. but that still does not prevent us from continuing to work every single day for the two-state solution. today, your focus is on settlements and on the issue of demolitions. israel’s decisions to declare more parts of area c as state land pave the way for further settlement activity and, as you know, settlements are illegal under international law, and the european union always refers to them in this way and restates this position. the european council has stated several times that our union opposes israel’s settlement policy. we oppose a separation barrier built beyond the 1967 line. we oppose demolitions and confiscations, evictions, forced transfers, including of bedouins, illegal outposts, settler violence and – let me remind all of us – we oppose all forms of violence on all sides, as i mentioned before, and we oppose the restrictions of movement and access. this is not simply because we care about international law (which we do) and respect for it (which we do), but also because these actions directly reduce the palestinians’ ability to use the land in area c, something which is vital to development and growth in the west bank and to the viability of the palestinian economy. israel, as an occupying power, has a duty to protect the palestinian population and to facilitate its socioeconomic well-being. you all know that the european union is doing a lot to promote development and improve humanitarian conditions in palestine. however, as a result of planning policies applied by israel, projects funded by the european union and member states in area c are often deemed illegal under israeli law and are therefore demolished or threatened with demolition by the israeli authorities. eu humanitarian aid always respects the principles of neutrality and impartiality. we follow the humanitarian imperative of giving support to the most vulnerable, whenever and wherever this is needed, so where humanitarian projects are concerned, it is not conceivable for us to ask for prior authorisation from the israeli authorities. it is our humanitarian duty. in the first quarter of this year, some 500 houses and other structures were demolished, and 650 people displaced. approximately 20% of those structures were eu-funded. we are raising the issue with israel in our regular dialogue, and we have established a specific consultation mechanism with israel to discuss obstacles to the two-state solution and to the socioeconomic development of the palestinians, including the issue of settlements and the issue of demolitions in area c. these mechanisms were used most recently last month on this particular matter of demolitions and dislocations and the issue was also highlighted in the council conclusions we adopted last january. tangible results have so far been very limited. member states have agreed to continue the dialogue for six more months while pushing for an immediate moratorium on adverse developments in area c, especially demolitions and confiscations. we are also engaging with member states to agree common messages on this issue, including on the possible restitution or compensation for the confiscated or demolished eu assets. demolition of a house or a humanitarian project has of course a very strong economic impact on those involved, and also on us, but this is not just about money and we know this very well: this is about the present for the people and the future of the political settlements. we also know very well that only a serious and meaningful peace process can lead us out of the current downward spiral. there is an urgent need to improve the situation on the ground, and at the same time we have to keep an eye on the goal. again, let me conclude on the bigger picture, because we are focusing tonight on one aspect which is important, relevant and serious, but we have to keep focused on the bigger picture. this is something you normally ask of me, but tonight i will be asking this of you. we continue to work on a daily basis on two states living side by side, in peace and in security, to end the conflict and all claims. you know that we are working on the report of the quartet together with the united states, russia and the united nations. the quartet report will address these issues and will also include some substantial recommendations for the way forward, and i will be very glad to discuss the report with you in the coming weeks in one of the next part-sessions, because we know very well that what is key is working at the concrete perspective of the two states and how to put that in place in the near future. i know this sounds like a daydream today, but we need to keep that daydream alive and to turn it into reality. we know very well, as europeans at least, that this is the only way out of the cycle that we are seeing today, and we are stubbornly working in that direction. i know that i can count on you and on your support to do this as we focus on the parts of the problem we are seeing, but let me ask you, at one of the next part-sessions, to come back to the process itself and the european union’s contribution, through the quartet report, to other initiatives that are also in place and being coordinated, such as the french initiative to hold an international conference, in coordination with the work we are doing in the quartet, on our contribution to solve the crisis in the middle east and to revitalise the political peace process to get to a two-state solution. again, i know very well that we are all on the same page on this, but we need not only to make a slogan out of it, but also to translate it from a parliamentary point of view into an active, constant daily work.

in writing. ‒ taking into account eu regulation no 575/2013 and directive 2013/36/eu, the directives apply to both credit institutions and investment firms. the amount to be reported in column 060 of this row: original deduction according to article 56 (b) of crr as of 2017, the two derogations will expire and this time limitation clause was originally included in the crr to give regulators the time to establish that prudential regulation tailored to the risk profile of commodity traders. i voted in favour of the report on the derogations for traders in goods because i believe that we need to support all traders in goods so that they can achieve a better return, a return that is favourable both to the member states and to the european union.
in writing. ‒ the requirements set out in the capital requirements regulation as well as in the capital requirements directive apply to both credit institutions and investment firms. the regime applicable to investment firms is derived from the regime applicable to credit institutions and is adapted according to the investment services they provide. we voted to develop a coherent prudential framework for all types of investment companies.
in writing. ‒ i support the proposed regulation that aims to extend the exemptions laid down in the crr for commodity dealers from the large exposures and own funds requirements and, accordingly, amend regulation 575/2013. the prudential framework applicable to investment firms (including commodity dealers) laid down in the crr and directive 2013/36/ec (‘the capital requirements directive’) is currently under review. because it is highly improbable that any legislation that may result from this review can be prepared, adopted and applied before the current exemptions expire (31 december 2017), in order to continue their activities they might be forced to increase the amount of own funds needed to perform their activities. therefore i welcome the commission’s proposal to extend the existing exemptions laid down in the crr and to take into account the amount of time that will be necessary to conclude the investment firms’ review and to prepare, adopt and apply any legislation that may result from that review.
in writing. ‒ the capital requirements regulation implies the 'requirement for own funds' principle, which requires credit institutions to have sufficient capital reserves to cover unexpected losses. the high exposure and own funds requirements were developed to limit the maximum loss a bank can suffer in the event of the sudden failure of the borrowed entity. the credit institution thus maintains its solvency. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties. however, the commission needs to review the framework on investment companies. a coherent prudential framework for those companies is necessary. therefore, since merchants of goods fall into this category, they agree to the extension of the derogations for them, until the legislative framework is clarified.
in writing. ‒ in march 2016 the commission decided to extend regulation 575/2013 that exempts commodity dealers from large exposure requirements and from own funds requirements. i have voted for this report that extends the exemption until the 31st of december 2020, in order to save commodity dealers from an unstable regulatory environment in the short term.
in writing. ‒ the requirements set out in the capital requirements regulation and the capital requirements directive apply to both credit institutions and investment firms. the prudential regime applicable to investment firms is derived from the regime applicable to credit institutions and is adapted according to the investment services they provide. the commission has decided to undertake a single review on a proper regime for merchants and on the prudential supervision of investment firms in general and to prepare a single report on the above issues. this was considered necessary to ensure the development of a coherent prudential framework for all types of investment firms.
in writing. ‒ i supported, in my vote today, the adoption of this report on the extension of derogations from certain provisions of the capital requirements for dealers in goods regulation, as i believe that predictability of legislation is absolutely necessary to ensure a healthy competitive environment. in this respect, the possibility that these derogations expire at the end of 2017 without being replaced in time by legislation adapted to this broad spectrum of economic actors, defined as 'commodity traders', would cause instability and lack of legislative coherence. the extension of these derogations until the completion of the review by the european commission and the adoption of coherent legislation will give economic operators confidence in the efficiency and consistency of european legislation.
in writing. ‒ the european institutions have developed a series of measures in recent years to avoid economic problems of the type that arose during the international financial crisis of 2008. these measures were aimed at more stringent regulation of the commercial sector, with a view to ensuring greater protection for consumers. one of those measures was the adoption of regulation (eu) no 575/2013 on capital requirements (crr), which was doubled by the capital requirements directive (crd) 2013/36/eu, documents applicable to credit institutions and investment firms, derived from the prudential regime for credit institutions. in those documents, there is a derogation for investment services in the field of securities from the compliance with the requirements for large exposures and, respectively, with the own funds requirements. the derogation, which is valid until 31 december 2017, was considered necessary to allow regulators the time to establish prudential regulation adapted to the risk profile of merchants. in view of the stage reached in the assessment of the necessary legislative framework, the commission considered that an extension of the derogation was necessary until the completion of the reviews already undertaken. as this is a request for the consistency of the union legislative act, i support the extension of the derogation.
in writing. ‒ the term 'commodity trader' is intended to cover a wide range of actors in the energy and commodities markets, as explained in this proposal for a regulation. investment firms may be assimilated, with the negotiation of commodity derivative contracts being their sole activity, or for others, represent only part of the activity of commodity production. the capital requirements regulation (crr) 575/2013 provides for a derogation for commodity dealers from the requirements for large exposures and own funds requirements with a deadline of 31 december 2017. to this end, the european commission has undertaken a one-off review and is preparing a report on the issues referred to, in order to develop a coherent prudential framework for all types of investment firms. i supported this report because it is appropriate to extend the existing derogations provided for in the crr. the extension should be granted taking into account the time needed to complete the review of the framework for investment companies and to prepare, adopt and apply the legislation that may result from that review.
in writing. i voted for the report on the derogations for traders in goods. the european commission has decided to undertake a single review on a proper regime for merchants and on the prudential supervision of investment firms in general, called the investment firm framework review, and to prepare a single report to that effect.

in writing. ‒ as a mean of respecting and safeguarding the fundamental rights of union citizens, the creation of a harmonized, high level of data protection covering police and judicial activities in the union is crucial. i have voted for this report on law enforcement cooperation and the creation of such agencies across member states.
in writing. ‒ merging europol and cepol into a single agency based in the hague would generate important synergies and efficiency gains. combining europol's knowledge in operational police cooperation with cepol's expertise in training and education would strengthen links and create synergies between the two areas. collaboration between operational and training staff, who will work within a single agency, will help to identify training needs, thus increasing the relevance and focus of training at eu level, to the benefit of overall eu police cooperation. this proposal for a regulation provides a legal framework for a new europol which succeeds and replaces europol and cepol as established. the proposal also strengthens the data protection regime applicable to europol's activities. thus, greater efficiency in eu law enforcement cooperation will also ensure stronger supervision and a clear data protection regime.
in writing. ‒ the council proposal aims to strengthen the level of data protection for police and judicial activities in the european union. in view of the common responsibilities of the union and the member states in the field of security and justice, it is important that there is close and effective cooperation between the supervisory authorities at national and european level. the new measures will allow europol to respond to threats more quickly and to set up specialised units more easily. i believe this is an important step towards greater efficiency in eu law enforcement cooperation. for this reason, i support the council's position by my vote.
in writing. ‒ this report aims to increase europol's effectiveness and accountability, with a view to stepping up efforts in the fight against terrorism, cybercrime and other crimes. europol should thus strengthen actions and cooperation between member states aimed at preventing and combating serious forms of crime affecting member states and eu interests. in addition to strengthening europol's mandate, the new regulation aims to facilitate the creation of specialised units to fight certain forms of crime or terrorism. it also sets clearer rules for existing centres and contains new rules to strengthen the agency's data management and protection regime by establishing a mechanism for scrutiny of its activities by the european parliament in cooperation with national parliaments and a complaints procedure for citizens. this new data management and protection system allows for links between the different surveys. moreover, information exchange agreements with third countries will fall within the scope of the regulation. europol will also be able to exchange information with private parties in certain cases. i therefore voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation establishing new competences for the eu agency europol.
mr president, research, student and student exchange, paid and unpaid internships, volunteering, all of this is preparing the young generation for the historic leap we must make and are already making - some of you may not be aware of it, but many are. the mobility of the young generation is very important both for increasing competitiveness and for raising the skills of the workforce, the more competitiveness we have, the more skilled the workforce will be and the better the outcome of work and the society will evolve. with this opening up of europe to students and pupils from third countries, we must of course take care to adopt effective measures to prevent those who enter the union territory under the pretext of study or volunteering or work from bringing extremism with them.
in writing. ‒ this directive aims to allow member states to reject an application only on a case-by-case basis, taking into account both the specific circumstances of each third-country national and the principle of proportionality, but only on the basis of evidence or serious and objective reasons. at the same time, it is necessary to monitor and ensure that member states implement that provision in accordance with that interpretation when transposing the directive and inform the european parliament and the council thereof, within the framework of their obligations under article 39. i voted in favour of this resolution on the entry and residence of third-country nationals for the purposes of research, studies, vocational training, volunteering, pupil exchange and au pairing, considering it essential to encourage teaching, research and vocational training, because this exchange does nothing but support the member states, but also the european union as a whole.
in writing. ‒ the situation of third-country nationals coming to the union for studies, research, vocational training through paid or unpaid traineeships, but also for volunteering or au pair work is characterised by two aspects that i consider important. firstly, this mobility creates a transfer between the european labour market, the research field and these young people in the sense of providing a favourable framework for completing their educational and professional development at a high quality level, and for the eu it would be remarkable to increase competitiveness on the market. secondly, as this recommendation for the second reading itself emphasises, member states must not neglect the profile of any young third-country national coming to the eu and their application should only be rejected on the basis of evidence or serious reasons which would make their presence inappropriate. i am referring, of course, to the possibility of a transfer of extremism from outside to the union. i therefore support this recommendation for a second reading on the conditions of entry and residence of third-country nationals for research, studies, vocational training, volunteering and pupil exchange programmes, educational projects and au pairs.
in writing. ‒ i believe it is fundamental to make the conditions of entry of third-country nationals as simple and harmonised as possible, and to strengthen provisions on the right for students to work part-time while studying, and the right for students and researchers to remain after completing their studies for an 18 months period. at a time of negative news stories concerning migration, this directive is a welcome step forward with regard to legal migration for students, researchers and other groups of young people. we need to see more legal migration instruments at eu level to tap into the great positive potential of migration. the broadening of the scope, the provisions on mobility, the provisions on working hours and allowing students and researchers to stay after completion of their studies or research are all elements which i support and will keep fighting for. i am satisfied with their inclusion in the final compromise text.
in writing. ‒ i support this directive because there are clear improvements in the mobility within the eu and working conditions of researchers, students and their families. for the first time we have common rules for au pair work and this directive also covers volunteers. students will be able to work 15 hours a week instead of the current 10 hours. researchers can work for six months instead of three. all citizens have the right to remain in an eu country for 9 months after the end of the job for which they came. the directive provides for intra-mobility which prevents member states from blocking it. au pair is a cultural exchange programme that offers people the chance to do something new and at the same time get paid.
in writing. ‒ i strongly support this report. the eu should offer more migration opportunities for young individuals, such as students or researchers. migration can be a constructive tool as long as the security of the union’s citizens is first considered.

in writing. ‒ the directive lays down the conditions for admission, entry and residence of third-country nationals in the territory of the member states for the purposes of research, studies, pupil exchange, vocational training, whether or not remunerated, voluntary service or au pair work. member states shall be authorised to reject an application only on a case-by-case basis and taking into account the specific circumstances of each third-country national and the principle of proportionality and on the basis of serious and objective evidence or grounds.

in writing. ‒ the central objective of this report is to establish harmonised rules at european level for third-country nationals to facilitate entry and stay in european territory for research, studies, vocational training, volunteering, pupil exchange and au pair work. the new rules clarify and improve the conditions for trainees, volunteers, pupils and au pairs from outside europe. the new rules will allow students and researchers to stay in the eu for nine months after completing their studies or research in order to find a job or develop a business. it also facilitates mobility within the eu from one member state to another, requiring only notification to the destination state without a new visa. moreover, researchers are entitled to bring their family members with them and they are entitled to work during their stay in the eu, and students are entitled to work at least 15 hours a week. european universities will have the capacity to increase their competitiveness on the international stage and become more attractive to ambitious students who have benefited from higher education in other countries. i therefore voted in favour of the report which sets out new rules for third country nationals on european territory.
mr president, the essence of eu cohesion policy is to help the poorer member states to get back on their feet. this is for several reasons: in addition to meeting the social need for an increase in living standards, it can also be seen as an objective to create fairer competition on the market. the common market is a very serious problem, given the enormous differences in income, infrastructure and service levels between the member states. it is important to make people aware that cohesion policy is not aid. unfortunately, we see that even leading politicians often use this word, which is a complete misunderstanding of the situation. without a successful cohesion policy, the infrastructure and living standards of the former socialist countries will be brought even closer to those of the old member states, leading to increased migration, dissatisfaction and disillusionment with the european project. it is therefore important to have the same level of resources in cohesion policy beyond 2020. it is therefore important to stress that the success of cohesion policy is also in the interests of the old member states.

in writing. ‒ accelerating the implementation of cohesion policy can only be a positive element for member states. i firmly believe that investments under the cohesion policy – through its eur 350 billion euro budget until 2020 – will aid member states in enhancing growth and job creation.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this motion for a resolution that calls on member states to use the esi funds to their full potential, in order to enhance social and economic cohesion and reduce territorial disparities by enabling all regions to become more competitive and to facilitate investment, in line with the europe 2020 strategy.
in writing. ‒ during the 2007-2013 programming period, the main obstacles and problems that hindered the implementation of cohesion policy in several member states and regions were insufficient information for potential beneficiaries, the cumbersome and time-consuming process of approving major projects, complex and lengthy procurement procedures, complex state aid rules, complicated authorisation procedures, excessive length of the authorisation procedure and difficult access to funding. we invite the commission to provide, for the 2014-2020 programming period, information on the obstacles faced by member states in implementing cohesion policy and an assessment of the impact of the exercise of ex ante conditionalities on the effective implementation of the policy. we welcome the establishment of a task force for better implementation of the 2007-2013 programmes in eight member states and ask the commission to inform parliament of the results achieved. the commission should continue, together with this task force, to support and accelerate the implementation of the 2014-2020 programmes in all member states and present to parliament an action plan on the task force's activities.

in writing. ‒ given that two years have already passed since the start of the new 2014-2020 programming period, the implementation of cohesion policy is lagging behind, with operational programmes largely approved since 2014-2015, yet a significant number of ex ante conditionalities have not been met to date. the 2014-2020 regulations have introduced several key reforms in the area of cohesion policy, but cohesion policy investments need to be aligned with other areas such as the digital single market, the energy union, social policy, macro-regional strategies, the urban agenda, transport research and innovation, in order to best contribute to the europe 2020 objectives of the member states. i voted for the motion for a resolution on speeding up the implementation of cohesion policy because i believe that the annual evaluation by the european commission can bring benefits for a better coordinated use of the european structural and investment funds.
president-in-office of the council.– mr president, let me be clear, the creation of the schengen area, in which the free movement of persons across internal borders is ensured, is one of the greatest achievements of the union. without any doubt, it has brought important benefits to european citizens and businesses alike. yet over the past months, the system has been severely tested by the migration crisis, leading several member states to reintroduce internal border controls. now as you all know, the aim is to ensure that any and all remaining obstacles are removed by the end of the year at the latest, for the costs of losing free movement within the schengen area would be huge. now to overcome what emerged originally as a patchwork of unilateral decisions, we are developing a coordinated european approach, within the framework of the schengen rules of course, and let me also underline that the practice of waving through has now ended. clearly, securing the eu’s external borders, ensuring efficient border controls and improving the functioning of the asylum system are prerequisites for restoring normal free movement within the schengen area. this is a shared responsibility involving all our institutions as well as the member states. in other words, proper control at our external borders is our common responsibility, hence the need to reinforce our collective ownership over that common good. now, as we all know, last december the commission presented a proposal for a european border and coast guard. it is imperative that we adopt this proposal as soon as possible so that it becomes operational and it is therefore of great importance to work together in order to start trilogues in june and strike a political agreement soon thereafter. in february, the european council made itself very clear. member states must grant access to asylum procedures for all applications made at their borders. at the same time they should refuse entry to third country nationals who do not satisfy the entry conditions of the schengen border code and who have not submitted an application for asylum despite having had the opportunity to do so. the european council also underlined the importance of restoring the normal functioning of the schengen area in a concerted manner while giving full support to member states facing difficult circumstances. i am of course referring to greece, whose external border has been under immense pressure. now fortunately this pressure has, since the eu—turkey statements of 18 march, significantly reduced. however, serious deficiencies in external border control persist today – even if many of them have been, and are being, tackled by greece. that is why the commission presented on 4 may a proposal on article 29 of the schengen borders code, a proposal recommending a coherent eu approach to the reinstatement of internal border controls until the structural deficiencies are remedied, as well as proposing border controls only at the sections of the border where they are necessary and proportionate. now in closing, the effective application of all these policies and measures taken together, and the effective application by all of us, should contribute to fully reinstating free movement within the schengen area and i sincerely hope that we will succeed before the end of the year.
member of the commission. – mr president, the schengen area, as you know, is an area of free movement without internal borders. we have repeatedly said here that it is maybe the most tangible achievement of the european integration. this commission, from the very beginning, has done everything in its power to make sure that we preserve it in accordance with the steps set out in our back to schengen roadmap. our objective is to return to a normal functioning of the schengen area with no internal border controls as soon as possible and within six months at the latest because the costs of internal border controls are already visible. we see transporters complaining about increasing delays and costs and we see the tourism industry in some member states suffering and this is only a small part – a fraction – of what would happen if border controls were systematically re—established. but the political cost of non—schengen would be much greater still. it would be a highly symbolic reversal of a major achievement of european integration. this is why we need to take coordinated action at european level, making use of the tools that the same schengen borders code provides us with so as to allow member states to do what is necessary in the current circumstances, while preserving schengen as a whole. this is what our proposal under article 29 of the schengen borders code is meant to achieve. let me first acknowledge that greece has made significant progress in the last few months. however, not all deficiencies identified in the management of external borders control have been remedied. this concerns in particular sea border surveillance, reception capacities and registration on the mainland of migrants who were not registered upon arrival in the islands. despite the reduction in the flows due to our cooperation with turkey, the sustainability of this reduction still has to be confirmed. moreover, a number of these unregistered migrants remain in greece or in other countries of the western balkans. they may seek to move irregularly to other member states. in other words, the reasons that led several states to unilaterally introduce temporary border controls still exist. the persistent threat of secondary movements puts at risk the overall functioning of the schengen area. therefore a coherent, coordinated and sustainable common approach to temporary internal border controls, as foreseen in article 29 of the schengen borders code, is needed at eu level. article 29 is a tool to safeguard the functioning of the whole schengen area and this is the first time that the commission has made use of it. as a result, we propose that the council recommend that austria, germany, sweden, denmark and norway maintain their internal border controls at specific border-crossing points for up to six months. controls will be regularly reviewed by the schengen states concerned and adjusted to the level of the security threat addressed. the states concerned will also report to the commission every two months. let me be clear about two things. article 29 is not a sanction against a member state nor a means to expel it from the schengen area. i want to be very clear on that. we do not propose the introduction of border controls at greece’s schengen border, namely at airports and ports. in addition, we clearly state that the controls introduced should be proportionate and limited to what is strictly necessary to respond to the serious threat and safeguard public policy and internal security. they should impede border crossing for the general public as little as possible. the commission will continuously monitor the situation and will report to this parliament and the council, after four months, on the possible need to adapt the application of its initial recommendation. the principles of necessity and proportionality are the guiding principles for this and any future decision. let me therefore reiterate that our proposal is an exceptional – temporary – measure to ultimately allow for the safeguarding and return to a normally functioning schengen area as soon as possible. it is expected that, by the end of the six—month period at the latest, the implementation of other tools will allow the lifting of all internal border controls and a return to a normally functioning schengen. i refer in particular to the european border and coast guard, to the further sustained implementation of the eu—turkey statement, and the full application of eu asylum rules, as well as the swift agreement by the co-legislators on the recently presented proposals for reforming parts of the common european asylum system, in particular the dublin system. we look forward to the council adopting the proposed recommendation tomorrow.

in writing. although the european parliament has repeatedly called for improvements to existing community legislation on parental leave, current evidence confirms that a gender imbalance persists in this area. childcare is most often undertaken by women and this is confirmed by the much lower percentage of women in employment with dependent children compared to men in the same situation. women are more likely to interrupt their careers or work shorter hours than men, which negatively impacts their career development and promotion chances, as well as a less remunerated career path with consequences for their retirement income. i believe that more efforts are needed to identify the most effective tools for improving work-life balance in european policies, with the aim of reducing gender discrimination in childcare and women's participation in the labour market, but also in terms of the distribution of family responsibilities between women and men.

madam president, we need mandatory automatic exchange of information on taxation and i am glad that we adopted this report today. the latest information from the panama papers scandal shows us over 200,000 offshore companies, 200 states and 21 different tax havens are involved. this is an unprecedented situation. member states do not yet exchange data automatically, which is why we need to oblige them, and that is what we have done today with this report. the commission announced the publication of the country-by-country public reporting impact assessment in april 2016. let's come with our feet on the ground! we do not have time for impact assessments, but we must proceed immediately with this mandatory automatic exchange of information. it was said that it would reduce competitiveness if this information came out. i'm not sure. transparency will lead to competition and companies paying their taxes and citizens... )
in writing. ‒ this proposal for a directive aims to strengthen cooperation between member states' tax authorities to combat tax evasion in the context of the importance of aggressive tax planning. the need for all taxpayers to pay their taxes equitably derives from the ultimate purpose of collecting these taxes, namely to obtain higher tax revenues, which generates a reduction in public sector deficits, which is to the benefit of citizens. the commission notes that the tax advisor did not provide any evidence that the mne group was a company with a dominant position in the union. it is also necessary to increase the transparency with which these groups operate, in particular by requiring multinational enterprises to provide information on an annual basis and for each tax jurisdiction in which they operate on the amount of income, profit before tax on income, income taxes paid and accrued, number of employees, share capital, retained capital gains and intangible assets. i voted in favour of this proposal because i believe that close cooperation between tax authorities based on increased transparency leads to the smooth functioning of the internal markets and a significant reduction in tax evasion.
in writing. ‒ one of the major issues of concern within the union, and globally, is the problems of cross-border tax evasion, which have become considerably more acute. multinational groups of enterprises located in or operating in the eu with a total consolidated revenue of eur 750 000 000 or more will be required to report on a country-by-country basis. the country-by-country report must be submitted in the member state in which the subsidiary parent of the multinational enterprise group or any other reporting entity is resident for tax purposes. we voted for this first step towards solving these problems by increasing transparency.
in writing. ‒ in order to counter the aggressive tax planning we need increased transparency with regard to tax information, notably by introducing country-by-country reporting (cbcr) for multinational groups. because under the current legal framework member states do not share cbcr with one another, i welcome the proposal to set out a mandatory exchange of information of country-by-country information between tax authorities, taking into consideration that tax transparency is only a first step to fight tax avoidance. however, the commission’s proposal regarding a threshold will only make it possible to tackle 10% of multinationals, about 1 900 companies. i would like to underline that i am in favour of lowering the threshold to eur 40 million, the threshold of the accounting directive and cdr iv, in order to target about 20 000 multinational companies. in parallel, i believe that the commission should also have access to the information exchanged between member states’ tax authorities in order to ensure compliance with the relevant competition rules. i support the publishing of the country-by-country reports by the commission, based on the information contained in the centralised register of country-by-country reports. in doing so, the commission shall comply with the provisions on confidentiality.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the report because there needs to be a mandatory exchange of information in the tax field. the panama case is one of many cases of tax evasion, economic crime. i have been and am a strong supporter of smes and in this area of tax evasion they are the ones who suffer the most. to reduce cross-border tax evasion, cooperation is needed and that is why i supported this report. an adequate level of information provided to member states' tax authorities and the commission in a responsible manner will discourage those who have become accustomed to running for profit, circumventing tax regulations and business ethics.
in writing. ‒ tax transparency is crucial in fighting tax avoidance. i voted in favour of this report because this is a necessary first step, however cbcr (country-by-country reporting) is needed.
in writing. ‒ the challenge posed by aggressive tax planning, cross-border tax avoidance and harmful tax competition has increased considerably and has become a major focus of concern within the european union and at global level. i have voted for this report that will oblige multinational groups in the eu that have a revenue equal or higher than eur 750 million to file a country-by-country report that will include every tax jurisdiction where the group has its activities.
in writing. ‒ it is of vital importance for the union that tax rules are designed in such a way that they do not adversely affect growth or investment, do not subject union enterprises to competitive disadvantages and do not increase the risk of double taxation, and that they are designed to minimise costs and administrative burdens for businesses. the directive on mandatory automatic exchange of information in tax matters lays down the rules and procedures according to which member states cooperate with each other and with the commission to exchange information which is foreseeably relevant to the administration and application of the internal laws of the member states concerning taxes and duties.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the fight against tax evasion needs to be intensified at european level. the economic crisis of recent years has made the people of the european community increasingly aware of the need to create a healthy tax environment in which all taxpayers must pay their taxes in a fair way. the report voted on today encourages the exchange of information between the tax authorities of each member state, with multinationals being obliged to provide all information about the company's activities. last but not least, this transparency will allow the state budget to increase, not only by absorbing more taxes, but also by reducing administrative costs.
in writing. ‒ i support the resolution for mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation because i believe that public authorities in member states need to better communicate and cooperate with each other in order to increase tax transparency. although such information is not available to the public, cbcr is necessary in order to fight tax avoidance. the lux leaks and the panama papers revelations have brought momentum on tax evasion and have given the european union opportunities to further push for the regulation of taxation at the eu level. the eu does not need to wait for a third leak in the area of taxation before finding solutions to the issues that we are confronted with.
in writing. ‒ the report on mandatory automatic exchange of information provides for the automatic exchange of information on multinational companies' tax returns between member states as from april 2017. thus, multinational groups of enterprises located in or operating in the eu with a total consolidated revenue of eur 750 000 000 or more will be required to report on a country-by-country basis. this report proposes that the commission be associated with the automatic exchange of information and that it have access to the statements of each country, while respecting the rules of confidentiality. moreover, the commission should have equal access to the information exchanged between the tax administrations of the member states in order to ensure compliance with the provisions of competition law. the commission should also report annually to the european parliament and the council on the annual assessments made by the member states of the effectiveness of the automatic exchange of information and on the practical results achieved. this practice could be a first step in the fight against cross-border tax evasion, aggressive tax planning and harmful tax competition and i therefore voted in favour of this report.
we want to know what we're eating. one third of the fish we eat in brussels is mislabeled. in other words, we don't know what we're eating and where it came from. a recent study published by the ngo oceana showed that one third of the 280 fish samples taken from restaurants in brussels, including european institutions, are incorrectly labelled. it's serious and it's another wake-up call that we don't know what we're eating. i ask the european commission to investigate where in the production chain there are errors in the production and distribution chain of fish and to use dna-based barcodes as a tool to identify the origin and tracing of fish products.
in writing. ‒ the european commission and member states are urged to improve traceability and controls. non-traceable seafood may include illegal fish which causes economic damage and constitutes a risk to the protection of marine resources as well as a health risk due to a possible lack of sanitary and health checks. imports from third countries must fully comply with eu rules and standards. improved traceability can boost the economic situation of coastal communities as well as fair competition for producers of high-quality eu seafood. awareness-raising campaigns should be strengthened. labelling requirements must guarantee the right of the consumer to accurate, reliable and understandable information and avoid any confusion. in the context of voluntary labelling, member states are asked to state all available information that enables the consumer to make an informed choice.
in writing. ‒ various studies have expressed concerns showing significant levels of mislabelling on fish products sold on the eu market, including in the restaurants of the eu institutions. i have voted for this motion for a resolution that will strengthen national controls in an effort to tackle fraud and identify the stage in the supply chain where fish is mislabelled.
in writing. ‒ the eu is the world's largest market for fishery products, which is supplied both by the eu fisheries sector and by imports from third countries. a good european fisheries labelling policy would be essential to stimulating the economic development of coastal communities by recognising the best practices of fishermen and the quality of the products they offer to consumers. consumers also have the right to be informed, with easy-to-understand explanations, including information on the geographical areas and coastline where the fish was caught, and should be able to rely fully on the entire chain that offers fishery products to the eu market. the eu and its member states have a duty to protect eu citizens from fraud and all imported products must comply with eu rules and standards.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the traceability of fishery products. traceability is essential, especially as fish and seafood are perishable products. i hope that both the european commission and the belgian authorities will take action to eliminate the irregularities in the labelling of fishery products.
in writing. ‒ european citizens have the right to enjoy quality food products whose origin is clearly indicated. unfortunately, this is not always the case at member state level, especially with regard to seafood. there are many cases where the labels of certain products misrepresent the true origin or quality of the product, offering a lower quality for the price of a higher one. this has already happened with the various tuna species traded at european level and is very serious. it is the duty of the european institutions to eliminate these reprehensible practices by introducing much stricter controls, both as regards quality and the elimination of risks to public health and as regards the exact determination of the origin of marine products. the origin of the products from third countries is often hidden, which results in the avoidance of the payment of the related duties and the falsification of the real prices, with negative effects on european producers and workers in the sector. the consumer must have all the information necessary to make a fully informed decision to purchase the product. in this respect, i support the adoption of the present resolution.
in writing. ‒ the aim of this motion for a resolution is to provide consumers with information on the geographical and coastal areas where fish were caught, given that the eu is the largest market for fishery products in the world, being supplied both by the european fisheries sector and by imports from third countries. in 2015, in the framework of a control plan aimed at determining the degree of mislabeled fish on the market, the european commission found that the declared species were confirmed in 94% of the samples taken. however, the results of several studies show significant levels of mislabelling for fish products sold on the european market. therefore, a robust traceability system is needed to provide consumer confidence, thereby strengthening the european market for fishery products and stimulating the economic development of coastal communities. in addition to stressing the need for member states to strengthen their national controls, the motion for a resolution also calls on the commission to examine the potential of dna barcodes that could help identify species. i therefore voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products in restaurants and retail.
madam president, china is not a market economy: it subsidises companies and meddles in the way in which they are run, and its export prices are not determined by the rules of supply and demand. in addition it dumps its overcapacity production in other countries, where it creates severe economic and social damage, putting at risk hundreds of thousands of jobs in the eu alone. it has happened in the case of solar panels, tyres and shoes, and now it is happening in the steel sector. this is why i believe that, just like the usa, we should not automatically grant market economy status to china. instead we should opt for a criteria-based assessment of this status, involving a case-by-case definition of dumping margins, and prepare in advance strong trade defence instruments that can protect our industries against global unfair practices.
in writing. ‒ the issue of market economy status (mes) for china is a key topic of current interest in the european parliament. we must therefore engage in a transparent and cooperative process that leads to a successful and mutually acceptable outcome. i strongly believe that any decision on mes should be based on a solid and comprehensive impact assessment in order to evaluate the consequences on jobs and sustainable growth in all eu sectors. there is an evident need for the eu to maintain an effective anti-dumping instrument mechanism that takes the real market situation in china into account. we need to be united in the fight for balanced and reciprocally beneficial eu-hina relations. our demands and proposals will ensure that fair conditions are upheld in the european union’s trade policy towards china, and that there will be no automatism which could put european jobs at risk.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution and against the idea of automatically granting china the status of a market economy. the resolution duly recognises the strong economic relations between eu and china and the importance of respecting international commitments, notably the provisions of china’s accession protocol to the wto, and i support this approach. at the same time, the eu legislation foresees clear criteria, which are not applied only to china, which guide the determination of whether a country can be considered or not a market economy. and china does not currently fulfil those criteria. together with an overwhelming majority of my colleagues, i therefore call upon the commission to take due account the interests of the eu as a whole and notably the need to defend eu jobs, ensure high environmental standards and promote sustainable economic growth.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this motion for a resolution following the evaluation made by my political group.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from voting on the joint resolution on china's market economy status because i believe that the current level of influence of the chinese state on its economy, together with its production capacity, provides the opportunity to offer dumped prices on the eu market, with multiple effects on the societies and economies of the member states. at the same time, the importance of economic exchanges between the eu and china is very high for the industries of both economies. in this context, and in the context of the forthcoming g7 and g20 negotiations, i believe that a detailed analysis of the types and implications of measures needed to protect eu economies and jobs should be undertaken.
in writing. ‒ the issue of granting china market economy status has been hotly debated in recent months. representatives of several european industries warned of the negative impact of granting this status on the european workforce. as the world's second largest economy and the largest supplier of manufactured goods globally, china could gain a significant undue advantage over the eu and its member states. there is no doubt that the chinese authorities have made significant progress towards meeting the requirements for such status since joining the world trade organisation in 2001. the changes needed in the functioning of the chinese economy have been highlighted by the five criteria established by the commission as early as 2008 and concern compliance with the supply and demand rule in product pricing, the use of an accounting type in line with the rules of independent auditing, the regulation and transparency of public subsidies, compliance with the internationally agreed exchange rules and the adoption of clear property and bankruptcy legislation. the chinese economy is currently in the process of transforming and implementing those criteria. i think it's premature to make a decisive decision that could negatively affect relations with such an important partner.
in writing. ‒ in 2001, china joined the world trade organisation and the accession protocol provides that by the end of 2016 at the latest, it will receive market economy status. the market economy status is not a symbol, it is the legal status within the world trade organization. where a country does not have this status, anti-dumping proceedings are facilitated for countries considered to be facing unfair competition. it is estimated that between 1,7 and 3,5 million european jobs could be lost if china is granted market economy status. it is also estimated that a potential decrease of 2-3% of european gdp would be expected if this status is granted to china. moreover, the five criteria set by the eu for the granting of market economy status are not currently fulfilled by china, therefore the eu should continue to impose anti-dumping and anti-subsidy duties on imports from this country after december 2016 as long as these conditions are not fulfilled. i therefore voted in favour of the joint motion for a resolution on china's market economy status.

madam president, in answer to concerns about food quality, food safety and animal welfare, origin labelling can provide consumers with a means of making informed choices about the food they wish to purchase and consume. it also seems that consumers’ interest in the labelling of the food they consume is considerably strong. that is why mandatory marking of foodstuffs should be used as widely as possible. nevertheless, in the case of more advanced levels of processing, requiring complex traceability measures, mandatory origin labelling can lead to significant increases in production costs. considering the limited willingness of consumers to pay higher prices for their products, and the fact that around 90% of companies in the food sector are smes, i believe that a voluntary approach would be the optimal way forward in such cases. voluntary origin labelling is already widespread and, as the commission has pointed out in its report, if used, it would not raise additional operational challenges for producers, while the costs passed on to the consumer would be kept to the minimum.
madam president, i am very pleased that we have adopted today this proposal, this resolution for the mandatory indication of the country of origin on food products and i am also pleased that we have succeeded in defeating the lobby of the food industry, which has been very strong these days. several feasibility reports on mandatory product labelling were published by the european commission in 2015, and these reports showed us that it would cost more for industries to put country of origin labels on products, and that this would lead to higher prices for products, and the higher prices should be borne by consumers. i don't understand why industries can't afford this increase, because it is their obligation to write down which country produced a particular product they put on the market and not consumers to bear this cost. furthermore, as far as romania is concerned - and my colleagues referred to their countries - it is very important for us and for the romanians to know where these products come from. for example, there is a campaign 'buy products made in romania!'. people want to do that, but often the milk in the yogurt or the cheese comes from other countries. we want to know where it's coming from.
in writing. ‒ although the regulation on food information to consumers provides for the need to inform the consumer, the feasibility of this measure is hampered by the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance of the meat. the indication of the origin of meat may constitute a non-tariff barrier, which will affect many european processors, leading to strong anti-competitive influences. the increased cost will also lead to a decrease in consumption with all its negative influences on the economy. for romania's situation, the context is different, as at national level romanian producers use voluntary labelling of the origin of meat, having in the romanian consumer a devotee of romanian products, but at european level romanian preparations that entered the european union late could be eliminated by long-standing and already strong brands on the european market. i am therefore voting against this motion for a resolution, since i believe that tightening the labelling rules would not have a beneficial effect on the market players: consumers, producers, processors.
in writing. ‒ country of origin labelling (cool) was already mandatory for beef and fish under eu law, and was extended to fresh pig, sheep, goat and poultry meat under the food information regulation. during negotiations on the food information regulation, parliament supported s&d amendments calling for cool to be extended to cover all meat, meat in processed foods and milk & dairy products. i believe cool is needed because consumers want to know where their food comes from, especially as it has environmental and animal welfare consequences; it would force producers to get a greater grip on their supply chain and limit the risk of fraud; it would help restore consumer trust in the food industry. cool is very popular with consumers: 90% support cool for meat in processed foods and 84% support cool for milk. it is also supported by many farmers and consumer organisations.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain foods, in order to ensure correct information for consumers and to facilitate the promotion of romanian products on the markets. there is demand for romanian products, whose superior quality is recognised, therefore mandatory country of origin labelling will ensure more effective promotion of these products on the external market. the commission notes that the product labelling system is based on the principle of 'one product, two times', and that the labelling system is based on the principle of 'one product, two times'.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this motion for a resolution that considers it necessary to indicate the origin of milk, whether sold as such or used as an ingredient in dairy products. the same applies for the origin of meat other than beef, pig, sheep, goat and poultry meat.
in writing. ‒ i support this resolution calling for the commission to propose legislation making the indication of country of origin or place of provenance available for drinking milk, and dairy and meat products, including meat in processed food, as it is in the interest of consumers to be able to make informed decisions about food consumption by enhancing transparency. indeed, different surveys clearly indicate that a majority of eu citizens are in favour of labelling meat and dairy products, showing that this resolution is very timely and needed.
in writing. ‒ the european union now has clear rules on the indication of the origin of foodstuffs made from unprocessed meat (beef, pork, sheep, goat or poultry), eggs, fruit and vegetables, fish, honey, virgin and extra virgin olive oil, wine and spirits. at the same time, dairy products and cheeses, as well as processed meat and other types of meat are not regulated to the same extent. this resolution seeks to include these types of food in the regulated category of the mandatory indication of the country of origin. the voluntary rules currently in place at member state level are considered insufficient. at the same time, however, a detail that has been neglected is the increase in the prices of the products concerned following the application of the new regulations. this is not in the interest of european consumers. for these reasons, i believe that the present resolution should take account of several aspects before establishing a binding regulation at european level.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the motion for a resolution on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain foods because it constitutes a non-tariff barrier, which will affect processors, the consequence being transmitted indirectly to national producers. moreover, a legislative proposal from the european commission on this subject will create strong anti-competitive influences and open the way to restricting and tightening national labelling rules, without beneficial effects on market participants such as: consumers, producers, processors. i consider this proposal unrealistic, based on populist demands. farmers and smes will feel a financial pressure that they would not have needed, as the commission's report clearly underlines that consumers are not willing to pay for the labelling of these products. european producers use voluntary labelling, with the indication of the national or even regional origin of the product, already having consumers who are localists, and these movements supporting the idea of mandatory labelling are clearly protectionist and not necessarily in the interest of the consumer.
in writing. ‒ the gender imbalance in parental leave persists even a decade after the member states have transposed the relevant directive. it thus makes it almost impossible to achieve the employment target of 75% for women set in the europe 2020 strategy. career equality for men and women is influenced by parental leave, and policies are needed to support women to enter and remain in the labour market and also to support their reintegration as mothers into the labour market. this agreement takes into account the main demographic, economic and gender equality challenges in the union, highlighting the importance of gender equality and equity in the distribution of family responsibilities between women and men. the importance of adopting family policies to facilitate a gradual return to work is also underlined, given that returning to work after parental leave can be a difficult and stressful situation. i voted in favour of this agreement because i believe that women's participation in the labour market makes a significant economic contribution to the union's economy and also to demographic development.
in writing. ‒ in the last few decades, the european union has adopted two pieces of legislation on leave for family reasons: maternity leave and parental leave. those acts no longer correspond to the economic and social context of the union. the employment target of 75% set in the europe 2020 strategy has already been achieved for men, but is unlikely to be achieved for women (currently 63,5%) by 2020 without measures to support women's participation in the labour market. i voted for equality in the distribution of family responsibilities between women and men.
in writing. ‒ i strongly believe that modernisation of different leaves and their coherence in the eu are necessary to ensure gender equality, increase participation of women in the labour market and ensure work-life balance. fathers should be encouraged to take parental leave, which should be adequately paid with individual and partly non-transferable rights. i support the call for an ambitious proposal on maternity leave and a directive on at least two-week paternity leave. it is fundamental to open up the discussion on necessary work-life balance initiatives and on the disparity of implementation of individual leaves. we must come as soon as possible with coherent legislative as well as non-legislative proposals. moreover, we must continue to push for the revision of maternity leave, and repeat the call for a paternity leave directive. this should be a positive and solid ground for the broader work on labour market conditions for work-life balance following publication of the road-map.
in writing. ‒ the new agreement on parental leave is intended in principle to extend the scope of parental leave to all member states. i support this extension of parental leave. however, this report stigmatises the low use of parental leave by fathers, as it is in line with gender equality in the distribution of family tasks between men and women. this text is therefore too intrusive, since parents must be free to make any arbitrations they wish in the allocation of parental leave. finally, the desire for uniformity in this text conflicts with the competence of the member states in the field of social security benefit schemes. this competence must remain exclusive, in order to respect the sovereign rights of states and guarantee the freedom of individual choice. i therefore voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report in the light of the practical situation of the application of the old framework and the application of directive 2010/18/eu. member states need to act towards gender balance in the issue of parental leave. eurostat shows that only a very small percentage, 2.7%, of men have taken parental leave, which shows a major imbalance in gender equality. through this revision of the framework agreement, member states are invited to find appropriate policies for the reintegration of women after maternity leave, the public sector being an important employer that can balance the overall situation. i agreed to the maternity leave allowance amendment at 100% of the reference salary so that it would not be discouraging for highly qualified parents to want children.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report. it is clear that europe needs to work on policies regarding parental leave in order to enforce gender equality and increase the participation of women in the labour market. at the same time, fathers should also have the opportunity to take parental leave with the appropriate paid leave.
in writing. ‒ over the past few decades, the european union has introduced two pieces of legislation on family leave: maternity leave (introduced as a directive in 1992) and parental leave (introduced as a directive in 1996). although these pieces of legislation were considered modern 20 years ago, they are no longer in line with the economic and social climate of the union of today. i have voted for this report that will assess the implementation of the legislation on parental leave by the different member states and to draw the necessary political conclusions.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament's report on the revised framework agreement on parental leave. the whole union is facing a serious demographic problem, with birth rates falling in most member states. family policies that are fair to men and women could improve women's labour market prospects, improve work-life balance and reduce gender disparities in pay, pensions and lifetime income and have a positive influence on demographic trends. a mixed model, consisting of maternity leave, paternity leave and a joint leave, namely parental leave, allows both parents to take joint decisions in an appropriate manner on how to manage their leave rights, in the best interests of the children and taking into account the characteristics of their workplaces. we encourage member states to adapt their design and eligibility criteria for quality and inclusive education and care for pre-school children to the increasingly diverse forms of work, thus helping parents to meet their professional commitments or find a job, while maintaining a strong focus on the best interests of the child.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it emphasises the right of all employed eu citizens to four months unpaid parental leave. moreover, the report sheds light on the implementation across eu member states of the legislation on parental leave and in doing so finds that fathers are still not using parental leave to an extent that could positively affect and promote gender balance in the work sector and overall gender equality. i therefore support the report’s call for reviewing parental leave legislation in order to set up the right conditions for equal childcare responsibility in the eu.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the arena report on the application of council directive 2010/18/eu of 8 march 2010 implementing the revised framework agreement on parental leave concluded by businesseurope, ueapme, ceep and the etuc and repealing directive 96/34/ec. the european union today faces a number of demographic challenges. therefore, the legislation on parental leave needs to be revised to strengthen the aspects of its duration, remuneration, transferability and scope (since childhood does not end at the age of eight). it is also necessary to review the legislation on maternity leave and european legislation on paternity leave should be adopted as a matter of urgency.
in writing. ‒ although much progress has been made in europe, women still have lower employment rates than men (63.5%) and a factor that contributes to this figure is women’s primary involvement in parenting and house care responsibilities. although, at the european level all employees have the right to four months unpaid parental leave, most member states comply with the minimum requirements for parental leave and fathers make use of very little of these rights. furthermore, women that take parental leave are faced with discrimination upon their return to the labour market and are given less favourable working conditions/contracts. these discrepancies are hard to understand, since the job performed by parents represents a measurable contribution to the economy and parental leaves have long-term benefits for children’s development. i support this framework agreement as i believe that family policies that are fair to both men and women will not only improve women’s prospects in the job market and reduce gender pay gaps, but also bring significant benefits to the economy of the european union.
in writing. ‒ the whole union is facing a serious demographic problem, with declining birth rates, so gender-equitable family policies should improve women's labour market prospects, improve work-life balance. moreover, gender disparities in remuneration, pensions and income should be reduced, thus having a positive influence on the demographic process. the employment rate target of 75% set in the europe 2020 strategy has already been achieved for men, but is unlikely to be achieved for women (currently 63.5%) by 2020. in addition to ensuring gender equality and women's access to the labour market, parental leave should enable parents to fulfil their responsibilities towards their children. i believe it is important to review the implementation of parental leave legislation and to draw the necessary policy conclusions.

in writing. ‒ trafficking in human beings is a violation of fundamental human rights, but also a violation of the personal integrity of the victim, being a serious form of organised crime. the main victims, 80%, are women, with gender being a factor of vulnerability. for women, factors that increase this vulnerability are barriers to access to education, the gender pay gap, unequal access to employment opportunities, underemployment, development strategies that do not focus on gender differences. these types of barriers, particularly those related to education, can influence women's perceptions, and there is a chance that they will not consider these experiences in terms of exploitation, but rather in terms of service providers. in order to have a clear and realistic picture, the union needs to improve its data collection methods, given that there are still a significant number of victims who are not identified, given that trafficking in human beings mainly affects 'hidden populations'. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that prevention is essential in combating trafficking in human beings, and that initiatives to reduce gender inequalities and empower women need to be put into practice.

in writing. ‒ the report assesses how the directive on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims has been implemented across eu member states. trafficking in human beings is a highly gendered phenomenon – 80% of victims being women and girls. the report stresses that member states should, in accordance with this directive, introduce a gender perspective into anti-trafficking measures, but that there is a need for clarification of what this means in practice in order to do so effectively. likewise, the report points to disparity across member states in terms of collecting data on trafficking in human beings due to a lack of common definitions and, in some cases, lack of gender disaggregated data. standardising data collection across the eu is essential for creating policies that can prevent such trafficking. thus, the resolution outlines important gaps in the implementation of the directive which need to be addressed, and it is for this reason that i endorse it.

in writing. ‒ trafficking in human beings (thb) is a large transnational phenomenon that brings profits of approximately usd 150 billion a year. although 80% of victims are girls and women, the majority of whom are being trafficked for sexual exploitation, victims of thb can also be found in other types of legal and illegal activities, such as domestic work, agriculture, criminality and forced marriages. thb is not only a gross violation of fundamental human rights and a crime that undermines the rule of law, but can also cause victims severe physical and psychological harm that could last a lifetime. i believe that the only way to tackle thb in the european union is for member states to better work together in order to prevent people from becoming victims. it is essential to raise awareness of this problem and to empower women and girls in order to reduce their vulnerability. furthermore, i think that coordinated systems of victim identification and victim assistance are due and a common set of guidelines in all member states is needed. i would like to express my support for this resolution as it takes us one step closer to ending trafficking in human beings.
