important. we are talking about a business contract, a business contract between two parties who have to take on both the benefits and the risks equally. in a commercial contract, the banks are the ones who give the credit, they get the interest, they get the insurance but at the same time they have to bear certain risks. it must be very clear to everyone that we are still talking about the effects of the 2008 crisis. we're talking about loans taken by european citizens in 2007-2008 (when interest rates were 10-11%, when house prices were very high), customers who had been paying these loans for years, who gave an advance of 20-30%. basically, the banks have been recovering their credit over the years, but because these customers couldn't pay their credit, the banks took their homes and left them in debt. it's a social phenomenon, it's a very big social tragedy in many countries, like croatia, like romania, that has to be managed by all the factors involved. we have to keep in mind that the root cause of the 2008 financial crisis was primarily banks that, overnight, transformed themselves from commercial banks into investment banks that gave mortgage loans, without taking any security measures, to people who could not pay back those loans in ten lifetimes, just because they could roll them over. this irresponsibility of the banks and this greed of the banking system has cost us all a lot. guess what! the banks were bailed out, the bank managers, the investment managers in those banks kept their financial benefits, but people were left homeless after paying for those homes for years, and not only were they left homeless, but they were still in debt. this situation cannot continue. you say that in croatia a billion is the price that the banks pay for this situation to be regulated and for the banks to take some of the burden of this situation. but i would also be interested in other figures besides this one, commissioner, because one figure is never enough. what is the value of the loans granted during the period? what is the profit rate of the banks in that period? what is the value of the housing stock that the banks have recovered from customers who could no longer pay their housing and how have they recovered it on the real estate market? there are a lot of negative phenomena associated with this crisis of foreign currency loans. there are, for example, in romania, situations where banks have taken the homes of those who could no longer pay, have given them to so-called executors, who have valued them on a black, parallel, real estate market at nothing, and were going to return to certain people who had connections with the banks that had given the original credit. it's a phenomenon that has affected a lot of people. it is a negative phenomenon, which distorts the market economy you refer to. it is not just about the free movement of capital. it's about the responsibility of the financial system, the responsibility of the banks and the measures they take when they have credit. nobody is stopping a bank from taking extra security measures, from letting the customer opt, for example, as it is in romania, for the law that just passed, the act of giving in payment, to opt to give the property back when they can't pay it anymore or to come up with extra guarantees. in romania, a very good law has now been passed, in our view, the law of giving in payment, which says that a citizen, if he can no longer pay his mortgage, his mortgage, should give the property to the bank and close his debt. of course, there was a lot of pressure: that it's not fair, that investors will no longer have predictability, but the situation is very simple. in the loan agreement, in the mortgage agreement, it's very clear that the mortgage covers the loan, the amount of the loan. therefore, when the property is returned to the bank, it is closed. the debt is closed. you say the banks are suffering very large losses. what is the loss, when an ordinary man pays 30% upfront, pays interest and installments for years, covering the difference in money, and at some point, he can't pay it back, after a year, two, three? the bank keeps the advance, the bank keeps the interest paid, and the bank keeps the property. what the loss of the bank is, i'm not very clear. i think there should be a clear contract, where everyone bears both the benefits and the costs of this contract, and the banks should remain commercial banks, never again be investment banks.

in writing. two issues are central to the discussion of virtual currencies. first, virtual currencies are a necessity of the present in which we live. because of their ease of use, alongside our traditional currencies, these virtual currencies are being used by more and more citizens around the world. they offer the advantage of anonymity of transactions and an increased degree of security of personal data. the second aspect concerns the legality of these currencies, i.e. the creation of a coherent legislative framework, adapted both to the present and to the future. currently, virtual currencies do not meet many legislative criteria, which makes it impossible to legalize them at present. however, even without existing legislation, transactions with virtual currencies are becoming easier and their use is growing, which is why we are forced to prepare a set of possible solutions to be discussed. the fluid, non-national nature of this type of currency and the inability of the competent institutions to monitor the flow of financial transactions force us to constantly reassess both the benefits and the disadvantages of these instruments. given the innovative dimension of virtual currencies, how do we respond to market demand in a regulated manner? more specifically, do we even know what steps we need to take to ensure smooth, undistorted regulation of this area?

madam president, european citizens expect the european union to have rules and standards to protect them. one example is the health crisis facing romania, as the country's third largest producer of disinfectants has diluted its products sold to 300 hospitals in romania. we're talking about tens of thousands of possible medical problems that this situation generates. it's extremely worrying, especially since they could have been avoided if we had proper legislation and serious controls in hospitals. the crisis romania is facing could happen in any other european country at any time, in the absence of firm measures applicable to all health systems. i therefore call on the european forums to develop a set of clear rules, applicable to all member states, so that such situations are no longer possible in any european health system. i believe that the european union needs to have more powers in the field of health in order to be able to adequately finance this area and support the development of a quality health system in all member states, including in my country, romania.

in writing. the single market is the backbone of european economic integration. the strategy for developing the single market is therefore welcome. efforts must focus on two priorities: removing any barriers to the free movement of goods, services, capital and labour; and stopping corruption and abusive practices of profit shifting from one country to another, as trade in intangibles is increasing. we must recognise that the single market is still fragmented for essential products and services such as electricity and natural gas, for which investment in the necessary connections is lagging. the european union also still adopts many regulations that reduce the competitiveness of european companies, especially small and medium-sized ones. the abusive transfer of profits from one country to another must be stopped as soon as possible, so as not to further destroy citizens' trust in the rule of law and in the state authorities.
in writing. ‒ virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology have a positive impact on citizens' well-being by helping to create secure, user-friendly systems with low transaction and operational costs, while ensuring privacy. the commission will also assess the impact of the new rules on the financial sector, including the impact of the new rules on the financial sector, on the financial sector's ability to provide financial services and on the impact of the new rules on the financial sector's ability to provide financial services. ledger technology facilitates the decentralised, fast, resilient recording of any type of transaction along with the history of previous transactions. it also provides for the possibility of merging traditional and innovative types of payment instruments into a single application, which would contribute to the development of electronic commerce and the deepening of the single market. smart regulation in this area to support innovation requires the development of regulatory capacity in technical expertise. i voted in favour of this report because i believe it is a timely report that will help to improve the level of financial well-being of citizens and also lead to the strengthening of the single market.
in writing. ‒ still in its infancy, the virtual currency industry has seen rapid development due to the potential of distributed ledger technology to accelerate, decentralise, automate and standardise data-driven processes, reducing the costs of asset transfer and ledger management. this technology can contribute positively to the well-being of citizens and to the economic development of member states by promoting financial inclusion and facilitating access to finance across a wide range of industries and services in both the public and private sectors. however, regulation and the creation of a robust legal framework have not kept pace with the rapid development of this innovative technology, increasing the risks of its use for illicit purposes. promoting operational transparency and developing effective regulatory solutions to ensure consumer protection, resilience and reliability of the system architecture are necessary to reduce uncertainty related to the evolution of this area and the vulnerability of users. i voted in favour of the report on virtual currencies, calling on the european commission to develop a coherent, comprehensive strategy to identify the benefits and risks of this technology and to strengthen regulatory capacity to oversee and ensure the security of markets and consumers.
in writing. – i welcome and support the inclusion in the report of a commission task force on virtual currencies, which would propose any necessary legislation to regulate the sector and to update current legislation, e.g. the money laundering directive/payment services directive. also, i support the suggestion to explore the promotion of an electronic wallet. the virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology have the potential to contribute positively to citizens’ welfare and economic development, including in the financial sector. however, virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology schemes entail risks which need to be addressed appropriately so as to enhance their trustworthiness. addressing these risks will require enhanced regulatory capacity, including technical expertise, and the development of a sound legal framework that keeps up with innovation, ensuring a timely and proportionate response if and when the use of some distributed ledger technology applications becomes systemically relevant. i also agree with precautionary monitoring instead of pre-emptive regulation in order to avoid stifling innovation. lastly, i support the development by the commission, in cooperation with the member states and the virtual currencies industry, of guidelines with the aim of guaranteeing that correct, clear and complete information is provided for existing and future virtual currency users.
in writing. ‒ the bitcoin was launched seven years ago; however it has not yet reached a critical mass and does not have the nature of a highly liquid asset. i believe that the underlying innovation, distributed ledger technology (dlt), will have a significant impact on the financial sector. the new technologies have the potential to contribute positively to consumer welfare and economic development, as well as bringing changes to the banking sector. however, some significant risks have already become apparent, like the abuse of certain applications for criminal conduct, including money laundering and terrorist financing. it is better to have precautionary monitoring instead of pre-emptive regulation.
in writing. ‒ the definition of virtual currency (vc) appeared in 2012 drafted by the european central bank as ‘a type of unregulated, digital money, which is issued and usually controlled by its developers, and used and accepted among the members of a specific virtual community’. distributed ledger technology (dlt) will enable a decentralised, resilient, rapid and secure means of recording transactions of any sort together with the history of previous transactions. i voted for this report that will introduce smart regulation of the dlt.
in writing. ‒ virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology have the potential to contribute positively to citizens' well-being and economic development, including in the financial sector. to date, no universally applicable definition has been formulated, but virtual currencies are sometimes referred to as 'electronic money' and are considered by the european banking authority (eba) to be a digital representation of a value that is not issued by a central bank or public authority, is not necessarily linked to a fiat currency, but is accepted by natural or legal persons as a means of payment and can be transferred, stored or traded electronically. i stress the importance of consumer awareness, transparency and trust in the use of virtual currencies. the commission should develop, in cooperation with member states and the virtual currency industry, guidelines to ensure that existing and future users of virtual currencies are provided with accurate, clear and complete information to enable them to make an informed choice, thereby increasing the transparency of virtual currency systems as regards how they are organised and used and how they differ from regulated and supervised payment systems from a consumer protection perspective.
in writing. ‒ a commission task force should be set up to monitor developments in virtual currencies and inform any necessary legislative proposals in this area. virtual currencies have implications for money laundering and other important issues related to monetary regulation, and this calls for a dedicated task force to provide the necessary analysis and advice.
in writing. ‒ information technologies have made remarkable progress in recent years, fundamentally changing our daily lives. such progress is also the emergence of virtual currencies that allow transactions to be carried out in information networks without the need to use national or regional currencies. the advantages of this procedure are the facilitation of financial transactions, mainly by reducing additional costs, but also the monitoring of financial flows, the increase of consumption and the fight against tax evasion. however, these transactions are currently taxed at an exaggerated level, which is affecting the development and expansion of the virtual currency sector. at the same time, there are also risks that this type of operation could be used by organised crime or terrorist groups for money laundering activities. all these problems could be solved much more effectively, however, by regulating the new field more carefully, using appropriate technologies (distributed ledger technology) proportionately and avoiding bureaucratization. this report recommends the creation of a horizontal working group on distributed ledger technology to develop smart regulation to encourage innovation and ensure integrity. it is a laudable initiative and i therefore support the adoption of this report.

in writing. ‒ the refugee crisis affecting the european union over the last year has had a significant impact on certain countries, which have had to take in more refugees than usual. one of these countries is sweden, where the number of refugees has increased exponentially in recent times, making it one of the favourite targets of asylum seekers. in particular, the number of refugees arriving in sweden increased by 60% between 2015 and 2016, with 39 055 asylum applications in october 2015 alone. in addition, in march 2016, the number of requests increased to 170 104, of which 73 331 were children, 36 181 were unaccompanied minors. faced with this influx, sweden has asked for the commission's support to be exempted from the proposed eu-wide relocation scheme for at least one year. the commission agreed to this temporary measure to allow sweden to provide asylum seekers with adequate access to healthcare, decent housing and education, in line with eu rules in this area. however, given the difficult situation currently faced by greece and italy, the exemption of sweden from the relocation scheme constitutes discrimination between member states. i therefore agree with the rejection of the commission's decision.
in writing. ‒ the development of the information society and electronic commerce, as well as the development of the interception capabilities of intelligence agencies, have led to an exponential increase in data transfers worldwide, but at the same time to an increase in the risks of misuse of this data. this type of abusive communication not only acts as a brake on the development of electronic commerce by undermining consumer confidence, but also sometimes constitutes a violation of the rights and freedoms of citizens and, in particular, a violation of the right to privacy. the commission has also concluded that the us privacy shield is not a sufficient safeguard against the unlawful conduct of third parties. i voted in favour of the resolution on transatlantic data flows because i believe that it is very beneficial for the eu countries, as the development of electronic commerce is essential for better cooperation between countries and, not least, for the development of the eu.
in writing. ‒ i believe it is fundamental to have clear and detailed information concerning the looming adoption by the commission of the adequacy decision concerning personal data transfers to the united states, called the privacy shield. however, as the text is now, it does not fulfil the criteria laid down for adequacy decisions in the eu data protection law, the court jurisprudence and the fundamental rights charter. the redress mechanism for individuals under the privacy shield is too complex and difficult to use and would therefore render itself ineffective. moreover, neither the us federal trade commission nor the us department of commerce nor the providers of alternative dispute resolution have investigatory powers essentially equivalent to those of european data protection supervisory authorities. i welcome such a regime with the us, but i believe it needs to respect the new data protection acquis of the eu, court jurisprudence, the fundamental rights charter and be completely legally watertight.
in writing. ‒ the privacy shield decision, adopted by the commission, is an improvement to the safe habour decision. however, many changes are necessary to since the text, as it is, does not fulfil the criteria laid down for adequacy decisions in the eu data protection law, the court jurisprudence and the fundamental rights charter.
in writing. ‒ this joint motion for a resolution on transatlantic data flows is an excellent example of the political parties of this house working together. while we recognise and welcome the commission and the us administration’s efforts to reach an agreement, some concerns remain especially in relation to bulk data collection, access to data by the us authorities, a very complex redress mechanism and the role of the ombudsman. through this resolution we urge the commission to deal with these issues as soon as possible because it hinders commercial exchanges with one of our largest trade and investment partners. additionally, it is necessary to submit the agreement on transatlantic data flows to periodical reviews particularly in light of the new general data protection regulation, which will apply as of 2018. i endorsed this resolution that sent a clear but also reasonable and constructive message to the commission, to our us partners and to all member states.
in writing. ‒ the european commission and the united states have agreed on a new framework for transatlantic data flows: the eu-us privacy shield. i have voted for this motion for a resolution that highlights the importance of the privacy shield framework enabling member states to examine and investigate claims related to the protection of the rights to privacy and family life under the eu charter of fundamental rights.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the right to privacy of our personal data is a hard-earned asset, a living guarantee of our status as european citizens, residents of democratic states. in a delicate security context, where the issue of terrorist threats is a daily reality, the transfer of relevant data between states is crucial. in this context, it is of particular importance that the exchange of information be regulated as clearly as possible by the adopted report, especially as we are dealing with a data flow that ensures close commercial and legal links in order to ensure economic development and the safety of citizens. i also appreciate that the report takes into account the 'privacy shield' mechanism which must meet international human rights standards.
in writing. ‒ the so-called privacy shield has been called into question in the same ways its predecessor, the safe harbour decision was. serious issues about fundamental rights and data protection law are at stake here. any agreement made with third countries must fully respect, and not undermine, the provisions of existing eu law.
in writing. ‒ information has become a vital component of today's society, especially in a context where most of our decisions are based on how well informed we are. the decisive role of information is also highlighted by the importance of information structures in ensuring global security. the rise of global terrorism has raised the issue of collaboration between relevant actors in the information field. the most relevant case in this respect is the cooperation between the european union and the united states in the field of transfers of personal data. the initial agreement between the two parties in this sensitive area, also known as the 'safe area', was rejected by the court of justice of the european union as not complying with european standards for the protection of personal data and privacy. the adoption of a new agreement, known as the 'privacy shield', has shifted the focus somewhat, but there are still issues with respect to compliance with the standards of the european data protection supervisor. in these circumstances, the agreement needs to be amended to comply with european law, the case law of the court of justice of the eu and the charter of fundamental rights. for this reason i support the rejection of this resolution, in order to clarify outstanding issues concerning the legitimate rights of european citizens.
mr president, the classic centralized energy system is a thing of the past. we're moving towards a decentralized, flexible, efficient, renewable energy-based system. the commission's communication on the new agreement for energy consumers is based on three pillars: better information for consumers to consume less, both energy and money; also the second pillar: more choice for consumers between heating options, for example, and the third pillar: maintaining the highest level of consumer protection. i support this report. we need to look at how we define energy poverty at union level, given that each country has different energy needs, given that the minimum income per capita differs from one country to another, or given that countries define the idea of reasonable costs differently. i hope that we will find a resolution, as i said, of energy poverty at union level that will bring us to implement this agreement.
in writing. ‒ this report focuses exclusively on household energy consumers and industrial consumers should be treated in a completely different context. the ongoing energy transition is leading to a shift from an energy system based on traditional centralised generation to a more decentralised, energy-efficient, but also more flexible and based largely on renewable energy sources. as regards the costs of switching to a new market structure in certain member states, the report draws the attention of the european commission and invites it to take these costs into account in terms of accessibility and competitiveness, with the ultimate objective of an economy based on 100% renewable energy sources. i voted in favour of the report on 'new benefits for energy consumers' because i believe that support for new types of energy, in particular renewable energy, is necessary for much better economic development both in the member states and in the eu.
in writing. ‒ taking into account all the technological developments that have taken place in recent years and the objective of having an economy based on 100% renewable energy sources that europe proposes, i support this report which highlights the need for a new organisation of the energy market. the european union must be a model for the world in making the internal energy market more efficient and in pursuing a forward-looking climate change policy. the main beneficiaries of this new energy policy must be citizens, who, through access to new technologies, will be able to reduce their bills and actively participate in the market through the efficient management of energy consumption. installing heating controls and thermostats can have a significant impact on energy consumption, but only if coupled with a serious housing rehabilitation project that many european cities need. people will not only save money, but they will make a significant contribution to reducing energy consumption.
in writing. ‒ as volatility in energy costs can have major repercussions on consumers, it is important that the european union and the member states have a firm policy to decentralise energy systems and increase efficiency and flexibility through the diversification of resources. in addition, improving and strengthening connections with member states and partner countries should be a priority for the development of bi-directional flows at each cross-border interconnection. reducing monopoly and encouraging citizens' participation, individually or collectively, in the energy market can contribute to the eradication of energy poverty and to consumer protection through the provision of stable, sustainable, affordable energy and energy-efficient products, services and buildings. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the effects of instability in energy policies are felt at the level of the well-being of european citizens. i have thus expressed the need to put the citizen at the centre of european energy policies, by developing functional energy systems based on collaboration between local authorities, municipalities and citizens.

in writing. ‒ the achievement of the energy union is one of the european union's objectives for the period ahead. however, we must not forget that the main beneficiaries of this project must be european citizens. energy suppliers currently charge high prices at national level because the common energy market has not yet been achieved and because they still benefit from the high concentration of national markets. this keeps european consumers captive to large energy monopolies, without the possibility to switch suppliers and benefit from such better prices. this leads to the idea that there is a 'energy poverty' at european level, which must be tackled by firm action by the european institutions. a commission action plan is needed to combat this negative phenomenon at union level and to encourage energy efficiency in buildings. in addition, small unconventional energy producers should not be discriminated against against against large producers within member states. the european union must be a shield for consumers against the abuses of the big energy producers and suppliers. that is why i support this necessary initiative.

mr president, the creation of the single market was made possible by the existence of a common objective, namely the elimination of barriers to trade. we have non-tariff barriers in the european union at the moment, which result in a burden or a cost for companies that want to enter the market, they bear most of these barriers; and i am referring to the complexity of the current vat regime, the tax agreements between some member states and multinational companies, all of which can be considered non-tariff barriers, unjustified and costing the citizen a lot because the citizen pays more for goods and services. the lack of information on the quality of support services and online procedures, for example, are again non-tariff barriers. they also represent barriers to competitiveness in each member state and in the union's single market. the completion of the single market for the free movement of goods and services, as well as for public procurement and the digital economy, is estimated to bring in over eur 600 billion.
in writing. ‒ a significant achievement of the eu is the creation of the single market, which was made possible by cooperation and a shared goal of removing barriers to trade. tariff barriers were successfully removed 50 years ago, but the challenge to remove non-tariff barriers continues and is what drives single market initiatives today. in many respects, the approach is consistent with actions taken in international trade, and while tariff barriers are easy to remove, the removal of non-tariff barriers is the most difficult challenge. the removal of non-tariff barriers will directly help eu businesses, with consumers as the ultimate beneficiaries. the removal of this barrier is therefore in the interest of all member states and of the european parliament. i voted in favour of the report on non-tariff barriers in the single market because i believe that it is necessary to remove the non-tariff barrier as soon as possible in order to be able to support businesses, but in particular to be able to benefit consumers throughout europe.
in writing. ‒ in 1992, the european union launched the concept of the 'single market', removing non-tariff barriers to trade in goods and opening up trade in services within the union. non-tariff barriers are measures or policies that restrict trade and have a similar effect on tariffs. today, the single market for services accounts for 70% of the european economy and only 20% of intra-eu trade, with the free movement of goods and services still hampered by non-tariff barriers. the removal of trade barriers will stimulate the economies of the participating countries by increasing export earnings and increasing the variety of products and services offered to consumers at lower prices as a result of competition from imports. we need greater involvement of member states in identifying areas where priority action is needed to maintain and develop the single market. i support this report because i believe that the removal of non-tariff barriers will help eu businesses, will boost the european economy and of course the ultimate beneficiaries will be consumers.
in writing. ‒ although the launch of the single market should have led to the abolition of unjustified tariff and non-tariff barriers, it is noted that they continue to exist in various forms. operational rules applied to suppliers of products and services may unduly or disproportionately restrict the activity of those operators, leading to de facto discrimination against them. in addition, non-tariff barriers that are not justified by proportionality, consumer protection, the environment or workers' rights create market gaps that can be to the detriment of citizens, whose access to certain goods and services becomes unaffordable. without pursuing the aim of reducing market regulation, it is necessary to harmonise those national rules and make information on divergent national regulatory requirements accessible through the development of e-governance systems. since uniform application at european level is a sine qua non criterion for the proper functioning of the market and the mobility of professionals, early examination by the european commission of eu legislative and policy action in emerging areas is necessary. i voted in favour of this report to reiterate the importance of solidarity in the framework of the european joint initiative, which, under article 3 teu, balances economic freedoms and social policies, affirming the union's status as a 'social market economy' that 'promotes social justice and protection'.
in writing. ‒ an insufficient or incorrect application of existing eu rules still hinders intra-eu trade and constitutes an obstacle to growth. however, a clear distinction has to be made between non—tariff barriers and other rules both at eu and member states level that are lawfully in place and which serve a public policy objective. i welcome achievement that we managed to introduce in the report, such as the balanced definition of non-tariff barriers as applied to the internal market, the clear recognition of the full respect of the right to regulate in the public interest, a balanced reference to the so-called ‘gold-plating’, which does not affect the right to lawfully adopt progressive legislation in case of minimum harmonisation directives, and finally the explicit mention of the importance of public services and the fact that related legislation does not constitute a non-tariff barriers.
in writing. ‒ this report on non-tariff barriers in the single market applies the external trade concept on ntb inside the eu, looking at remaining obstacles to the completion of the single market.
in writing. ‒ i have abstained in the vote on this report on non-tariff barriers in the single market.
in writing. ‒ businesses and citizens face major obstacles to cross-border activities in the single market due to the lack of availability and quality of information, support services and online procedures, which lead to a considerable administrative burden and significant compliance costs. the monitoring of barriers and costs is fragmented and unsystematic, and there is a lack of quantification and clear identification of barriers and costs, which makes it difficult to prioritise measures. member states should regard the single market as a common initiative to be maintained in a coordinated and collective manner and as a condition for increasing the competitiveness of the eu economy. the ultimate burden of unjustified non-tariff barriers is borne by consumers, as new entities are denied access to the internal markets and face high costs, lower quality and a reduced range of options.
in writing. ‒ i support this resolution because it stresses member states protectionism regarding trade competition and lack of consistent enforcement of existing regulation as key obstacles, preventing the single market from becoming fully integrated. that is not to say that non-tariff barriers (ntbs) should be completely removed, as the resolution rightly states, however, it remains important to identify the cases in which ntbs are inflexible, discriminatory or work against the principles of proportionality. indeed, removal of some ntbs would significantly benefit eu consumers who would have access to cheaper and greater variety of goods and services.
in writing. ‒ non-tariff barriers are measures to free trade, composed of instruments such as licences, quotas, standards and other administrative and bureaucratic measures designed to regulate flows in accordance with the interests of an economic actor. the completion of the european union's single market has led to the removal of tariff barriers between member states, but non-tariff barriers continue to represent important obstacles to intra-community trade flows. this is affecting economic growth and the interests of european consumers. at the same time, however, it is true that a number of such barriers derive from the principle of subsidiarity itself, which allows regulation at different levels, including national and local, through public policy and in the public interest. some of these regulations may constitute temporary non-tariff barriers in an attempt to protect the interests of citizens of certain member states. respect for the rights of workers cannot be included in the category of non-tariff barriers. they must not, however, become protectionist measures that are opposed to the concept of the single market. member states should work together to gradually harmonise their practices, as far as possible, with a view to ensuring the prosperity of their citizens.
in writing. the report on non-tariff barriers in the single market finds that, despite the elimination of tariff barriers on 1 july 1968, the free movement of goods and services in the single market has continued to be affected by non-tariff barriers, such as technical rules and regulatory and non-national regulatory requirements applying to suppliers of products, service providers and conditions of service or bureaucracy. i voted for this report which considers that non-tariff barriers are a disproportionate or discriminatory regulatory action, especially for new firms wishing to enter the single market. the rapporteur stresses that in particular the lack of implementation and divergent application of the services directive constitute obstacles to the single market and calls on the commission to remove them.

in writing. ‒ the challenges of contemporary society demonstrate the need for constant adjustment and rethinking of the european strategy so that the social economy is a genuine factor of economic and social development in europe. striking a balance between the market economy and social and environmental protection mechanisms could have the effect of tackling unemployment, poverty, inequalities, social exclusion and wage dumping. at the same time, the european single market, by promoting respect for fundamental social rights, legal mobility and improved working and living conditions, will be an important element of solidarity and cooperation between member states. without aiming at total market liberalisation, both unjustified barriers and justified barriers should be removed and information on them centralised in order to further the achievement of a fair single market as a common good of all citizens, workers, economic operators and member states. i voted in favour of this report because i wanted to reiterate the importance of striking a balance between fundamental economic and social rights. economic growth and the promotion of quality jobs must aim at the rapid achievement of a social market economy based on knowledge and sustainable growth, while maintaining an effective system of social protection.

sustainable development goals of last year mark a welcome shift from a focus on diseases to a more integrated approach to addressing people’s health needs. if we want to end aids and many other diseases, we must help third countries develop the capacity to provide basic healthcare, clean water and sanitation to all their citizens. this needs to be a collaborative effort. domestic funding for this purpose, particularly in middle-income countries, also needs to be increased. in the eu we have made good progress: they have in particular eliminated mother-to-child transmission, and thus exposure of children to hiv/aids. new infections are declining. treatment coverage and access to care is high. a rather significant outstanding challenge remains: over 300 000 people in the eu need lifelong treatment; 30 000 people still get infected every year. even so, hiv can be prevented. hiv/aids treatment costs billions of euros. the commission works closely with member states and civil society to strengthen prevention, improve testing and support universal access to treatment and care. we must reach out in particular to eastern europe and central asia, where the epidemic is still on the rise. again, this needs to be a collaborative effort. tailor—made action for each of the most affected countries needs to be intensified.
on behalf of the epp group. mr president, i welcome the presence of the commissioner in the plenary and share many of the views he has expressed. the new report by the united nations secretary-general, 'accelerating the response to end the aids epidemic', warns that the major gains made in the last 15 years in the fight against this threat to public health could be lost if no action is taken in the next five years. the report also urges states to respond by increasing investment and strengthening action, particularly in the area of prevention. i remind you that since the beginning of the epidemic, nearly 71 million people have been infected with the hiv virus, half of whom have died over the years because of lack of timely detection, treatment or proper care. there has been encouraging progress, especially since 2011. access to antiretroviral treatment has been provided to over 15 million people living with hiv, leading to significant increases in life expectancy, decreased deaths and access to treatment. however, the impact of social factors such as poverty, inequality and discrimination, especially among vulnerable populations, should not be overlooked. and when i say 'vulnerable population' i mean the categories of people who should no longer suffer from discrimination and, of course, i mean children first. statistics show that between 2000 and 2014, their numbers decreased, but discrepancies still exist, especially in developing countries. i think we need to have a much more ambitious plan of action, we need to target vulnerable populations, we need to create a social protection tool, we need to ensure that people living with hiv have access to lifelong treatment and adequate health care.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would first like to thank the other political groups for the excellent cooperation we have had and commissioner andriukaitis for being with us today to discuss the policy coherence of the union for development (udp). cpd is a subject that is both very important, complex and poorly understood. it is about the coherence of all our policies, and so it is tempting to want to deal with everything. it seems to me that parliament's report has not succumbed to this temptation and has tried to focus on a few key elements, both to move the debate forward and to contribute to the implementation of the cpd. within the union, coherence is very important: the different institutions want to be consistent with each other; we also want our policies to be consistent with each other. the most difficult question is how to implement this coherence in the service of development so that we do not undo on the one hand what we are doing on the other. the commission's 2015 report is positive: there has been considerable progress, which of course needs to be both continued and strengthened. in the resolution of parliament we have concentrated on two essential points. firstly, there is the interaction between the cpd and the 2030 development agenda. while other international actors have already started to think deeply about the transformation of the cpd into 'policy coherence for sustainable development', the european union has yet to adopt a clear position on this point. the drafting of this report and the workshop we organised were an opportunity for parliament to launch this process of reflection. the fact that the european commission is embarking on a similar process could call into question the very principle of the dpc and the biennial report, placing it in a broader perspective. designing the cpd as part of the 2030 development agenda also means rethinking the development goals at the global level to move away from this donor-receiver approach and towards goals that apply to all. the concept of cpd is still unknown at international level. we will not succeed in integrating cpd into the sustainable development goals if the other key development actors - the us, japan, brics - do not join in this effort. the union has a key role to play. it must continue to promote the universalisation of the concept of dpc among our partners. the european parliament must be involved in this process, as it is now an important player in the dpc. the second crucial element in this year's report is to find ways of improving the use and effectiveness of the instruments of the cpd. i think it is important to stress that the implementation of the cpd is still laborious, but it should also not be forgotten that it is a complex exercise. i did not call for the creation of new instruments for the dpc, because the necessary instruments already exist. but we must find a way of using these tools in the most consistent and effective way possible. this requires that the responsibilities for implementing the cpd are clear and unquestionable. the only way to give the dpc a decisive boost is to put it on the agenda of a european summit. i know that the idea may be laughable, but a few years ago, people also laughed at the idea of organising a european defence summit. if we are to be serious about the progress of the cpd, it must be discussed at the highest political level. a european summit would also create a process of reflection at interinstitutional and member state level. this summit would provide clear guidance on how to operationalize the cpd. it must be able to extricate itself from the development bubble in order to exist in other areas. it is not about development, it is about coordinating all other policies for development. so we need to think about cpd differently. since the 2013 report, new instruments have been created. i am thinking in particular of the contribution of the european union delegations to the biennial report. this exercise is a positive development, which should be extended to all delegations. in addition, given the extremely important role that heads of union delegations can play in the implementation of the spc on the ground, this issue should be included in the agenda of the annual meeting of heads of delegations in brussels. delegations have a global view of the union's policies in a given country and can therefore help us to identify inconsistencies and how to correct them. of course, i cannot mention here all the instruments of the cpd and how to improve them. we still have a lot of work to do in the area of impact studies, for example, which are not carried out systematically. but i also want to say that some of the instruments are working, and very well. i am thinking in particular of joint programming, which includes not only all the activities of the union but also the activities of the member states, to ensure greater coherence. i cannot, of course, go into all the priority areas of action in the report. should the priorities of the cpd be changed or added to? i think we will be able to answer this question once we have started the process of reflection in the framework of the implementation of the 2030 development agenda. finally, i would like to add that i wanted to emphasize this year the importance of the cpd in the union's external policy. the refugee crisis and the destabilisation facing the union in its neighbourhood have called into question its very foundations, in particular solidarity and free movement. external action is the area on which the dpc must concentrate. stabilizing our neighborhood must therefore be a top priority. we have the comprehensive approach, which is an ideal instrument for the cpd, and this approach should be further strengthened with the adoption of the comprehensive strategy this month. we must make this instrument the hallmark of the european union's external action. the comprehensive approach, when properly implemented, should also enable us to prevent crises and ensure an effective transition between a military or civilian operation and the implementation of other instruments to pursue progress on the ground. the sahel is a good example. when the union mobilizes all its tools in a region facing poverty, internal conflict and radicalisation, it can make a difference.
mr president, nowadays it is more than obvious that a coherent development policy is needed in order to successfully tackle the most urgent social problems across the globe and, what is more, to achieve peaceful, just and inclusive societies. the challenges of the past years have already shown us that building synergies between different eu policies leads to improved results. however, a coherent policy management also demands a global framework which can deal with the complexity of the task, to ensure coherence between many factors: global goals and national contexts; international agendas and processes; and between economic, social and environmental policies. the eu and its global partners have to constantly support an approach based on collaboration, mutual accountability and human rights, in order to ensure that economic, environmental and social progress will be sustainable.

rapporteur. – madam president, first of all, i would like to thank all of the shadow rapporteurs who contributed to this report on international financial reporting standards (ifrs). it is the first time that the european parliament presents its strategic view on the issue of ifrs. these standards are the bedrock of all investment decisions in the global capital markets, and of the evaluation of company management on behalf of its shareholders. for over a year, we have held many debates, seminars and hearings, with different stakeholders, standard setters, academics and experts. let me focus on the main points of this report. we think that the concept of public good for the ifrs should be clarified, as well as the potential conflict between the private nature of the iasb, the standard setter, and the public good nature of the ifrs that are applied today in more than 110 countries and jurisdictions. there are differences between how we in the european union understand the concept of true and fair view, the principles of prudence and stewardship, which are the basis of accounting standards, and the accounting setters view on this concept and principle. we insist on the need for an impact assessment for every new accounting standard or change of a current accounting standard. we think about the future of efrag, the private technical advisor of the european commission in the process of ifrs endorsement in the european union, and about the possibility on the long-term to transform efrag into a european agency. we also ask for the strengthening of the role of the european parliament, both in the process of setting accounting standards and in the endorsement process of ifrs in the european union.

in writing. ‒ illicit trade in tobacco products is an activity with a negative impact on both public health and revenues to state budgets. smuggling of cigarettes undermines tobacco control policies, favouring access to tobacco products at lower prices which generates significant revenue losses for the european union, given that the related taxes and customs duties are not paid. as a result, the union and its member states are losing more than eur 10 billion annually. the protocol to the who framework convention includes a complex set of measures, rules and policies to combat illicit trade in tobacco products, by pursuing a safer process in the tobacco supply chain, by creating a global traceability and tracing system. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that ensuring the highest standards of public health protection is paramount and that enhanced international cooperation is needed to combat illicit trade in tobacco products.
in writing. ‒ the world health organisation’s protocol on the illicit trade in tobacco products is designed to eliminate the producing, shipping, receiving, being in possession of, distributing, selling or buying of illicit tobacco. this will be achieved by targeting the supply chain, through the creation of an international tracking and tracing system, strengthening licensing and record-keeping requirements, and increasing the regulation of sales and international transit. to curb the existing illicit trade, the protocol will introduce dissuasive law enforcement measures and enhance international cooperation. since, tobacco products have severe public health impacts worldwide and are toxic, mutagenic, carcinogenic and addictive, i consider it of the utmost importance to ensure that there will be no further increase in consumption of tobacco products and so i vote for the recommendation that the european union should immediately ratify this protocol. decreasing the availability, affordability or attractiveness of tobacco products, and by further developing stricter tobacco control, the european union can better protect health, healthcare systems and national budgets from the damage caused by tobacco consumption.
in writing. ‒ the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control is the first global health treaty. illicit trade in tobacco products is a criminal activity with serious public health implications. the eu estimates that member states lose around €10 billion a year in taxes and duties due to this trade. this means that about 1 out of 10 cigarettes is sold illegally. i voted for the establishment of an effective global regime to combat this phenomenon which affects the lives of european citizens.
in writing. ‒ in accordance with council decisions 2013/744/eu and 2013/745/eu, the protocol to eliminate illicit trade in tobacco products to the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control was signed on 20 december 2013, subject to its conclusion at a later date. the aim of the protocol is the elimination of all forms of illicit trade. in order to address this, the protocol targets the supply chain of tobacco products via a series of measures by governments: creation of a global tracking and tracing regime and establishment of a global information sharing point. the protocol will establish offences, address liability and seizure payments as well and the disposal of confiscated products. the protocol concedes the irreconcilable conflict between the tobacco’s industry’s interests and public health’s interests. i voted in favour of the conclusion of this protocol.

in writing. ‒ the use of tobacco products is a practice that poses serious risks to the health of citizens. the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control (who fctc) is the first international framework document to address the tobacco epidemic, adopted in 2005. smuggling of cigarettes produced outside the eu is a criminal activity that undermines control policies and brings huge financial losses due to non-payment of taxes and customs duties, estimated at over eur 90 billion per year. the protocol to eliminate illicit trade in tobacco products was adopted on the basis of the ccct in november 2012 and is the only multilateral regulatory initiative in this field. however, its entry into force is conditional on its ratification by 40 states, and eu-wide ratification would be an important step in this direction. the protocol aims to establish a global system for tracing and tracing tobacco products, licensing, record-keeping, regulating internet sales, defining offences and mutual customs administrative assistance. i believe that ratification of this protocol will help to combat the trafficking of tobacco products and to protect the health of european citizens.

in writing. ‒ international regulatory cooperation is vital to the automobile trade and helps to ensure common technical standards in road transport. the recent emission scandals involving the car industry highlight the urgent need to improve implementation and monitoring of regulations, including at international level, in order to ensure safety and performance for consumers and deliver genuine environmental benefits.
in writing. ‒ the automotive industry and related sectors are an important part of the european union's economy, providing jobs for 12 million people and representing 4% of eu gdp. globally, eu member states are among the world's leading automobile producers, with a significant contribution to research and development and to the euro area trade balance. in this context, it is in the eu's interest to support the removal of barriers to trade, regulatory cooperation and the interconnection of world markets. in this way, common rules will promote transparency, efficiency and competition in the economic environment, while ensuring the protection of health and safety. the global regulatory framework offered by the un economic commission for europe (unece) contributes to technological harmonisation, to reducing production and certification costs and to avoiding administrative duplication. support for revision 3 of the unece agreement concerning the adoption of uniform specifications for wheeled vehicles and the conditions for the mutual recognition of approvals granted on the basis of these specifications is an essential condition for supporting the european automotive industry and i therefore consider that the adoption of the present recommendation is necessary.
in writing. ‒ the trade agreement between the european union and its member states, of the one part, and colombia and peru, of the other part, was signed in brussels on 26 june 2012 and, with the accession of croatia, it will be allowed to participate in the agreement in question. it has a positive impact in the two states, colombia and peru, fostering socio-economic development, integration into the global economy and an increase in the quality of life. as a result, the agreement includes a number of provisions on the origin of goods, technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, competition, intellectual property and public procurement with a view to strengthening a transparent partnership based on mutual benefits. it is necessary to take legal measures to allow croatia to participate in the eu-colombia and peru free trade agreement in order to ensure a level playing field and fairness for all member states, which is why i voted in favour of this agreement.

in writing. ‒ enhanced cooperation on international matrimonial property regimes is a decision taken as a result of the deadlock in negotiations between all member states on the commission's initial proposals in 2011. enhanced cooperation is seen as the appropriate solution, as an option of last resort, where the objectives pursued by such cooperation cannot be achieved within a reasonable time by the union as a whole, and the participation of at least nine member states is required. this form of enhanced cooperation must be a lever for achieving the union's objectives, protecting its interests and contributing to the integration process. i consider that enhanced cooperation on the matrimonial property regime of international couples, including both matrimonial property regime and registered partnership property effects, is necessary in so far as certain bottlenecks cannot be overcome and the objectives pursued cannot be achieved within the time-limits laid down, which is why i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution.
in writing. ‒ in the field of family law, after consulting parliament, legislative acts are adopted by the council unanimously. however, it soon became clear that not all member states would agree to the proposals. enhanced cooperation thus emerged as the ideal solution, as 23 member states agreed in principle to adopt the two acts. such enhanced cooperation must be an option of last resort, respect the treaties and union law, facilitate the achievement of the union's objectives and not undermine the internal market or economic, social and territorial cohesion. i voted for the introduction of enhanced cooperation, to avoid the blockage of negotiations between all the member states.

in writing. ‒ illicit trade in tobacco products is an activity with a negative impact on both public health and revenues to state budgets. smuggling of cigarettes undermines tobacco control policies, thus promoting access to tobacco products at lower prices which generates significant revenue losses for the european union, given that the related taxes and customs duties are not paid. the protocol to the who framework convention includes a complex set of measures, rules and policies to combat illicit trade in tobacco products, by pursuing a safer process in the tobacco supply chain, by creating a global traceability and tracing system. the protocol emphasises the importance of judicial cooperation in criminal matters through its provisions, regulating the granting of licences, internet sales, duty-free sales and international transit. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that it is essential to ensure the highest standards of protection of public health and that international judicial cooperation in criminal matters is necessary to combat illicit trade in tobacco products.
in writing. ‒ this is a consent file for ratifying the who framework convention on tobacco control, fctc protocol. this protocol is currently the only multilateral regulatory initiative in this field. not only is illicit trade in tobacco products harmful to public health, but it also results in huge losses in revenue to the eu. this protocol consists of a complex set of measures and rules to tackle illicit trade, such as establishing a global tracking and tracing system to make the supply chain more secure. this proposal is in line with the eu’s comprehensive strategy to combat cigarette smuggling. other provisions include licensing, record keeping requirements and regulation of internet-sales, duty-free sales and international transit. it establishes offences, and addresses liability and seizure payments, as well as the disposal of confiscated products. i welcome the achievement of the first multilateral initiative to tackle illicit trade of tobacco and cigarette smuggling by securing supply chains. this is also a very important from the side of public health as well as fight against tax evasion.
in writing. ‒ the aim of the protocol is the elimination in the future of all forms of illicit trade. this could be done by the creation of a global tracking and tracing regime and establishment of a global information sharing point. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the world health organisation (who) framework convention on tobacco control is the first global health treaty created in response to the globalisation of the tobacco epidemic. i support this recommendation that aims to eliminate the illicit trade of tobacco products, in particular cigarette smuggling by enhancing judicial cooperation in criminal matters.
in writing. ‒ i am extremely satisfied that today we voted in favour of the ratification of the protocol. illicit trade in tobacco not only causes billions of lost revenue to the budgets of member states. more importantly, it undermines our public health policies and violates the rules that the eu and member states have on manufacturing, distribution and sale of legitimate goods. cigarette smuggling makes possible the circumvention of legislative restrictions and pricing policies that are designed to deter smoking, especially among youngsters. therefore, the control of the supply chain is of fundamental importance not only for combatting illicit trade, but also for reducing tobacco use in general. the illicit tobacco trade is also a main source of revenue for organised crime, and, in some cases, terrorist groups. the global and highly complex nature of the illicit tobacco trade makes it hard to tackle. this is why a coordinated international response and improved global regulation of the legal tobacco trade is such an imperative. i hope that with the ratification and later the implementation of the protocol we will succeed in changing this situation.
in writing. ‒ the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control is a first global response to tobacco and aims to tackle the causes of this scourge. the protocol to eliminate illicit trade in tobacco products is currently the only multilateral regulatory initiative in this area. on 20 december 2013, the protocol was signed by the european union, but it still needs to be ratified by 40 parties involved to enter into force. this protocol aims to reduce tobacco-related mortality and disease in the world. moreover, illicit trade in tobacco products, in particular smuggling of cigarettes to or within the eu, is considered a criminal activity that causes significant revenue losses, in particular taxes and customs duties for the eu and the member states. it is estimated that the european union and its member states suffer losses of over eur 10 billion each year. therefore, given that most of the illicit products originate from third countries, the report underlines that enhanced international cooperation is essential to counter illicit trade. in this regard, i voted in favour of adopting the protocol to the who framework convention on tobacco control.
