in writing. ‒ the international accounting standards board (iasb) was founded on the 1 april 20012 and is an independent accounting standard body of the international financial reporting standards (ifrs) foundation. i support this report, which aims to further address issues regarding the endorsement process of ifrs in the european union.
in writing. ‒ the european union's influence on international accounting standards (iasb) has contributed to the development of high-quality common accounting standards worldwide. the union has, in turn, since 2005 started to incorporate these standards into european legislation, which contributes to the development of the single capital market, financial services and the supervisory framework. at the same time, the development of those standards was aimed at ensuring a higher degree of transparency and accountability and at preventing the emergence of conflicts of interest. the adoption of common accounting standards also contributes to financial stability and sustainable economic development in the eu. last but not least, the harmonisation of these standards with those in partner countries such as the united states will strengthen the relations between the two parties. i believe that the adoption of this document will cement the existence of common accounting standards worldwide, facilitating a wide range of economic activities beneficial to eu member states and european citizens.
in writing. i voted in favour of my colleague theodor stolojan's own-initiative report on the assessment of international accounting standards. the rapporteur emphasises the important role of accounting standards in the development of a single capital market in the eu, particularly in the context of the capital markets union project. the rapporteur believes that the application of international financial reporting standards in the eu has helped to strengthen the single market and has also strengthened the competitiveness of the european economy, as it has enabled companies to attract capital and investment from global capital markets. the rapporteur also notes that the financial crisis has shown that financial reporting standards need to be revised and improved.
mr president, the emergence of terrorist and guerrilla groups in somalia, nigeria and the sahel/sahara region has led to a dramatic change in the security climate. we contribute, the member states contribute almost two billion euros through the african peace facility. the member states of the union together constitute the largest financial contributor to the un peacekeeping budget. but there is a lack of transparency of eu peacekeeping operations, and as such, we don't know exactly what happens to the money, and the peacekeeping instrument that we fund is not sustainable, it's not controllable. we don't know where it leads or what the consequences will be. so we want more transparency and we want reporting of what's happening with the money. the african union should also be encouraged to take greater responsibility for security in africa.
in writing. ‒ peacekeeping operations (psos) are forms of crisis response in support of an organisation such as the un or the african union (au) designed to prevent armed conflict, maintain or build peace, to comply with peace agreements, but not least to deal with emergencies and complex challenges. the aim of the pso is to contribute to the creation of a climate of long-term stability, security and prosperity. good governance, justice, respect for the rule of law, civil protection, respect for human rights and security are key conditions for this, and the success of reconstruction, reconciliation and economic development programmes will contribute to achieving sustainable prosperity, but at the same time will lead to the achievement of peace. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the stability of the european and african neighbourhood is very beneficial to all eu member states, and that the eu's cooperation with the un and the au does nothing but consolidate this peace, which has recently been very fragile because of terrorist and guerrilla groups.
in writing. ‒ with the increase in fragile states and ungoverned spaces, the security climate in africa has changed dramatically in recent years. the un remains the principal guarantor of international peace and security and has the most comprehensive framework for multilateral cooperation in crisis management. there are 16 un peacekeeping operations with a staff of over 120,000 people. 8 of these missions, as well as 87 percent of the un peacekeeping forces, are on the african continent. i voted for a coherent long-term approach to peace and for continued dialogue between the eu and the african union.
in writing. ‒ given that the purpose of peacekeeping operations (psos) is to respond to crisis situations in order to contribute to the creation of a climate of stability, security and greater prosperity in the long term, i consider that respect for peace agreements is vital for the stability of the african and european neighbourhood.
in writing. ‒ this report is tackling the issue of the european cooperation in the framework of the un initiatives for peace support operations in africa, including as well the eu csdp missions and operations in the region. this initiative report comes with recommendations for the eu to improve its engagement in africa in the field of the peace support operations. having in mind the spectacular security changes in africa over the past decades and its consequence for the eu, the report seeks to describe how the eu can help africa ensure its own security. i supported the report as i consider africa a priority, including as well the aspects related to security.
in writing. ‒ the issues concerning european cooperation in the framework of the un initiatives for peace support operations in africa, including as well the eu csdp missions and operations in the region are tackled in this report. considering the security changes in africa over the past decades, the report seeks to describe how the eu can help africa ensure its own security. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ peace support operations (pso) encompass activities of all civil and military organisations that deploy peacekeeping missions. i support this report that aims to enforce peace agreements, prevent and stop armed conflicts and restore, maintain and build peace.
in writing. ‒ acknowledging the importance of a long-term approach towards guaranteeing peace in africa, and driven by the adequacy of the measures proposed with this aim in the report, i have resolved to support the resolution. the report notes the need to reinforce eu involvement with peace support operations in africa following strategies effectively coordinated with those of the un and the african union. not only should overlaps be avoided, but particular focus should be placed on promoting capacity building rather than substitution, with the ultimate goal of ensuring the continent’s autonomy in conflict resolution. furthermore, accountability mechanisms regarding funding utilisation ought to be further refined.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the van orden report on peacekeeping operations and cooperation with the un and the african union. despite fierce criticism, eu peacekeeping operations in africa are essential. but we have to learn from our mistakes and make these missions effective. i would like to stress that special attention must be paid to the security situation in the sahel-sahara region, which can generate significant migratory flows to the european continent. only by ensuring peace on the african continent, complemented by development aid, can we talk about a chance for stability and democratization on the african continent.
in writing. ‒ the european union is an important international actor, interested in maintaining world peace and combating negative phenomena that threaten international security. for this reason, member states have frequently supported un peacekeeping missions. the missions deployed on the african continent in recent decades have been aimed at strengthening state structures affected by internal fighting between various factions, combating the phenomenon of terrorism or combating oppressive regimes. the missions were carried out in cooperation with nato structures or through the capabilities of some of the member states. in recent years, the development of the structures of the african union has led to a partnership with this regional organisation, with a view to developing the capacity of those states to manage adverse situations affecting their security on their own. to achieve these aims, financial resources allocated under the european development fund (edf) through the african peace fund have been used to support structural reforms in african states. particular attention should be paid to the security situation in the sahel-sahara region, which can generate significant migratory flows towards the european continent. only by ensuring security on the african continent can these states develop in all respects, and the eu can support this complex process.
in writing. ‒ in the context of the spread of terrorist groups in africa, peacekeeping and counter-terrorism operations have become a necessity in many regions. today, peacekeeping operations are increasingly characterised by the deployment of several un missions in the same theatre of operations, bringing together different actors and regional organisations such as the african union. for these actions to be successful, these partnerships need to be effectively coordinated to avoid overlaps. in this context, an effective allocation of tasks between states and organisations is needed. furthermore, un and african union missions need a global approach. in addition to the organisation of diplomatic, military and development missions, other elements such as a thorough knowledge of the security environment and the exchange of information and technologies are essential. there are also eu instruments in the field of security, in particular missions and operations under the common security and defence policy, which could be used in these regions. for these reasons, i voted in favour of the report on peacekeeping operations eu cooperation with the un and the african union.
i agree with the position expressed in the report and i myself believe that we must act by legislative means to put an end to unfair trading practices in the european union's food supply chain. it is quite clear that wholesalers are abusing their dominant position in the market to an extreme extent, thereby putting the capital-supporting undertakings which are placed at their disposal in an impossible position. small and medium-sized enterprises are the engine of the european economy, and small food producers and retailers are the foundation of european food. we cannot leave this to market self-regulation, which requires national and eu regulators. the primary consideration should be the interest of european citizens in facilitating access to safe, healthy and nutritious food. unfortunately, it seems that self-regulation in the market is not moving in this direction and it is our responsibility to contribute to restoring the balance.
mr president, unfair trading practices are a serious problem and they must be stopped. a commission report from january 2016 confirms that these unfair practices can exist at all stages of the food supply chain. there's an imbalance of income and power in this chain. this imbalance is disadvantaging small and medium-sized enterprises, small producers. and small producers make up over 90% of the economic structure of the european union. they're the most vulnerable right now. their ability to survive on the market is jeopardised precisely because of unfair trading practices. they are jeopardising their ability to come up with new initiatives, or to do trade, or to expand across borders into the internal market of the european union. or that's not how a free market works. therefore, eu competition law needs to be aligned to combat unfair practices.
in writing. ‒ unfair commercial practices (ucps) are contrary to good faith and fairness and are imposed unilaterally by one trading partner on another, affecting good commercial conduct. ncds are a serious problem and occur in several economic sectors, with negative effects on the eu economy as a whole. today, at european level, there is no eu legislation addressing unfair trading practices between companies in the food supply chain. at national level, however, most member states have approached ncps using a variety of approaches based on the problems encountered. although measures to combat unfair trading practices have evolved significantly in recent years, i believe that a framework legislation to combat ncps at union level is needed, ensuring greater transparency and fairer conditions for european citizens to buy and sell in the common market. at the same time, i would point out that this new framework instrument should not affect the level of protection in countries with national legislation on the fight against intra-corporate ncps. i support this ep motion for a resolution because the purpose of the report is not only to inform us and analyse the problem of unfair practices, but also to identify new solutions that can be applied in this area for a better functioning of the eu internal market.
in writing. ‒ unfair trading practices have negative effects on the eu's entire economy. a 2011 survey shows that 96 per cent of respondents in the food supply chain said they had already been subject to at least one form of unfair trading practices. self-regulatory systems are not sufficient to solve this problem. i voted for the introduction of clear sanctions for anyone who applies such practices and for firm and consistent action to eliminate this phenomenon once and for all.
in writing. ‒ i believe that this resolution is a signal that the european parliament is sending in support of farmers. it is a positive signal for producers of consumer goods, who are often not protected in relation to large commercial networks. it is important that these people's efforts are properly rewarded, just as it is important for consumers to benefit from quality products at decent prices. i hope that the responsible officials of the european commission will act as quickly as possible on the requests made in this resolution. the resolution also serves romanian farmers, who we already know often have difficulty selling and distributing their products on fair terms.
in writing. ‒ the czesak report states that all voluntary schemes in place (such as the supply chain initiative) to tackle unfair trading practices (payment delays, restricted access to market, abusive changes to contract terms, pressure to cut prices, etc.) are insufficient and that eu proposals for an eu framework doubled by a strong enforcement mechanism, including penalties, are needed. i support legislative/regulatory measures at european level to tackle utps and strong enforcement mechanism and penalties. i supported the report as i want the eu to put an end to unfair commercial practices against small and medium—sized producers and farmers when they engage in commercial relations on a highly concentrated market.
in writing. ‒ given the importance of this report, i voted for it in view of the negative effects that unfair trading practices can have on the european economy. they may lead to a loss of investment and innovation capacity of smes and could also affect their decision to expand. i too believe that firm and consistent action is needed to eliminate unfair trading practices from the eu food supply chain once and for all. given the scale of the problem, provisions need to be adopted at eu level to ensure the proper functioning of markets and fair and transparent relationships between all parties involved in the food supply chain. unfair trading practices should be clearly defined and clear penalties should be provided for anyone who applies such practices. and national agencies should be responsible for the enforcement of the rules and should be able to open investigations on their own initiative and deal with anonymous complaints.

in writing. ‒ access to the free market for small food producers and traders is currently affected by a number of unfair trading practices in their relations with participants in the food supply chain. these practices occur in the presence of imbalances between the financial resources of the two parties and are manifested by setting unfavourable prices, delays in payment, restricting market access, abusive contractual clauses in relation to small producers, who are forced to accept this way of working, without having the necessary means to defend themselves. the situation is widespread, despite regulatory measures taken by member states, which rely on voluntary and self-regulatory systems. firm and consistent measures are needed to eliminate these negative practices from the union food supply chain. they involve a clear definition of unfair trading practices and clear sanctions to deter them, applied by the competent national agencies. the current report envisages the introduction of the necessary mechanisms for the implementation of these measures, which can support small and medium-sized producers. that is why i support the present form of the document.
in writing. ‒ this report highlights that unfair trading practices are a serious problem that can be found in many sectors of the economy. this threat is particularly relevant to food supply chains. unfair practices may consist of: delaying payment, restricting market access, unilaterally changing contractual terms, changing them with retroactive effect or pressuring to lower product prices. the rapporteur notes that these practices are the result of imbalances in income and power relations within food supply chains and stresses that the most appropriate means must be found to ensure that food producers and distributors are adequately protected against these practices. furthermore, it is underlined that the initiative on supply chains and other optional national and eu systems should be developed and promoted more intensively. it is also necessary to develop effective control mechanisms so that complaints can be lodged anonymously and deterrent sanctions can be imposed with coordination at european union level. for these reasons, i voted in favour of the report on combating unfair trading practices in the food supply chain.

in writing. ‒ by 2050, the world's population is expected to increase, and the demand for food will increase in direct proportion by 70 per cent. today, there is a positive trend in healthy food on the european market, a demand that unfortunately farmers cannot meet due to several factors such as: reduced availability of land, ecological losses and environmental degradation, water shortages, energy needs, and the emergence of new pests. the majority of farmers and landowners are small enterprises and the additional costs threaten their survival on the agricultural market. strong farmers need state-of-the-art technology, high-performance financing solutions and continuous education. technological innovation is a key part of the solution. the eu has prepared for the next period the horizon 2020 framework programme which is the union's largest research and innovation programme, with funding of around €80 billion. i support this report because i believe that the need to improve productivity, competitiveness and environmental performance is not just a matter of economics, but rather a moral obligation of the ep to optimise and increase agricultural production in the most sustainable way possible for the wellbeing of european citizens.

question asked in accordance with the 'blue card' procedure. madam president, in your speech you referred to those countries that do not want to accept migrants. i would like to ask you how you comment on the intransigent position of the president of romania, mr iohannis, in this regard.
blue-card question. – because of the economic situation, because of the social situation, because of the civil wars taking place nowadays in some countries in africa, europe is going to see more and more people trying to come to europe in the years ahead – especially from africa. do you not think that in the end the european union has to come up with a long-term strategy and policy to meet this important challenge? it is not only practical measures or effective solutions that need to take place now: we need a long-term strategy for this.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, sometimes listening to some of the comments, let me be very frank, we had doubts and thought that maybe a careful reading of the proposal itself could be useful, to start from the facts. in the debates this afternoon you mixed many different things. mr verhofstadt was asking at the beginning – it is a pity he is not here – whether this is a duplication of the deal with turkey. the two situations are completely different. as frans mentioned at the beginning, from turkey we have mainly syrian refugees. it is temporary – hopefully temporary, we are working also on that, this is another story – a flow of refugees, asylum seekers. that falls into one specific international legal framework. we are trying to deal with that in a sort of immediate and also – let me use this word that i do not like at all, but that is the reality of our policies today – emergency mode. what we are putting on the table here is something completely different. it is something that starts from the fact that with africa we have a common interest in working on the development of the continent with a sense of partnership. some of you asked how are the african interlocutors reacting to this? very well. yesterday i was in new york at the security council. african countries, but not only african countries, latin american countries, were saying: this is the right way to go because finally you are not only investing in development – which is the right thing to do, by the way, in itself. and incidentally, i am proud to say that the european union is the first donor worldwide, it is the first – and if you want, i can give you the figures for it also being the first donor to africa – the first donor internationally with more than half of the official development assistance worldwide: eur 68 billion in 2015, over eur 20 billion oda to africa every year, and this is going to stay. i am proud of that. this is the right thing to do anyway but there is another issue. please go to ethiopia and talk to the women that came back voluntarily, not from europe but from the gulf because they were becoming slaves, while we support projects from the ilo to reintegrate them into their communities, offering training and job opportunities. listen to their stories and then come back to me and say that we are doing deals on their shoulders. no. we are protecting their lives and their rights. go and talk with the young girls from nigeria who turn into sex slaves in europe and tell me that the deal we want to strike with nigeria is not to protect their rights and their lives. i am sorry, but you do not protect the lives of people only by saving them at sea. you also save their lives at the beginning of the journey. go to lampedusa and listen to the stories that the survivors tell you, or if you cannot fly there, watch the movie ‘fuocoammare’ (fire at sea). there was a showing of it a couple of months ago in the european parliament in brussels. listen to those words that tell you that these people are turned into slaves from the very beginning of their journeys. they are in chains crossing the deserts, locked in jails in libya, locked in the boats that then sink. we have a human responsibility – and our african partners as well have a human responsibility – to protect their lives. this is what we are talking about, and doing this together with international agencies starting from the international organisation for migration (iom) and the unhcr. so what we are talking about is job creation, perfectly rightly, for african women, for african youth – go to agadez, that was living from tourism before security made it impossible – about first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i will make just a few remarks in addition to what high representative mogherini said. it is my deep conviction that the only way we can maintain a humane refugee policy, based on our most fundamental values, is if we make a clear distinction between people who deserve international protection and people who come to europe because they see economic opportunity in europe. all too often – and we have heard it again here today – people pretend that everyone arriving on europe’s shores is an economic migrant. i have heard some of your members saying it today. this is a cheap way of getting rid of your moral and legal responsibility vis—à—vis people who deserve international protection, but it is made possible because, until now, we have not been good enough at making a clear distinction between people who deserve international protection and people who do not. why? because for too many years greece and italy were left alone with a problem. they asked time and time and time again for a european solution and the only answer they got from the rest of europe was that ‘it’s not our problem, but your problem, so take care of it’. so now we need to solve it and the only sustainable way of solving it is by doing it in a european way. we can solve it, and get pan—european support for a humane refugee policy, if, and only if, we sort out the issue of economic migration in a sustainable way, and the compact with african countries is one element for doing that. that is why i passionately believe in this way forward. i have heard no one who criticises it giving us a better idea. if you have a better idea, share it with us. but to simply say, ‘let everyone into europe’ is the shortest way to ending our humanitarian policy, the shortest way to ending the reception of refugees in europe and the shortest way to giving populists the opportunity to say that everyone who comes here is an opportunist looking for a better future at our expense. tell that to a family fleeing from raqqah, fleeing from aleppo, from barrel bombs. tell them that they are economic migrants. it is a scandal. so that is why we believe international protection and, more importantly, that we create opportunity in african countries so that economic growth does not disappear into the pockets of the elite but goes to everyone with talent and every young person has an opportunity to build a life for themselves in their country of origin. that is what we need to do and this is surely not going to be done on its own. we need the member states to contribute. the biggest problem here is not just a lack of finance. it is the lack of clear direction, of coordinated efforts, of doing the same thing from all 28 with the european bring some order into this. finally, let us never forget that we are talking about human beings. we are not talking about numbers or objects. we are talking about people who have dreams – like you and capita more refugees than any other european country – more than 160 000. now that they have the impression that we are slowly getting this under control, you see the mood in the swedish society shifting towards, ‘ok, let us make a success of this’, companies offering thousands of intern places for refugees, schools accommodating many new pupils and communities welcoming new citizens. i hope member of the commission. – mr president, first i want to thank you for the opportunity to discuss the future of the european space policy and space sector here in the european parliament. i want to thank, in particular, the foreign affairs committee for its work on space capabilities for european security and defence that was coordinated by mr zdrojewski, with input from mr marinescu who represented the committee on industry, research and energy. i have to say that this debate is timely as we are now preparing the space strategy for europe that will be presented and adopted in the autumn of this year. this is also timely because these are challenging – but really exciting – times for space in the world and in europe. europe is today the second biggest player in space. space is crucial for security and defence, but it also generates an important spill-over effect in many other sectors, enabling business development, jobs creation and growth. of course, things are changing as the global context is evolving fast, competition is building up and the market is increasingly driven by the private sector. european companies need a market large enough to sell their products, yet this is not always the case, of course, today. our strategic assets such as critical technologies components and systems are really crucially important here. despite its increase, the budget available for space remains small compared to our competitors. we have to face these challenges together. europe cannot afford to treat it as ‘business as usual’ because competitors and partners are really moving fast. this is why the commission announced its intention to work towards the new space strategy for europe, and we intend to be inclusive – involving, of course, the member states, the european space agency, eumetsat, the industry and, of course, parliament. i therefore welcome our debate today and wish to engage more with you over the next month on space issues. but before i come to the space strategy, let me say just a few words on our european flagship space programmes, copernicus and galileo, because they are moving forward. as i commented several months ago, four out of six copernicus services are fully operational and the community of users is growing. we launched successfully another satellite in april. egnos is operational and two weeks ago we had another successful launch for galileo, which brings the number of satellites in orbit to 14. we really can, and should, be proud of that. of course, i have to mention the initial services which will start later this year. we hope to launch four more satellites in november. the main challenge now is to work to exploit these achievements for new or better services, products and applications. space solutions and technologies can have a decisive impact on high political priorities such as climate change, air quality, border management, transport, environment issues and security. actually, the largest impact may be outside of the space domain, per se. most of the growth and economic value will come from the commercial downstream uses of space. market uptake of our programmes is therefore at the heart of this strategy. we will propose measures in that sense. the role of the commission in the public sector should be as an enabler. we should promote favourable conditions and encourage businesses to develop innovative products and services. innovation clusters and business incubators will be supported. this will benefit smes and, of course, start—ups. we are also looking at how we can use smart financing and synergies among different eu programmes to increase the uptake of space. our top priority for copernicus is ensuring fast and easy access to data and services anywhere in europe, so we envisaged supporting the development of several industry—led platforms, making the most of the available data—processing technologies. we will identify any legislative, administrative and technical barriers that need to be addressed. on galileo, together with the gsa, we will continue to make chipsets and receivers galileo— and egnos—compatible and develop the relevant applications. our intention is to promote the use of egnos and galileo in various sectors, focusing of course on those with the highest potential. but we also need to take a strategic view. our main objective should be to bring the benefits of space to european society and to the european economy. we need a strategy to address the current and emerging challenges. we need a strategy that covers all the relevant public and private actors in europe. we want to mainstream the use of space to support public policies, providing effective solutions to the big societal challenges such as – as i said before – climate change, security, migration, and the digital agenda. we want to promote a globally—competitive european space sector that is innovative, agile and entrepreneurial, and create more jobs and, of course, more growth in europe. we want a space environment that is sustainable and remains accessible, safe and secure. this is the vision of the strategy that we are working on. we expect it to cover five main areas. first, as already said, we want to maximise the benefits of galileo and copernicus. second, we want to respond to emerging needs – for example, we may consider how space could better contribute to security policy, border surveillance and maritime security. we are also looking into the international developments taking place and how space technology could help our climate change agenda, notably with regard to co2 emissions. third, we want to boost the competitiveness of the european space industry throughout research, innovation and the modernisation of the industrial base. that means using opportunities from new business models to encourage greater involvement and risk—sharing by the private sector and a smart financing approach. fourth, we want to address the strategic aspects and dualist dimension of space. this means supporting the resilience and protection of critical space and ground infrastructure, including in the context of the current space surveillance and tracking framework. we are assessing how we can support europe’s independent access to space. when talking about security and strategic aspects of space, and similarly to what is said in the report of mr zdrojewski, i consider that space based capabilities and services can, and should, play a key role in the context of european security and defence. i particularly note the references in your report to govsatcom capacities, sst, precise navigation and earth observation. this is also an element discussed in the context of the announced european defence action plan which i am preparing together with vice—president katainen. finally, we want to strengthen the role and impact of the eu as a global actor. in april, we launch a broad public consultation process open until 12 july, to help us shape the strategy. to sum up and conclude, i see space as an enabler for solutions to key political priorities and societal challenges, as a vector for growth, enabling new services, new business opportunities in space, as an industrial sector in its own right, which is facing increasing challenges and needs to be supported, and as a strategic asset supporting europe’s autonomy of action on the global stage. the opportunities offered by space programmes will only be felt if they are used widely by both public and private users. that means stronger and more coordinated efforts at all levels – european, national and local. so we have to work together to bring the benefits of space closer to our citizens.

in writing. space policy developed in the context of the cold war, when the united states and the soviet union began the conquest of outer space, engaging in a space race. of course, the global political and technological landscape has changed fundamentally in the last 70 years. today, space policy means strategic opportunities in key areas such as telecommunications, transport and energy, weather and climate monitoring and, not least, security. but european space policy must be understood in a much broader geopolitical context. the eu does not yet have the profile of a major player in this area, although there have been sustained efforts since the early 2000s. on the one hand, these efforts must be seen in a highly competitive geopolitical environment, in which the eu must maintain a firm and coherent position for reasons of security and defence. on the other hand, it is not desirable for the eu to cause unexpected developments or global risks through its space policy. in this context, the line between risk and opportunity is very fine and must be rigorously analysed.

in writing. ‒ the agreement on the expansion of trade in information technology products aims to eliminate customs duties on all information technology products that are covered. the duty-free regime conferred by this agreement has an important role in strengthening and expanding trade in the information technology sector. approximately 200 tariff lines are concerned, covering computers, telephones, but also production factors, components and machines for the manufacture of computer products. as a result of the negotiations, 65% of tariff lines will be completely eliminated by 1 july 2016, with the aim of eliminating almost all customs duties on imports of the products covered by the agreement by 2019. the expansion of trade in information technology products is a step forward in the process of reducing tariffs, with a major positive impact in boosting employment as well as in boosting the growth of gross domestic product, which is why i voted in favour of this agreement.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because, first of all, we need to protect the environment, but at the same time we need to help the victims of such a maritime accident, and this can only be done through a coherent policy framework on liability and compensation for environmental damage caused by the transport of dangerous and harmful substances at sea. in accordance with the 1996 convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea, it is the last of the international maritime organisation's conventions dealing with compensation and liability for damage caused by the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea. as regards the 2010 convention, it establishes the strict liability of the owner of a ship carrying dangerous or noxious substances for any damage resulting from an incident related to the transport of substances at sea and on board that ship. both conventions overlap with the scope of directive 2004/35/ec on environmental liability of operators carrying out professional activities, including maritime transport.
in writing. ‒ the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea - hns convention - represents a relevant international legal instrument in terms of transport and environment. the ratification of the 2010 protocol, which represents practically the ratification of the hns convention in its new form of 2010 is considered to be very important for the eu, as it provides for improved protection of the victims of damage in connection with the carriage of hns by sea, but there are divisions in terms of the period in which that should be done and the terms that the council established for it. in order for the convention to enter into force, some member states would like a swift ratification, while others are not yet ready to ratify. i support a swift ratification of this protocol, but council should reconsider its position, and should see that it is not beneficial to create legal uncertainty and divisions between legal regimes in member states in an issue that has so many cross-border implications.

in writing. ‒ the hns convention also known as the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea was set-up in 1996. i have voted for this interim report that aims to ensure that the establishment of a uniform liability regime, with the exception of aspects related to judicial cooperation in civil matters, is done in the most effective and fair fashion.
in writing. ‒ the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea – hns convention – represents a relevant international legal instrument in terms of transport and environment. the ratification of the 2010 protocol, which represents practically the ratification of the hns convention in its new form of 2010 is considered to be very important for the eu, as it provides for improved protection of the victims of damage in connection with the carriage of hns by sea, but there are divisions in terms of the period in which that should be done and the terms that the council established for it. i therefore welcome a swift ratification by all member states. the council should reconsider its position, and should see that it is not beneficial to create legal uncertainty and divisions between legal regimes in member states in an issue that has so many cross-border implications.
in writing. ‒ the 2010 hns convention ensures uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation for accidents caused by ships carrying dangerous and harmful substances at sea in the eu. sufficient funds are made available for compensation to victims, and it is therefore considered that an international regime, rather than regional solutions, is more appropriate to ensure uniform application of the rules on compensation and liability for marine casualties. this interim report should not be seen as an obstacle to the establishment of a uniform liability regime, but rather as an effort to ensure that this process is carried out with maximum efficiency and fairness, without affecting the uniformity, integrity and effectiveness of the common rules of eu law, but also without creating excessive disparities for the victims of pollution and for the shipping industry. i voted in favour of this report because we need to protect the environment but at the same time we need to help the victims of such a maritime accident, and this can only be done through a coherent political and legal framework on liability and compensation for environmental damage caused by the transport of dangerous and harmful substances at sea.
in writing. ‒ the environmental liability directive does not provide for compensation to victims beyond the limits of the ship owner's liability. the existing legal framework in the eu also does not include any requirement for compulsory insurance, whereas the convention specifically sets out this obligation for ship owners, coupled with the right of claimants to bring direct actions against the insurer. an international regime, rather than regional solutions, is more appropriate to ensure the uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation for accidents caused by ships carrying dangerous and harmful substances at sea within the eu, given that this is a global commercial activity. i voted in favour of a uniform liability regime for environmental damage caused by the transport of dangerous and harmful substances by sea, given the worldwide dimension of this phenomenon.
in writing. ‒ the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea – hns convention – represents a relevant international legal instrument in terms of transport and environment. the ratification of the 2010 protocol, which represents practically the ratification of the hns convention in its new form of 2010 is considered to be very important for the eu, as it provides for improved protection of the victims of damage in connection with the carriage of hns by sea, but there are divisions in terms of the period in which that should be done and the terms that the council established for it. in order for the convention to enter into force, some member states would like a swift ratification, while others are not yet ready to ratify. i support a swift ratification of this protocol, but council should reconsider its position, and should see that it is not beneficial to create legal uncertainty and divisions between legal regimes in member states in an issue that has so many cross-border implications.
in writing. ‒ the hns convention also known as the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea was set-up in 1996. i have voted for this interim report that aims to ensure that the establishment of a uniform liability regime, with regard to aspects related to judicial cooperation in civil matters, is done in the most effective and fair fashion.

in writing. ‒ tackling cross-border tax avoidance practices must be a priority for the european authorities, taking into account situations where taxpayers act without respecting the real purpose of the legislation, taking advantage of differences between national tax systems to reduce their tax contributions. this distorts business decisions in the internal market and, if not addressed effectively, could create an environment of unfair tax competition. the panama scandal once again confirms the need for legally binding rules to enable member states to effectively combat the avoidance of obligations by businesses, so as to maintain their collective competitiveness and respect the single market, the freedoms enshrined in the treaty, the eu charter of fundamental rights and eu law in general. i voted in favour of this report because this initiative brings added value compared to what could be achieved by a multitude of national methods.
in writing. ‒ aggressive tax optimisation by multinationals costs governments worldwide between $100 and $240 billion a year. this represents between 4 and 10% of worldwide corporate tax revenues. this significant loss reduces the capacity of states to develop projects for employment, poverty reduction and development of high-performing health systems for all. the main objective of this report is to ensure that companies pay their taxes where they make their profits. i voted for a coordinated and harmonised approach to the implementation of tax systems.
in writing. ‒ the fight against tax evasion by multinationals is fundamental in regaining the confidence of european citizens. moreover, i agree with the more comprehensive position on profits that should be taxed where they are created. firstly, i support a stricter interest limitation rule. i am in favour of the new common definition on permanent establishment that should be applied by member states, both in relevant legislation and bilateral tax treaties, in order to ensure consistency and to make sure profits are taxed where the economic activity takes place. i also believe that we should develop a common method of calculation of the effective tax rate in each member state, to make it possible to draw up a comparative table of the effective tax rates across the member states. until now, multinationals have used patent incentives to artificially reduce their profits. this has an adverse impact on genuinely innovative countries. these multinationals should be subject to an exit tax where they repatriate proceeds from patents to countries with lower tax rates. consequently, i agree that the commission should bring forward a proposal on a withholding tax to make sure profits are taxed before leaving the union.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report because i believe in strengthening economic and monetary union through harmonisation of european taxation. i also believe that the taxation issue must be tackled in an efficient and harmonised way across member states to ensure the smooth functioning of the single market and the success of capital markets. this report is an encouraging step towards making multinationals pay their taxes fairly, in proportion to their profits, but also towards limiting tax evasion and eliminating tax havens that put pressure on smes and encourage unfair competition. this would avoid the harm created by instruments that artificially reduce the volume of multinational profits. clear and harmonised legislation would promote the transparency of the european economic environment and foster employment, combat poverty and develop high-performing health systems for all.

in writing. ‒ a study made by the organisation for economic cooperation and development (oecd) estimated that aggressive tax optimisation made by multinationals causes losses to state budgets of somewhere between 100 and 240 billion each year, worldwide. i have voted for this report that will ensure that enterprises pay their taxes where they make their profits.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it encourages tax practices that are beneficial to the internal business environment of the european union. it is commendable that the european parliament has approved rules for the implementation of fair and efficient taxation of businesses within the eu, the rules being developed in line with the european commission's action plan. one of the new provisions adopted in this report aims to eliminate double taxation, a practice used to avoid tax obligations by businesses in the member states. in this respect, the report envisages the introduction of a switch-over clause which, by being applied in business credit agreements, will help avoid the risk of profit shifting from high-tax jurisdictions to low-tax territories. i also welcome the adoption of the general anti-abuse rule designed to complement the laws of the member states in order to prevent abusive tax practices by companies.

in writing. ‒ endocrine disruptors present major risks to human and animal health. recent findings confirm that chemicals have particularly severe effects on thyroid and brain functions, metabolism, and homeostasis. under the legislation in force, the commission is required to adopt delegated acts establishing the scientific criteria for the determination of the properties of endocrine disrupting substances. the commission has unfortunately not issued these delegated acts within the deadline, despite having a clear, precise and unconditional obligation to fulfil its task, as set out in the judgment of the general court of december 2015. i voted in favour of this resolution because i consider it inadmissible that an institution which has the role of guardian of the treaties should paradoxically fail to fulfil its obligations under the current regulations and i ask the commission to adopt immediately scientific risk-based criteria for the determination of the properties of endocrine disrupting substances.
in writing. ‒ so-called endocrine disruptors are chemicals capable of interfering with the hormones of animal species, including humans, and are believed to be the cause of many serious diseases (for instance hormone-dependent cancers, infertility, obesity, diabetes, neurobehavioral disorders, etc.). they are found in a multitude of consumer items, cosmetics, pesticides and plastics (such as bisphenol a - bpa). the biocides regulation and the plant protection products regulation provide for special treatment of pesticides and biocidal products. under those regulations substances recognised as endocrine disruptors would not be allowed on the eu market. as a result of this provision the commission was obliged to find a way to distinguish endocrine disruptors from other chemicals by laying down scientific criteria to identify them. i strongly condemn continuous and incomprehensible delays in defining clear rules on chemicals which are believed to cause many serious diseases. i support the call on the commission to comply with the general court ruling by submitting strict criteria for endocrine disruptors based on science and not on socio-economic considerations.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteurs on the material they have put on the table today. the european union is defined mainly by the free movement of persons, goods, services and capital. today we have a more than acceptable free movement of persons within the union, even though not all member states are in the schengen area. unfortunately, the administrative obstacles to the cross-border use and acceptance of official documents have a direct impact on the free movement of citizens. it is necessary to further identify practical tools that make life easier for citizens across national borders. 'unity in diversity' must also be found in the bureaucratic sphere, thus overcoming the language barriers created in the absence of standard forms. simplifying these procedures responds to the needs and wishes of citizens, while at the same time representing an important step towards deepening and strengthening european integration. a gradual approach is needed in starting this process, starting with testing a narrower area such as civil status documents, and then it is mandatory to move towards an extension of the scope. however, we must be extremely careful not to let the mirage of simplification override the principles of security and legal certainty which have been the basis for the introduction of legalisation formalities. i therefore remain firmly convinced that the proposal provides a new impetus to the free movement of persons.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, in the context of an increasing number of europeans working, studying or living in member states other than their own, the european commission's proposal to simplify the process of accepting public documents is of major importance both for citizens and for the functioning of the european single market. whether it's tourists who need health insurance, employees who need to prove they've paid some taxes, or students who interact with university administration, bureaucratic requirements act as a real brake on european freedoms. the commission's proposal is therefore a necessary but not sufficient step for the current mobility needs. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. in addition to relieving european citizens of the stress of unnecessary red tape, the costs they are forced to bear will be substantially reduced. i also welcome this initiative because of its contribution to the idea of trust between the authorities of the member states and towards european citizens, who are increasingly mobile.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, again, this is one of the issues on which i am working very closely with my colleagues in the commission. the commission and high representative/vice-president mogherini and the european investment bank are currently examining how to have more efficient eu economic diplomacy. economic diplomacy is about using all levers that are at our disposal to promote our economic interests abroad. this means removing barriers and creating incentives to trade and investment by opening global markets, fostering cooperation on economic governance, regulatory convergence or a level playing field, concretely supporting the internationalisation of eu businesses and improving the coherence and effectiveness of the external action of the eu in the economic field. economic diplomacy is therefore at the forefront of the jobs, growth and investment agenda, one of the top priorities of the juncker commission. in a world where most of the future economic growth is expected to happen outside the eu, we must make optimal use of all the levers at our disposal to promote eu prosperity in a global context. to this end, we need to develop a more cohesive and coherent approach that targets strong economic and political outcomes using our trade, investment, industry, innovation, foreign and development policies. eu economic diplomacy also has a financial dimension and access to finance for business internationalisation should be boosted, notably through eib actions. the commission services, the eeas and the european investment bank are already active in working towards removing barriers and creating incentives to trade and investment by opening global markets, fostering cooperation on economic governance, regulatory convergence or a level playing field with key economic partners. they are also supporting the internationalisation of eu businesses. we do this inter alia by negotiating and implementing trade and investment and sectoral agreements, by cooperating on sectoral policies across the world through diplomatic démarches by our eu delegations or at political level when we have summits or high-level meetings with partner countries, and by deploying and financing initiatives to support the internationalisation of businesses and smes. this can be done, for instance, via market access, partnership, support to eu chambers of commerce abroad, business missions and regulatory cooperation and projects. but we can still do more to further improve the coherence and effectiveness of the eu’s external action in the economic field. first, we need to have a clear view of the eu’s economic interests and strategic objectives with key partners. and then we need to use the policy tools and instruments at our disposal to pursue these objectives and ensure coherence and synergies. proper consultation, coordination and unity must be ensured with parliament, member states and industry, as a united eu is stronger and has more leverage. an inter-service group on economic diplomacy has been set up with representatives of the commission services, the eu external action service and the eib to examine and make proposals on the above-mentioned agenda. this group has already helped strengthen our internal coordination. one of the next steps will be to equip eu delegations with better guidance and instructions on how to support eu economic interests abroad. we are also reflecting on how to improve coordination with member states and eu industry to work the together on the same objectives and divide work in an optimal way, including in respect of concrete support for the internationalisation of eu companies, where we need to avoid duplication. for this, we will discuss with member states and industry representatives both in brussels and in european capitals, but also in third countries where economic diplomacy is being carried out on the ground. the role of eu delegations is therefore key. the european parliament’s role in eu economic diplomacy is also key, as you have relations with parliaments of most countries in the world and can pass important messages when visiting them. we need to pursue the same objectives and work together to defend eu economic interests abroad. so, honourable members, i will stop here and i am very interested in hearing your views on what more we could do and maybe learn from best practices you have seen during your visits and activities abroad.
madam president, commissioner, economic diplomacy is not a new concept and is not being discussed for the first time in the european parliament. i remember mr tajani's work as commissioner and vice-president of the commission, when he already initiated action in 2013 on an interesting programme for economic diplomacy so that the european union could become a stronger player in the world. in its definition, economic diplomacy is actually an external political function that ensures that actions are aligned with very clear objectives to promote the economic well-being of european citizens. economic diplomacy aims to use foreign policy instruments to support the economic interests of entrepreneurs in the member states. to achieve its objectives, the european union should promote global competitiveness and take the lead in strategic sectors such as industry, innovation and energy. in my meetings with several commissioners, including mr juncker, i have often raised issues relating to concrete measures, the reindustrialisation of the european union, the internationalisation of business and, in particular, support for smes to expand their activities in third countries. you have also specified it, commissioner, but you have not said how. because without having concrete budgets for the internationalisation of smes, we will not be able to do it with words. my question is very explicit and i hope to receive an answer as clear. what diplomatic instruments in the economic and trade sectors do you want to develop now that the european union is in extremely important negotiations with large markets: the united states, canada, china, japan? commissioner, as vice-chair of the sme intergroup, i had the opportunity to meet with many sme associations, i was myself a sme-ist and sme minister. what economic diplomacy tools do you intend to develop to support smes in expanding their business and marketing in third markets? what can be done to have innovative, competitive, robust smes in the global market? you have a plan? a diplomatic strategy would generate revenue and promote european values by creating a level playing field. economic diplomacy is useful and would reinvigorate europe on the world stage.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and all the colleagues who support this initiative. it may sound strange, but i'm glad there's another commissioner here, because i think each commissioner speaks his own language and doesn't connect with the projects. commissioner, you can argue to mr juncker that we need reindustrialisation, that we need a strategy and that all the projects that the commission generates must have a link between them. the strategic investment fund must be connected for railway equipment, for investments, for the railway industry. we can't work separately and not connect these programs. yesterday we talked late about economic diplomacy. that's what this is about! make an industrialization strategy through economic diplomacy so that european industry can withstand the unfair competition created by state-subsidized industries on a global scale!

in writing. the european railway equipment sector is a driver of industrial growth and innovation in europe, while also contributing to job creation. rail transport is the lowest carbon dioxide emitting mode of transport. the creation of modern railways and of equipment and accessories can provide europe with a technological and innovation lead. investment in research and innovation is indispensable to preserve the international competitiveness of the european railway sector. both national governments and the eu need to support and encourage innovation, according to the eu 2020 strategy. without adequate funding, the objective of an integrated rail network cannot be achieved. particular attention should be paid to the effective implementation of the european fund for strategic investments as a tool for raising private capital for the railway sector. in view of the reduction of public expenditure in this area, substantial private investment in railway projects is required for a long-term european development strategy. in addition, it is necessary to modernise existing railway equipment and for member states to replace worn-out equipment with modern and long-lasting products. there is therefore a need for an effective railway infrastructure capable of serving the general interest of european society in the long term.

in writing. ‒ mobility of union citizens is a reality: some 12 million of them study, work or live in a member state other than the one of which they are nationals. today, when citizens and businesses in the european union exercise their right to free movement or the freedoms of the internal market, they face administrative difficulties. the report refers to civil status documents and several other documents frequently requested by citizens, concerning, for example, residence, nationality and criminal records. i voted to remove these obstacles to citizens' mobility within the european union.
in writing. ‒ more than 12 million european citizens study, work or live in a member state other than the one in which they were born, and every day more than five million europeans cross the union's internal borders to work in another member state. for this reason, hundreds of thousands of official documents enter the legalization or certification cycle each year in order to be recognised in member states other than the one in which they were issued. as such, i support the rapporteur's proposal to reduce the additional cross-border formalities for the recognition of these documents as a measure to facilitate the free movement of citizens.

in writing. ‒ i supported this report in my vote today because it supports the final form of the negotiations between the european parliament and the council on the legislative act promoting the free movement of eu citizens by simplifying the formal acceptance of certain official documents between member states. the presentation of official documents requested by one member state and issued by another is a bureaucratic problem for european citizens wishing to move to the territory of another member state and entails very high costs for the latter. in this respect, simplifying procedures, eliminating the need for legalisation and apostille, as well as for certified translation, will make the procedures that european citizens have to go through much easier. also, the introduction of multilingual forms for most official documents, although these will also have to be accompanied by the required documents, will help avoid ambiguities and reduce the resolution times.
in writing. ‒ one of the principles underpinning the european union is the freedom of movement of citizens of the member states. in this respect, an important component is the simplification of the acceptance of certain documents issued by those states. unfortunately, there are currently still many obstacles to the normalisation of this important process, which creates difficulties, in particular for those who wish to study and work in another member state, but also for other public documents concerning marital status, residence, nationality and criminal records. the current proposal for a regulation provides for exemption from the legalization and apostille of those documents, traditional procedures for cross-border official documents. simplifications are also provided for in relation to legalized copies and authorised translations, in particular by creating multilingual standard forms and pre-translations, annexed to national official documents. at present, diplomas and training certificates, certificates of disability, documents relating to undertakings are not included in the regulation. however, the regulation is an important step forward and may be revised in the future in line with the evolution of conditions at eu level. i therefore consider this to be an obvious step forward and support the adoption of this document.

in writing. ‒ this regulation is the fourth relating to the reform of the court of justice. the third reform concerned an increase in the number of judges at the general court to 56. this increase was subject to the condition that the civil service tribunal be abolished, with civil service disputes transferred back to the general court. the present regulation is therefore a follow-up to the third regulation reforming the court of justice. in parallel with the second step on the increase in the number of judges at the general court, from 40 to 47, the civil service tribunal, which has seven judges, is to be abolished. the court of justice’s proposal merely proposes the repeal of the legal provisions relating to the civil service tribunal, along with a small number of consequential amendments and transitional provisions concerning the transfer of ongoing cases.

in writing. ‒ it is important that there is and is a clear definition at union level of the rules and procedures that are correlated with their rights and obligations. a high degree of transparency, efficiency and rapid problem-solving by the institutions must be ensured. at the same time, it is necessary to take into account that, although a number of sectoral administrative procedures have developed over time, they are not able to ensure the coherence of the system, thus making it difficult for citizens to understand their rights under european law. i voted in favour of this resolution because it calls for a common set of administrative procedures to cover the gaps in this system, which will certainly lead to greater legal certainty.

in writing. ‒ an efficient administration of the union is essential to the public interest. an excessive number of rules and procedures, as well as their absence, can lead to poor administration, which can also be generated by the existence of contradictory, inconsistent or unclear rules and procedures. the european parliament calls on the commission to adopt a regulation laying down the procedural rules governing the administrative activities of the union's administration. the objective of the regulation is to guarantee the right to good administration enshrined in article 41 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union through a transparent, efficient and independent administration. it shall not apply to the administration of the member states.
in writing. ‒ i support the approval of a regulation on the union’s administrative procedures, as the lack of it has often left european citizens’ procedural rights insufficiently protected in a context where growing eu competences have increased citizens’ administrative engagement with european institutions. the development of a significant number of sectorial procedures over the years has not always achieved the greatest coherence and consistence in the overall legal system, and thus the need for a comprehensive regulation seems clear. the treaty of lisbon provided grounds for the adoption of an administrative procedure regulation, and in its resolution of 15 january 2013 the european parliament called for the adoption of a regulation on a european law of administrative procedure. such a regulation, being promoted at present, aims at establishing a set of administrative norms the union must comply with when carrying out its administrative procedures. this regulation shall not apply to member states’ national administrations, but to the administrative activities of the union’s institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. it shall apply neither to legislative or judicial procedures, nor to procedures leading to the adoption of non-legislative acts directly based on the treaties, delegated acts or implementing acts.
in writing. ‒ this proposal pressures the commission to come up with a legislative proposal to regulate the administrative procedure of the eu institutions. i see a need to reform the union’s administrative procedure, as i do not believe that the current framework maximises time and provides sufficient legal certainty for eu citizens when dealing with eu bodies. a large number of european citizens are still not aware of their rights at eu level and do not understand the administration process when dealing with our institutions. therefore, parliament is taking this initiative very seriously and i give my full support to an important step towards more efficient administration and transparency.

in writing. ‒ the european railway supply industry (rsi) covers high-speed, conventional and urban passenger and freight trains. it includes the manufacture of locomotives, rolling stock, track, and electrification, signalling and telecommunications equipment, as well as services for maintenance and parts. i voted for this motion for a resolution, which stresses the need to achieve the objective of establishing a single european railway area that is crucial to maintaining the global dominance of the european rsi.
in writing. ‒ the european railway equipment industry comprises the production of locomotives and rolling stock, rails, electrification, signalling and telecommunications equipment, as well as maintenance and spare parts supply services. the industry accounts for 46% of the world market for rail equipment, employs 400 000 people, but, together with operators and infrastructure, it provides over 1 million direct jobs and 1.2 million indirect jobs in the eu. investment in research and development, innovation capacity, market defragmentation and the creation of clusters are essential foundations to maintain the international competitiveness of the european railway equipment industry and to contribute to the 20% reindustrialisation target in the union. the commission should consider setting up a european-level forum bringing together established or newly established companies with innovative ideas for the railway sector, in particular in the field of digitalisation, with the aim of exchanging good practices and facilitating partnerships. as s&d coordinator for the itre commission, i draw attention to the importance of manufacturing in the single market trains, trams and other modern means of rail transport, together with all necessary auxiliary equipment. in this way we would contribute to increasing the competitiveness of industry and preserving jobs within the union.
in writing. ‒ stressing the positive impact that the rail supply industry (rsi) has on european growth and climate change, this resolution has my full support. already the railway sector is the source of 1 million direct and 1.2 million indirect jobs across the european union. for the sector to continue to generate employment, in the future we need to invest in it by supporting research and developing new innovative technologies that will increase our global competitiveness. our competitiveness in the rsi is further dependent on access to international markets. eu trade strategy should therefore focus on securing the principle of reciprocity with third countries. moreover, as called for in the resolution we should be ambitious about the prospect of creating a single european railway network that will increase efficiency, and hence our competition skills, reduce administrative costs and overall drive a shift towards a sustainable and energy-efficient europe based on a strong railway sector.
in writing. ‒ the railway sector is one of the main components of the transport system at european union level, both in terms of freight and passenger transport. at the heart of the development and efficiency of this sector is the european railway equipment industry, which ensures the production of the rolling stock and the necessary devices (locomotives, rails, electrification, signalling and telecommunications equipment) for the proper functioning of the entire sector in the long term. in this respect, it can be said that the sector is of strategic importance for the european industrial renaissance, for the achievement of the commission's 20% industrialisation target. in this context, there is a need to maintain the global competitiveness of the european railway equipment industry, to adopt a renewed eu agenda, but also to invest in acquiring the necessary skills, to support smes and to improve the climate on european markets in favour of suppliers and to encourage demand for rail products. investment in rail projects, both at eu and global level, can support this process, but only if there is stable political support for the sector. i believe that the european rail industry deserves to be supported and that is why i support this resolution.

madam president, while 9/11/2001 was the work of teams of al-qaeda operatives sent to the united states, today most acts of terrorism are the result of radicalised nationals who one day decide to kill as many people around them as possible. why and how do they get radicalised and, even more important, how can we prevent that radicalisation? however, let us not forget that radicalisation does not come out of the blue, usually it is the result of increasing pressure exerted through siren calls and propaganda instigating hate and praising mass killing as a pressure-release, using in most cases the relative anonymity of the net. some people, usually from outside our countries, are doing that and we must, apart from countering their narrative and even discrediting it, find those people and deal with them according to our laws. because letting those people get radicalised and not interfering with that and concentrating our efforts on preventing them from committing the horrible crimes they are determined to commit is not enough. sooner or later they will find a way. but if we actively engage in dismantling those sources of radicalisation both in mosques and on the net, in cooperation with the muslim communities themselves, and engage in the active countering of their narratives of hate for a long period to come, then we stand the chance to do away with this phenomenon. after all, some years ago a well-known author of espionage books, tom clancy, if i am not mistaken, described exactly such a case when a recruiter of jihadists was discredited in the eyes of his followers ended up being captured. his imaginary plot has become reality today, why not his recipe?

in writing. ‒ since 2004, the eu has developed the european neighbourhood policy (enp) to prevent new dividing lines between the newly enlarged union and its neighbours, and to enhance their prosperity, stability and security. since 2006, lebanon has been one of the 16 neighbouring partners with whom the eu, in the framework of the union for the mediterranean, establishes a bilateral policy based on the values of democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights. the protocol to the eu-lebanon euro-mediterranean agreement aims to establish the financial and technical rules allowing lebanon to participate in certain union programmes considered relevant for that mediterranean state, such as economic cooperation and financial assistance. lebanon is home to approximately 1.1 million syrian refugees, which is an economic and administrative burden for a country with a population of just four times that number. in the context of the deteriorating situation of syrian refugees, this protocol facilitates the technical procedure for the provision of eu financial assistance, taking also into account that for 2016 the european commission allocates eur 87 million for humanitarian assistance in lebanon.
in writing. ‒ the republic of lebanon is an important strategic partner of the european union and its member states, which has repeatedly demonstrated its seriousness in respecting its international commitments, in particular in the framework of the european neighbourhood policy (enp). the lebanese republic is the main destination for syrian refugees due to its geographical and cultural proximity to syria. according to the statement of the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, federica mogherini, of 11 may 2016, there are more than 1,5 million refugees in the republic of lebanon out of an estimated population of 4,5 million. in this context, the beirut government was forced to take measures to ensure that asylum seekers could be received, housed, have access to education, healthcare and the labour market. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that it is necessary to establish the main measures of economic, financial and technical cooperation with a view to providing technical assistance to this partner with whom we share a long-standing friendship.
