in writing. ‒ i have supported this report, in which parliament reaffirms its long-standing support for the establishment of an independent and effective european public prosecutor's office. the establishment of a european public prosecutor's office is a basic prerequisite for the intensification of transnational law enforcement efforts, both in the area of crimes against the security of european citizens, cross-border crime and in the tax area. the report calls on the commission to present adjusted estimates of the budgetary implications of the new structure in a cost-benefit analysis and to present the results of the 'situation assessment' to parliament. last but not least, for more effective collaboration and information exchange, the report supports the idea of a joint seat for the european parliament and eurojust.
in writing. ‒ i support this report, as it is very important that the eu and all its member states detect and prosecute in an effective manner fraud affecting the eu’s financial interests, thus protecting the taxpayers of all member states who contribute to the union’s budget. this is especially relevant since organised cross-border crime has increased in the past decade and is committed by extremely mobile, flexible groups, which are active in many member states and areas of crime. i stand behind the idea of establishing an efficient and independent european public prosecutor’s office in order to straighten the fight against fraud in the european union. as stated in this report, the european public prosecutor’s office should have sufficient investigative measures available to conduct its investigations thoroughly and should cooperate and share information with eurojust, in order to increase the efficiency of its work.
mr president, when dealing with massive job losses caused by changes in world trade and technology, i believe we need to follow a comprehensive approach. first, we need to demonstrate true compassion and take care of those who are hurt by open trade or changing global economic patterns. we should also insist more on active employment policies and training for workers to help people get back into the labour market. however, training can only function efficiently if we have dynamic and competitive economies to create new jobs and bring back the dismissed into the labour force. i think the report duly recognised this, and i was glad to vote for it.
mr. president, in september, caterpillar announced that it would lay off 10,000 people. in france, alstom is also about to cease production at one of its combines after 130 years of activity. it is true that industries, especially extractive industries, have been facing a shortage of supply for several years and as such production is declining. and in my country, romania, the hunedoara power complex announced that it would lay off over 800 employees, and the oltenia power complex laid off over 1 300 employees in the first six months of this year. of course we are in solidarity with them and on the state's money they must be prepared to be able to do other jobs, to have other work. but we need innovation, we need 21st century industries, and as such, that's what we need to focus our money on, not to maintain industries that we no longer need. so innovation, 21st century industries, and that's where our money should go.
in writing. ‒ given the exposure of european industry to global competition, i believe that only an ambitious innovation policy, favouring the manufacture of high quality, innovative and energy-efficient products and promoting new production processes, will enable the european union to stand on its own feet in an increasingly competitive global context, thus allowing european industries to create r & d partnerships or strategic alliances and not limit their analysis to the internal market.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this resolution because i support the need to re-industrialize europe and increase jobs. european industry needs to maintain its competitiveness and its ability to invest in europe. in addition, european industry also faces social and environmental challenges that it needs to overcome. unfortunately, some companies follow strategies that focus only on short-term financial gains, which tend to negatively affect innovation and employment. there is a need for reindustrialisation, but also for the development of technical skills for a competitive industry. i believe that it is essential, in order to maximise the net job creation potential of the green economy, that the existing workforce has adequate opportunities to acquire the new skills needed for the circular economy. good collaboration between education systems, universities and the labour market is also vital for the creation of innovative interactive networks.
in writing. in the context of the recent caterpillar cases, europe urgently needs a new european reindustrialisation policy. the eu needs to develop border adjustment mechanisms to avoid ecological dumping and dumping of cheaper but poor quality products. these products do nothing but destroy european standards and affect the competitiveness of european industries. if the eu imposes a set of environmental and social standards, then the same european union must protect its industry and anticipate socioeconomic situations that lead to the dissolution of industrial capacities and the loss of many jobs. europe urgently needs to propose a strategy to cope with global competition from low-cost exporting countries on the european market, countries with a policy of rapid expansion across all continents and political and financial support from their governments. i ask the commission to start the consultation process with the social partners as a matter of urgency on the effectiveness of legislation on the legality of collective redundancies. i call on the commission to propose a revision of the european works council directive and to come forward with a legislative proposal on the information and consultation of workers, anticipation and management of restructuring.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this motion for a resolution that calls for a reindustrialisation policy in the eu following the redundancy plans of caterpillar and alstom.
in writing. ‒ the 2015 paris agreement is the first multilateral climate change agreement covering almost all global emissions. the agreement is a success for the whole world and a confirmation of the eu's orientation towards a low-carbon economy. the energy union project provides a broader framework within which the eu can provide an appropriate enabling environment for the energy transition. according to the international energy agency, full implementation of climate plans will lead to usd 13,5 trillion in investments in energy efficiency and low-carbon technologies between 2015 and 2030, with an annual average of usd 840 billion. in addition, the future energy union research, innovation and competitiveness strategy will take advantage of synergies between the energy sector, the transport sector, the circular economy, as well as industrial and digital innovation. this should lead to increased competitiveness of current and future european low-carbon and energy-efficient technologies.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution which offers immediate solutions to two situations with complex economic and social implications, but which at the same time sends a signal of solidarity with the regions of europe facing relocations of large enterprises. we are all aware that european industrial production is declining and that we need a european reindustrialisation policy to prevent this from happening again. in this respect, the document adopted today reiterates the need for a european reindustrialisation policy that promotes cooperation between old and newly established companies, which can create a much-needed oxygen bubble in the business environment. in this context, the european parliament calls on the european commission, in collaboration with the member states, to promote innovation and the digitalisation of european industry, taking into account the labour market offer, and thus create the conditions for new job creation.
in writing. ‒ in contrast, with the negative effects of globalisation materialising at an exponential rate, a reindustrialisation of europe is absolutely necessary. the european reindustrialisation policy must obviously focus on making human capital profitable, as it is the source of innovation and creativity. to this end, companies need to promote proactive behaviour and invest in a human-centred development model. it should be noted that the assumption of social responsibility by all european companies is the foundation for the viable and sustainable reindustrialisation of europe. compliance with a stakeholder engagement standard would lead, at a minimum, to the protection of workers, to the respect of their fundamental rights and to a viable and sustainable management of their careers, to ensuring cooperation and to valuing the involvement of all stakeholders in the decisions and actions of companies, to the development of fundamental and experimental research projects funded by structural funds and european investments in the sustainable development of european entities, communities and regions, etc. we hope for a coherent strategy on european reindustrialisation policy so that european entities can address global social and environmental challenges.
in writing. ‒ the caterpillar and alstom cases reflect an intensification of restructuring in several eu countries as a result of changes in the economic environment. in this context, member states will face significant economic challenges in the near future and must take all measures to improve the productivity and innovation levels of industry. i also believe that informing and consulting workers is an essential element of the social models in the member states. for this reason, stressing that the eu and its member states must coordinate their policies to ensure that they have sustainable and competitive manufacturing industries, i am voting in favour of the resolution.
president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, once again i am representing the vice-president of the commission/high representative. she is not able to be here and therefore as usual she has asked the presidency to speak on her behalf, and it is a great honour for me to participate in this important debate about syria. unfortunately, i have to start by recognising the fact that what we see in syria right now is the biggest humanitarian catastrophe of the century, and it is getting worse by the day. our exchange serves as an important input to the discussion among the eu foreign ministers at the next foreign affairs council in mid-october. in spite of the international community’s efforts to restore a nationwide ceasefire and press the parties in the conflict to come back to the negotiation table in geneva, the violence has escalated once again during the last two weeks. we have all seen the dreadful pictures of entire families caught in debris inaleppo under waves of bombardments. we all condemned the despicable attacks on the humanitarian aid convoy on 19 september and the deaths of the eight workers of the syrian red crescent, who lost their lives while trying to save others. last month in new york, at the un general assembly, a number of attempts were made to get the us—russia deal on the cessation of hostilities back on track. the high representative/vice—president has been actively involved in this effort through meetings with the syrian opposition, us and russian ministers as well as with the main regional players in the conflict. two international syria support group ministerial meetings were organised, which tried to salvage the cessation of hostilities and reduce the violence in the country. neither meeting led to a positive outcome. in fact the syrian parties are now further away from a negotiated solution for a political transition than before. let me reassure you that we are incessantly at work to contribute to the ending of the conflict and of the suffering of the syrian people. the political answers in the case of the syrian conflict are never straightforward or black and white. as we are working towards a renewed strategy for syria, let me recall the three policy tracks established by the international syria support group and the eu’s contribution to each: the humanitarian track, the ceasefire and the political track. firstly, the humanitarian track remains a core mission for the european union. we are – and always will be – the main donor of humanitarian aid for syria. the commission reactivated the echo office in damascus earlier this year. no matter what happens, our first duty is to provide support and hope to the syrian people, be it to the refugees in turkey, lebanon and jordan, in europe or inside syria, and especially in the besieged and hard-to-reach areas. we need to continue to do all we can to push for unhindered humanitarian aid deliveries throughout syria and an end to the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure. we continue to work with the united nations and with syrian organisations in this field, including inside syria, to deliver the aid needed. therefore high representative mogherini and commissioner stylianides launched an eu initiative on aleppo over the weekend, based on two main elements: first, let in humanitarian aid. we are working to facilitate the urgent delivery of basic lifesaving assistance to civilians in eastern aleppo. if the un ceasefire of at least two days is agreed, an inter—agency aid convoy will be ready to reach east aleppo from west aleppo to let out the wounded and the sick. we are working to ensure medical evacuations from east aleppo, with the focus on women, children and elderly people. this will be done in close cooperation with un agencies and other international agencies. in the last few days, the high representative has discussed this proposal with a number of international players, including the united states, russia and iran. the commission has also made eur 25 million available in an emergency fund for addressing priority needs, including health, water, food supplies and services. the eu will not be directly involved in operations on the ground but will provide pre-funding and assist in the facilitation operation, reaching out to partners on the ground, as well as to regional players in support of the initiative. but addressing the current emergency is not enough. the syrians in syria need access to services, education for their children and hospitals for the injured. they need jobs and functioning local economies if we want to build a strong society, if we want to avoid more refugees fleeing syria and if we want to avoid the radicalisation of the next generation of syrians. in the absence of a top—down political solution, we need to start building peace from the bottom up by helping local communities and civilian administration to start functioning and provide services to the local population in areas where this is possible. this is in line with the foreign affairs council conclusions of may 2016 that commit us to investing in civil society and support for local resilience inside syria. secondly, on the ceasefire, the eu as such is not a military player in the conflict. the greater responsibility lies with those who are supplying military assets and personnel. they have the leverage to push for an end to hostilities if they choose to, so we must continue to reach out to these regional actors. none of them will want syria to fall apart, but syria will fall apart if the war continues. we need to convince all actors that a political solution is the only option ahead of us. no side will win this war on the field. military offensives cannot bring victory nor impose peace, but only prolong the bloodshed. it took 16 years for the lebanese people to put an end to their civil war. we cannot afford such a scenario in syria. this leads me to the final and most important track: the political track. in these times of despair for the syrians, we must not lose hope in a political process and must never stop working for it. as the un special envoy, staffan de mistura, has recently explained in the un security council, losing hope equals abandoning the syrian people to death and devastation. many are working and many are now looking to europe for answers. high representative mogherini and her officials are engaged in a constant dialogue with the united states, russia and the countries of the region. we are thinking out of the box about what can create the conditions for the syrians to start talking seriously about their future within the parameters that have been set by previous attempts in geneva and by the un security council. we are aware of the different concerns and interests of the parties in the conflict and their own political objectives in syria. however, none of them can justify the indiscriminate targeting of civilians and the atrocities committed. in boston ten days ago, the foreign ministers of the united states, the united kingdom, france, germany and italy, and high representative mogherini, called on russia to take steps to restore the credibility of our effort, including by halting the regime’s bombardment of its own people. the high representative is also in direct contact with the syrian political opposition. we will continue to engage with them and support their quest for democracy, the rule of law and comprehensive and genuine political transition in the country while also committing to work towards the preservation of state institutions and the protection of minority rights. it is vital to maintain their engagement in the political process and to support the moderate opposition, otherwise we will face a growing process of the radicalisation of the syrian opposition, especially the armed groups, that could have long—term destructive consequences for the entire region. it is the european union’s political and moral duty to light the candle of hope again for the syrian people.

madam president, in expressing commitment to a carbon—free future, the signature of the cop21 agreement represents a remarkable global achievement. what we have to do now is to translate this commitment into action; to implement what has been included in the agreement, but also to go beyond what has already been agreed. one such area would be carbon pricing, an issue rather left out of the paris agreement, but which could bear crucial importance in emissions reduction. as opposed to emissions trading schemes – which in the past have often proved less effective because of the inflation in the tradable permits handed out – carbon taxes would represent a more effective way to reduce emissions: they would transform the cost of pollution from a negative externality into actual costs, favouring a change in polluting behaviour. additionally, revenues from such costs could, in the end, be used for the financing of new renewable energy infrastructures, thus starting a new virtuous cycle.

in writing. ‒ the dramatic situation in syria continues to be of concern to the international community and the european institutions. the way in which the various factions involved in the internal military conflict and supported by certain international actors fail to respect ceasefire agreements negotiated at the highest level is deplorable. the result is an increasing number of civilian casualties and refugees, especially in the context of the siege of aleppo by government troops and the shelling of humanitarian convoys. instead of a joint offensive against the islamic state and other terrorist groups, russian and iranian-backed government troops and us-backed rebels are choosing to confront each other to the detriment of any peaceful solution. the european union, as an international actor neighbouring this conflict zone, condemns the violation of international humanitarian law and urges the parties to the conflict to cease hostilities as soon as possible and to work towards a sustainable future for the syrian state, in line with un security council resolution 2254. in this context, the co-chairs of the international syria support group, the united states and russia, have an important responsibility for the resumption of negotiations. i support the adoption of these resolutions.
mr president, the european union is the global leader in combating climate change. at the paris conference we committed ourselves to reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 20% compared to 1990. what message are we sending to the people, to the politicians, to the investors, to the society? that we have no time to lose, history is not waiting for us, and let's get off the train because the train has already left, let's get off the train that leads, whether we like it or not, to a low-carbon economy. only then can we begin a process of reindustrialization for the 21st century. i want to make it clear that i am not in favour of introducing a tax on all financial transactions to finance climate change and here i voted against this paragraph. we have to be creative and find other sources of funding.
in writing. ‒ given that tackling climate change is a global priority, ensuring energy security, sustainable economic growth and sustainable job creation, i believe it is important to adopt a holistic and systemic approach to the development and implementation of policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions on the one hand, and on the other hand i believe that research and innovation in the context of climate change policies and adaptations, as well as low-emission and resource-efficient technologies, are fundamental to tackling climate change in a cost-effective way, reducing dependence on fossil fuels and promoting the use of secondary raw materials.

in writing. ‒ human activities represent the main cause for global warming, with widespread and substantial change occurring in natural and human systems all over the world. i have voted for this motion for a resolution that urges countries to reduce their greenhouse gases, which are the main cause of the greenhouse effect.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on the implementation of the paris agreement and the 2016 un conference on climate change in marrakesh, morocco (cop 22). as a member of the delegation to cop22 and as shadow rapporteur for the cop22 resolution in the itre commission, i stress that we must ensure energy security, sustainable economic growth and sustainable job creation alongside the fight against climate change. climate investments require a stable and predictable legal framework as well as clear policy signals. until a level playing field is achieved, the eu should maintain appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure the competitiveness of its industries and to prevent, where appropriate, carbon leakage, taking into account the need for coherence between energy, industry and climate policies. a more ambitious target for energy efficiency in the european union can contribute to achieving an ambitious climate target, and at the same time reduce the risk of carbon leakage. i also stress the need to prevent and alleviate energy poverty in order to protect and help vulnerable and poor households.
in writing. ‒ i supported this resolution and i am in favour of a rapid ratification of the paris agreement by all parties. it is critical for the environment, and for the european industries working hard to reduce their emissions, that there is a global framework in place. a binding agreement which includes all major emitters should reduce unfair competition for european producers and help limit temperature increases to less than 2° above pre-industrial levels. failure to reach this 2° target would be likely to cause significant environmental, economic and social pressures in the medium and long term.
in writing. ‒ the adoption of the paris agreement was a watershed moment in the international community's fight against climate change. its implementation will determine how our children will live in the decades to come. the european union and its member states were among the main supporters of the adoption of the agreement, which has 187 signatory parties and is a balanced, ambitious and fair document. the setting of a global average temperature increase ceiling of 1,5 degrees celsius above pre-industrial levels is an important commitment of the signatory states. in the context of the 2016 un conference on climate change (cop22) in marrakesh, the current resolution draws attention to the need for eu member states to ratify and implement the paris agreement without delay, assesses the state of implementation of the kyoto protocol, highlights the role of non-state actors in reducing emissions, the importance of climate finance and diplomatic dialogue with other international actors. the importance of adapting industrial production, energy policies, research, innovation and digital technologies, and support for developing countries in this area is also mentioned. i support the adoption of this resolution, which is so relevant to achieving the targets of stopping climate warming in the next period.

in writing. ‒ i voted for this report because i believe it is important for consumers to be protected by only allowing products that do not affect their health to be placed on the internal market. food is one of the main routes of human exposure to chemicals through the materials with which it comes into contact. in the current context, it is important to guarantee a high level of consumer protection in order to ensure the effective functioning of the internal market for mcas. better harmonisation at eu level, the development of uniform safety standards and better coordination in terms of risk assessment, traceability, enforcement and compliance checks on compliance with the legislation in force are needed. as regards the marketing of mca materials in the eu, the criteria for documentation and official registration of business activity need to be facilitated in order to avoid gaps in risk assessment. i consider this report to be an important step towards achieving very important objectives such as guaranteeing and protecting human health in the eu, ensuring the effective functioning of the internal market and facilitating the implementation of legislation.

in writing. ‒ before its consumption, food comes into contact with many materials during its production, processing, storage, preparation and serving. these materials are known as food contact materials (fcms). i have voted in favour of this report that will set out general safety requirements applicable to all fcms.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which highlights many of the concerns related to food contact materials. i particularly support the emphasis on safer alternatives to endocrine disrupting chemicals. once again, i urge the european commission to provide the necessary support to reduce and prevent our exposure to the potentially harmful effects of endocrine disruptors. whilst human health is the overriding priority, this report also contains constructive approaches for reducing costs to industry. savings could be passed on to consumers if eu-wide standards replaced the current patchwork of varied rules and different standards.
in writing. ‒ the european union is the guarantor of the protection of the health of the citizens of the member states and of the marketing of products that meet food safety standards. food contact materials (fcms), including food packaging, kitchenware, utensils, must have an appropriate chemical composition to avoid the transfer of harmful substances into food. to this end, the eu adopted in 2004 regulation no 1935 to ensure the safe management of plastic, ceramic, cellulose or smart material compounds in accordance with the relevant studies. for the rest of the cmos, standards are set at national level, which creates real difficulties at community level, especially on the free movement of goods. in order to harmonise these standards, this resolution proposes a common approach to the recycling and use process, in line with the concept of the circular economy, more complex joint tests at european level to avoid endocrine disruptors, in-depth research on nanomaterials, the revision of the regulation on ceramic products and more rigorous controls. it is a resolution aimed at eliminating the health risks of the mcas, which is why i support its adoption.
mr president, the responsibility for the correct application of union law, which means union legislation, directives, regulations and the union treaty, is shared between the member states and the commission. the commission is the guarantor, the guardian of the treaties, and it must take on this role more firmly. in 2014, the commission received around four thousand complaints for potential breaches of union law and launched around nine hundred new procedures for the non-application of union law by member states in the fields of environment, health, consumer protection, internal market and so on. what do i want to emphasize now? two things: 1) member states must transpose union legislation in a timely and correct manner, they must do so by clear laws and not by complicated ones because things only work with clear laws; 2) we here in parliament should stop stumbling into complicated resolutions and statements with plus, and, especially, if that people don't understand, but adopt clear laws.
in writing. ‒ given that the main responsibility for the implementation and correct application of eu law lies with the member states, but also taking into account the important role of social partners, civil society organisations and other stakeholders in the development of legislation and in monitoring and reporting on shortcomings in the transposition and application of eu law by member states, i believe that existing eu legislation should be supplemented where there are gaps or interpretation issues that bring more accessibility, clarity and consistency in the interpretation of existing rules, for the benefit of citizens and businesses, as well as the administration and its officials.

in writing. ‒ the number of formal infringement procedures in 2014 decreased due to the effectiveness of the eu pilot procedure. this is great news, but much remains to be done. one deplorable fact is that parliament still has only limited access to vital information and thus cannot play the role of ‘monitoring the monitor’ efficiently and effectively.
in writing. ‒ in response to the request from the european parliament and member states, the commission draws up an annual report regarding the monitoring of the application of eu law. i have voted in favour of this report, which states that the environment, transport and the internal market and services were the policy areas with the most infringement cases in 2014.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on monitoring the application of union law: annual report 2014. the new interinstitutional agreement on better law-making contains provisions aimed at improving the implementation and application of eu law and encouraging more structured cooperation in this regard. we support the call in the agreement for better identification of national measures that are not strictly linked to union law (a practice known as 'super-regulation'). we stress the importance of enhanced transposition and the need for member states to notify and clearly indicate national measures supplementing the provisions of union directives. when applying eu law, member states should avoid adding unnecessary burdens to eu legislation, as this leads to a misconception of eu legislative activity and increases unjustified scepticism towards the eu among citizens. we would point out, however, that this in no way affects the prerogatives of member states to adopt, at national level, stricter social and environmental standards than those agreed at eu level.
in writing. ‒ the commission’s 32nd ‘annual report on monitoring the application of eu law’ shows that the number of formal infringement procedures has decreased in the last five years, although environment, transport and internal market and services remained the policy areas in which most infringement cases were open in 2014. according to the commission, the decrease in infringement procedures reflects the effectiveness of their dialogue with member states. however, the european parliament has little access to this type of information, and it is difficult for us to evaluate to what extent this reduction is due to a more effective dialogue with member states. consequently, i support this report as i strongly believe that the european parliament could play a more prominent role in the analysis of how accession countries comply with eu law. furthermore, i agree with the rapporteur`s conclusion that the enforcement of eu law is still not sufficiently transparent and i believe that measures should be taken to increase transparency.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, let me first thank you for introducing this very important topic of sustainable finance. vice-president dombrovskis and i are jointly responsible for the capital markets union and this obviously has a close link to the sustainable finance issue. last year we witnessed some landmark international agreements with the adoption of the sustainable development goals (sdg) and the paris climate agreement (cop21). implementing a transition towards a more sustainable world requires determined efforts in many policy areas. in terms of public finance, the eu is leading the way due to its commitment to spend at least 20% of its 2014-2020 budget on climate-related projects and policies. work is ongoing to increase the availability of green funds through the european fund for strategic investments (efsi). but we need to move beyond public finance and to further reach out to private investors. the financial sector has a role to play. the capital markets union initiative addresses the importance of long-term and sustainable investments. in the most recent cmu communication, the commission has indicated a need for a broader strategy on sustainable finance. this is necessary to support investment in clean technologies and ensure that the financial system can finance growth in a sustainable manner over the long term. the commission also monitors developments in the green bond market. a study on the potential of the bond market to finance resource-efficient investments is under preparation. the final report will be ready in november. the commission has also adopted initiatives to increase company transparency, such as the directive on non-financial reporting that will be transposed by the end of 2016, and the related non-binding guidelines, currently under preparation. last july, a political agreement on iorp2 was achieved that will require occupational pension funds to consider taking into account environmental, social and governance factors in their investment decisions. the commission is also assessing the follow-up to the recent public consultation on long-term and sustainable investment which emphasised the importance of environmental, social and governance issues for the long-term performance of companies and investors, and the challenges institutional investors faced in this area. since sustainable finance has no boundaries, work must also be done at global level. the commission supports the work of the fsb industry-led task force which will provide recommendations on climate-related financial disclosures early next year. we will take these into account as much as possible when preparing the upcoming eu guidelines on non-financial reporting. at the same time, the commission is a member of the g20 green finance study group (gfsg), which recently identified options on how to mobilise private green investment; we will also continue this work under the german presidency. beyond relying on public finance and mobilising the private sector, the commission is also looking at how, and to what extent, climate change implications could affect the financial sector or even be a source of systemic risk to it. some eu institutions and central banks of eu member states have already begun analysing this. last february, the european systemic risk board proposed enhanced disclosures and the incorporation of climate-related prudential risks into stress tests as policy responses to mitigate risks for the financial system. this may be a suitable trigger to integrate considerations about long-term environmental risks and opportunities into the mindset of private investors. undoubtedly more needs to be done at eu level, and in a comprehensive manner. that is why the commission will establish an expert group on green finance that will help formulate the eu strategy. this group will provide advice on how to mobilise private capital for sustainable and green investments; and to better understand and deal with the financial risks related to the transition to a low-carbon economy. the expert group will be composed of senior experts representing various stakeholders of the green and sustainable finance spectrum. honourable members, i am interested to hear your views on the ongoing work streams and also i am expecting some input from your side for future work streams.
on behalf of the epp group. mr president, there is no doubt that we are all experiencing the effects of climate change and no country is immune from these effects. even in a country like my country, which is far from oceans, we have climate change that simply cannot be explained. therefore, all efforts that are made to mobilise the financing needed to change the structure of economies from economies that are very fuel-intensive and generate greenhouse gas emissions to economies that substantially reduce these greenhouse gas emissions are welcome. i would like to draw attention to a number of initiatives that the european commission has in this area, as mentioned by mr katainen, vice-president of the european commission. indeed, there is a fundamental question that we have to answer: how do we bring private capital into this financing? we know very well: private capital will not enter this financing unless it also sees a favorable return for investors. that is why our efforts to achieve the single market for capital in the european union and other efforts are welcome. let's not forget that there was a commitment, made many years ago, by all the countries in the world, to make a fund of about a hundred billion dollars to finance the transition to an economy that responds to the challenges of climate change, and basically, not much of that commitment was realized at that time by the countries. within the european union, we have a lot of funds that can be used from both the european union budget and from the resources of the member states, which can be used to encourage this transition to a green energy economy. but i would like to mention here that the populations, the population, the citizens, have had a negative reaction to certain incentive schemes that we have devised, especially for those who invested in green energy (wind and so on), where they simply created incentives that were much too high for what was normal. so i think we need to be very clear here, to think about what the optimal incentive size should be for those who invest in green energy.
madam president, i am not in favour of unnecessary legislation being adopted by the eu. i am in favour of the principle of subsidiarity, but i must say that in this case i am convinced that the adoption of legislation makes sense. as soon as we have a single customs territory, a single customs legislation, a single customs code, it seems logical to me that there should also be a single set of sanctions that will apply throughout the eu. in short, the penalty for a particular offence should be the same throughout the eu, if possible. it's a fundamental principle of the rule of law. a similar offense is to be punished by a similar penalty. so that is why i support the amendment, why i agree with the idea, although i am generally reluctant to accept new european legislation. if we look at the actual implementation, i have to say that the proposal put forward by the commission is unfortunately not very good and here, like my predecessors, i commend the work of the rapporteur of the imco committee in particular, who in my view has succeeded in removing a number of the legal problems of the legislation. i agree with the text that came out of the imco committee. one thing at least: the penalty is to be imposed for wrongdoing, the objective liability which was in the commission's original proposal is, in my view, absolutely unacceptable and has seriously harmed the entrepreneurs. so perhaps, commissioner, in the future, we should have better legislation than you propose here.
madam president, commissioner, i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteurs and, of course, the position of the colleagues who have spoken. i do not think we can speak of a customs union either when we have fully harmonised legislation throughout the european union, but the enforcement and, indeed, the verification of compliance with customs rules and the imposition of sanctions is a matter for each individual state. and we now know concretely that we have differences -- and big differences, not very small. this, in my view, disadvantages primarily small, small and medium-sized enterprises. the same formalities, the same documents, the same steps are to be followed by the economic operator, but when he passes through one customs office or another, the sanction is different if things go wrong at a control. i therefore support the principle of taking action to bring about a certain level of alignment in the 28 member states, because that is why we have a single market, to have national procedures, of course, but to have harmonised levels of sanctions for customs infringements. i believe that this provides legal certainty for businesses and could create a more level playing field, which would encourage businesses, especially smes, to invest in all member states and stimulate economic growth. i have personally tabled amendments and i hope that this report will be voted on and that we will take steps, because i do not think that we will end the customs union with this report alone. and i also think, at the same time, that the member states must, and it is also the role of the commission, to adopt greater transparency and see better enforcement of customs legislation. finally, we must all move towards measures that also improve the compliance of companies with customs legislation, but not encourage the crossing of certain borders just because the penalties are lower. i support the report and congratulate mrs callas.

in writing. ‒ even though it has been several years since the economic crisis that affected all the states of the world, it still puts pressure on national economies. eu member states are forced to take austerity measures to balance their budgets, and the implementation of the european structural and investment funds is necessary. these funds are needed as national budgets are under pressure and countries are struggling to find sufficient funds to co-finance regional policy projects. the change in the amount of payments could be very beneficial for states experiencing economic difficulties, which involves a temporary increase in payment appropriations. i voted in favour of the report on certain member states experiencing or threatened with serious difficulties with respect to their financial stability because i believe that the eu needs to come to the aid of all member states experiencing financial instability, which is beneficial first of all for the states that need these credits, but not least it is beneficial for the eu.
in writing. ‒ after this period of financial and economic crisis in which member states have taken austerity measures to balance their budgets, the eu needs to implement its main funding instrument: the european structural and investment funds (esi funds) to help them in regional policy. in addition to romania, four other member states (ireland, portugal, cyprus and greece) were eligible for an increase of the payment under article 24 of regulation (eu) no 1303/2013. romania, ireland, portugal and cyprus have completed their economic adjustment programmes. of these, only greece is still subject to an adjustment programme and is receiving related financial assistance until the third quarter of 2018. in view of the fact that greece continues to face serious difficulties with respect to its financial stability, the period of application of an increase in the amount of payments for member states experiencing temporary budgetary difficulties should be extended. i therefore support the commission's proposal without amendments under an accelerated procedure.
in writing. ‒ the financial and economic crisis is putting pressure on national economies and member states have taken austerity measures to balance their budgets, leading to budgetary difficulties in finding enough funds to co-finance regional policy projects. countries such as greece, cyprus, ireland, romania and portugal were eligible for additional payments in the period from 1 january 2014 to 30 june 2016. greece is the only country where a financial assistance programme is currently being applied, the others being beyond the period of application. i voted to change the period in which a country receiving financial assistance is eligible for additional payments. this could lead to an increase in administrative capacity to achieve a higher absorption of funds.
in writing. ‒ the recent financial and economic crisis puts pressure on national economies. national budgets are under strain. consequently, in many member states, investments by the european structural and investment funds are the main or sole source of investment. however, for countries experiencing budgetary deficits, it might be difficult to find funds for the national co-financing of cohesion policy projects. articles 24 and 120(3) of the common provisions regulation (cpr) intend to help member states receiving financial assistance and experiencing budgetary deficits. article 24 allows for so-called ‘top-ups’ – increased payments under esif. currently, only greece has a financial assistance programme in place under article 24 of the cpr. given the fragile economic state of greece, the commission proposed the continuation of top-up provisions which would otherwise have stopped if the commission had not come forward with a legislative proposal before the end of the accounting year (30 june 2016). after a review, the commission had to come up with a proposal for a possible extension of co-financement rate for cyprus before 30 june 2016. the legislative proposal foresees the extension of 85% of co-financement until the end of 2014-2020 financial period. i supported the proposal in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ the financial crisis continues to put pressure on national economies. under this pressure, countries face difficulties in accessing european structural and investment funds. if the funds are not absorbed, member states may receive additional financial assistance. the commission shall carry out an assessment and, if the economic situation in the countries concerned so warrants, the financial assistance shall be extended. greece, cyprus, ireland, romania and portugal were eligible for extended financial assistance during the period from 1 january 2014 to 30 june 2016. financial assistance for all these countries, except greece, has expired. i support this report containing the commission's proposal because it proposes to change the duration of a country's eligibility for additional payments. the commission also proposes that member states continue to be eligible until 30 june of the year following the calendar year in which they cease to receive financial assistance.

in writing. ‒ the main objectives of the proposal are to bridge the gap between different legal regimes through a common platform of rules and to enhance the level playing field between economic operators in the customs union. to this end, it includes a common list of infringements and establishes a common scale of administrative sanctions. having divergent sanctions poses problems to economic operators, to international trade relations (pressure from wto is quoted in the impact assessment), and creates uneven compliance costs and administrative burden that could make some member states more ‘attractive’ (forum shopping). i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report because it is important to clarify the scope of the eu's customs infringements directive and the related sanctions. it is important to ensure that only infringements committed negligently or intentionally constitute infringements, which is why the definition of negligent behaviour plays a key role in this directive. as far as sanctions are concerned, it's important that we have the same sanctions in all 28 states. i think it is necessary that there is no disproportion of penalties applied to the same type of error. we must no longer allow goods to be routed indirectly only to certain border points where sanctions are lower or even non-existent. the report's proposals can ensure that businesses better comply with the european customs code and can also ensure an increase in fair competition in the internal market.
in writing. ‒ having divergent sanctions poses problems to economic operators and to international trade relations and creates administrative burdens. this report is a compromise text that aims at addressing these issues. i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ one of the foundations of the european union as well as the backbone of the single market is the european customs union. i am in favour of this report that reiterates the need for an integrated approach with regard to the enforcement of customs legislation as well as the standardization of applied sanctions when the rules are infringed.
in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the legal framework of the union for customs infringements and related sanctions. i believe that ensuring the uniform application of penalties for non-compliance with customs legislation is extremely important for all eu operators, but also for the stability and predictability of markets. the discrepancies between the various member states destabilise the competitive market, giving advantages to only a few operators. this creates mistrust among member states' administrations, but also at the level of companies or small businesses, of the eu's ability to ensure fair competition. i therefore support this report, which supports the adoption of a directive to harmonise non-criminal sanctions for breaches of customs legislation.
in writing. ‒ the customs union is considered to be an essential component of the european union and the single market. however, there is currently no integrated approach to customs compliance that includes the application of penalties, as this area varies according to national legislation. since the rules of the customs union and customs policy are an exclusive competence of the union, a unified approach to customs compliance is needed to ensure a level playing field within its territory. such an approach is also in line with the eu's wto obligations to adopt convergent sanctions regimes. the commission proposal calls on member states to have effective, proportionate and dissuasive customs sanctioning systems that converge through the application of a modernised customs code and the use of electronic means. such measures would encourage trade and increased compliance, ensure penalties commensurate with the evasion of duties and distinguish between criminal and civil penalties. however, customs authorities would be the only ones able to decide on the application of extenuating or aggravating circumstances in the administration of sanctions, which raises the issue of mutual trust between member states. since this matter needs to be resolved, i support referring the report back to the committee responsible for adjustment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament's report on the union's legal framework for customs infringements and related sanctions. the customs union and trade policy are the exclusive competence of the european union; therefore, the eu alone can develop a common approach to ensuring compliance with customs legislation. member states have committed themselves to endeavour in particular to achieve two objectives: to ensure that customs administrations interact and produce results as effectively as if they were a single administration, to ensure checks with equivalent results and to support legitimate commercial activities, as well as the necessary protection of the financial interests of the union. however, without an integrated approach to enforcement, including the application of sanctions, the customs administrations of the member states cannot act as a unit, especially given the major differences between the sanctioning systems of the member states, highlighted by the report of the customs sanctions project group in 2010. the european commission published on 13 december 2013 a proposal for a directive on the legal framework of the union for customs infringements and related sanctions.

in writing. ‒ organised crime is one of the main threats globally. organisations constituted by criminal groups have intensified their illegal activities in recent years and new action is needed to sanction their actions. it is therefore necessary to create a framework for the correct transposition of existing rules, the monitoring and evaluation of their effectiveness. member states should therefore transpose all existing instruments at european and international level in the fight against organised crime, corruption and money laundering. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that a multidisciplinary approach is needed to prevent and combat organised crime and at the same time to achieve a strengthened partnership between national authorities and the relevant eu agencies.
in writing. ‒ corruption is a threat to democracy, the rule of law, social equity and justice, it erodes the principles of effective administration, undermines the market economy and endangers the stability of state institutions. most anti-corruption actions have been mainly punitive measures, the effect of which has not been far from expected. global anti-corruption policy must be expressed most effectively through a european action plan to eradicate organised crime, corruption and money laundering. i support the ep motion for a resolution on the report on 'fighting corruption and the follow-up to the crim resolution'. eradicating corruption will boost economic activity. this will make the european union stronger, the economic market of the member states more attractive to foreign investors, increase private sector revenues, improve the quality of services provided to the population and make it possible to promote social policy more effectively, develop the health and education systems. these actions are impossible without adequate support from the commission, which must propose legislative measures to fill any gaps that may exist in the fight against organised crime and corruption and to improve cross-border judicial cooperation.
in writing. ‒ organised crime is a global threat that requires a joint response coordinated by the eu and its member states. organised criminal groups have demonstrated a particular tendency and capacity to diversify their activities, thereby adapting to different geographical factors and economic and social contexts, exploiting their weaknesses and vulnerabilities, acting simultaneously in different markets and taking advantage of differences in the legal provisions in the legal systems of the member states. organised crime, corruption and money laundering pose serious threats to the eu economy, significantly reducing tax revenues for member states, but also for the eu as a whole. re-evaluating the legislative framework to fill any gaps is a priority. the phenomenon of organised crime has a cross-border dimension and requires more effective cooperation at eu level. i voted for the creation of an appropriate eu-wide system for the exchange of information between judicial authorities within the union.
in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report is a follow-up to the parliament report adopted in the last legislature on organised crime, corruption and money laundering (the ‘crim’ report). the report was drafted in anticipation of the commission’s 2nd anti-corruption report (still not published), takes a fresh look at the recommendations set out in the crim report, and seeks to draw conclusions on the recommendations which were followed up and those which were not. at a time when all the talk is of a ‘terrorist threat’, it is crucial not to forget the importance of having a serious strategy backed up by serious action to tackle the growing prevalence of organised crime and corruption infiltrating many levels of society in the eu. i voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ migration is a global and multidimensional phenomenon caused by a number of negative factors, but which can have an impact on demographic trends and economic development. in this context, the european union, but also its member states, must set an example in the promotion and protection of human rights. respect for the rights of migrants, irrespective of their status, is a priority for the union. i voted for closer cooperation with the relevant international organisations in defence of migrants' rights. identifying specific measures that governments can take to increase the potential of legal migration is necessary to stimulate development.
in writing. ‒ the report makes an analysis of the main root causes of the migration phenomena in third countries and stresses that according to the unhrc, the 65 million displaced people are affected by humanitarian conflicts resulting from conflicts and worldwide economic situation and that they should see their dignity and human rights respected. members call on governments to address the human rights protection gap, which migrants continue to face and to abolish punitive legal schemes which criminalise migration. the report also underlines that ‘the concept of safe countries of origin’ should not prevent individual assessments of asylum application and asks for migrants who need international protection to be identified and for their application to be considered. moreover a call is made on states to ratify all international treaties and conventions and to apply the standards applicable to migrants’ rights which may be found in a variety of legal international instruments. i supported the adoption of this report in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ unhrc estimates there are 65.3 million displaced and over 10 million stateless people worldwide. according to the un, there are 244 million international migrants. migration is therefore a global issue. significantly, migration is a human right enshrined in the geneva convention and undhr. however, many refugees, asylum seekers and irregular migrants are criminalised and penalised. development aid is key to tackling the migration crisis. member states should honour their pledge of 0.7 gni for development aid. this aid should consider the root causes of migration and its global context. the flow of migration is largely within the global south, with most refugees hosted by developing countries. therefore, aid should address sources of conflict and migration in host and transit countries, and mostly in the countries of origin of the migrants.
in writing. ‒ i am in favour of this motion for a resolution that stresses that human rights are essential to all human beings regardless of their ethnicity or religion, following the migration of persons that have been forced to leave their countries due to conflicts, persecution, violations of human rights and/or extreme poverty.
in writing. ‒ this report highlights the difficulties migrants face both in their countries of origin, which is why they are forced to seek refuge in other countries, and in countries of transit and destination. international law in general and human rights in particular provide for the right of any person to benefit from migrant status when the situation calls for it, and i support by my vote today the call for both eu member states and the international community to do more to protect these people and ensure that the rights they have are respected. the report also highlights that many migrants end up in developing countries, which face major difficulties in managing these flows. in this regard, i believe that supporting these countries in ensuring adequate treatment for all migrants must continue to be a priority.
in writing. ‒ migration in general is a global, multidimensional phenomenon generated by a multitude of causes (economic, social, political) which also produces positive effects as a result of globalisation and the interdependencies of markets. from a human perspective, migration contributes to demographic developments and to economic and social growth, provided that the fundamental rights of those who migrate are respected. in this regard, migration policies should contribute to the full integration of migrants into host country communities so that they can benefit from their potential (social, cultural, economic, creative). of course, these national policies must be coherent and comprehensive, taking into account all the dimensions and implications of the migration phenomenon, the result of cooperation and collaboration between all those interested in this complex phenomenon.
in writing. ‒ this report underlines the need for urgent action to address all human rights violations faced by migrants, which are most acute in situations of pressure due to security challenges and natural disasters. according to the unhrc, the 65 million displaced people are affected by humanitarian conflicts resulting from violent conflicts and worldwide economic situations. the report asks the european union and its member states to lead by example in promoting and protecting the human rights of migrants, notably within their own borders, and to systematically incorporate migration issues as a component of their political dialogue with all countries. the report calls on the eu to provide technical assistance to improve national and local migrant integration policies and to step up its foreign policies in bringing peace and stability to those areas where war and conflict trigger enormous migration flows to the european union. i support this report as we need as much visibility and acknowledgement as possible towards the issue of human rights violations faced by migrants, as well as solutions to what triggers the enormous flows of migration to the european union.

in writing. ‒ the global supply of lng is expected to increase dramatically in the next few years (50%) and consequently the price of it will most likely go down, which according to the commission represents a major opportunity for the eu, particularly when it comes to gas security and resilience, and especially for those member states currently heavily reliant on a single supplier, and hence vulnerable to supply disruptions. the report recommends that in order to exploit the full potential of lng and to make the eu an attractive market for suppliers, the union needs to ensure that the necessary infrastructure is in place. however, as existing lng infrastructure in the eu is currently heavily underused, the report underlines the need to, before supporting new regasification terminals and from a cross-border perspective, promote the most efficient use of existing lng terminals, also to avoid technology lock-in or stranded assets in fossil fuel infrastructure. the eu should also step up its efforts to cooperate closely with international partners to promote free, liquid and transparent global lng markets.

in writing. ‒ the report on the situation of connectivity in central and eastern europe is a first and major step towards reducing the significant disparities accumulated between this region and the west. it recognises that, despite efforts undertaken by the commission through its cohesion policy, several eastern member states are lagging behind in terms of infrastructure projects and attracting the eu funds available for these. in light of this, the report is proposing that the commission comes with a strategy for central and eastern europe, integrating all large infrastructure projects, taking into account both the differences between various regions and the long-term objectives of the eu. at the same time it proposes means by which european traffic can be diverted towards more transport modes, taking thus into consideration environmental concerns and congestion problems. not least, the present report brings a new perspective to tourism by soliciting that european infrastructure projects be connected with tourism objectives, underlining the close relationship between this industry and transport.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the own-initiative report on improving the connectivity and accessibility of transport infrastructure in central and eastern europe. high-quality transport links are essential for economic activities in europe and for the quality of life of our citizens. at the heart of fostering economic, social and territorial cohesion in and between eu member states are easily accessible and well-connected transport networks, which include the local, regional, national and cross-border dimension of freight and passenger transport.

we have been talking for a long time about a mechanism to check the rule of law and respect for human rights, respect for the law in the member states. it is necessary such a mechanism and i am totally to implement it. it's a monitoring mechanism, a tracking mechanism, but also a correction mechanism, obviously, because that's the goal, to correct what's wrong, and to sanction if necessary. and we're talking about states where democracy is still fragile -- like the post-communist states -- mainly about these. i am glad that parliament is not alone in this fight, that there will also be non-governmental organisations, that there will also be independent experts in respect for the law and respect for human rights. also, if the mechanism of sanctioning those states that do not respect the standards of democracy and the rule of law proposed by the commission will also lead to savings, as the report shows, then we will achieve two objectives.
in writing. ‒ europe has a long tradition of democracy, the rule of law and citizens' rights, beginning with athenian democracy followed by roman law. although the eu currently has some tools to ensure respect for the principles of democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights, gaps remain. it is imperative to adopt a framework that enables the eu to address not only certain breaches of its laws but also serious risks to democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights. i voted for the adoption of an eu pact for democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights, a pact that will lead to respect for the eu's fundamental values in practice, not just in theory. a number of additional non-legislative measures are needed to ensure a comprehensive view of the respect for the values on which the eu is founded in addition to this pact.
in writing. ‒ even if the eu has several existing instruments at its disposal to ensure the principles on democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights are upheld, substantial gaps remain and in practice, such instruments are often limited in scope, inadequate and ineffective, or they are unlikely to be used. in some cases, their uneven application is perceived by many as politically motivated, arbitrary and unfairly targeting certain countries. there is no integrated mechanism for the systematic, impartial and complete monitoring of all eu member states and institutions. therefore it is imperative to adopt a framework that enables the eu to address not only infringements to specific eu laws, but also (risk of) serious threats to democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights. european values are given the highest importance in the treaties, it is high time they also got the highest importance in practice.

in writing. ‒ plant health is very important for plant production, public and private green spaces, natural ecosystems, ecosystem services and biodiversity in the eu. therefore, strengthening prevention, surveillance and rapid action measures in the event of outbreaks of plant pests within the eu is of major importance, starting from detection of eu quarantine pests in areas where they were not known to be present, surveillance, early eradication of new pest outbreaks, public information on the economic, social and environmental impact of plant pests, correlated with financial support for undertakings and competent phytosanitary authorities in the member states.
in writing. ‒ plant health is a matter of the utmost concern for the european union and the common agricultural policy (cap), which supports the sustainable development of the agriculture, horticulture and forestry sectors. the main threat in these sectors is represented by pests, which are insects, fungi, bacteria or viruses that can cause significant damage to crops, especially when they come from other continents. to this end, the european institutions may regulate the treatments required to increase the resistance of native plants or may require more rigorous controls to be carried out on plants coming from other geographical areas. this last category of measures can provide very effective protection against the spread of harmful organisms and plant diseases. the commission has therefore proposed a higher level of plant import security, depending on the risks involved in each case. for imports of lower risk plants, it was proposed to include the introduction of plant passports to avoid any possibility of spreading pests. in extreme cases, temporary bans, compulsory phytosanitary certificates and contingency plans for emergencies are provided for. i support the adoption of this necessary report.
in writing. ‒ i support the report as it clearly focuses on the need to increase investment in the eu in order to create more growth, convergence, quality jobs and fight poverty and inequality. hence, i strongly support the introduction of the social imbalance procedure into the economic coordination and the proposed european minimum income framework to fight social exclusion in the eu. the eu and the member states need to better implement the revised economic policy mix, which aims at increasing investment linked to eu2020 policy objectives including quality employment, education, innovation and growth enhancing policies. the single market is a pillar of the eu economy, therefore i am in favour of an inclusive single market, with enhanced governance, which favours better regulation and competition, which i believe is a crucial instrument to improve growth, cohesion, employment and competitiveness and to preserve the confidence of the business sector and consumers. the commission should monitor the progress made by the member states, the formal inclusion of the single-market pillar in the european semester is very important to enable continuous monitoring of single-market indicators, allowing for systematic follow-up and assessment of member states’ progress on csrs.
in writing. ‒ i believe that the european union and the member states should better implement the revised economic policy mix which aims at increasing investment linked to eu2020 policies objectives (more growth, convergence, quality jobs and fight poverty and inequality).
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report on the european semester for economic policy coordination that calls for the implementation of sustainable reforms to improve growth, cohesion, productivity and competitiveness following the slow growth rates of only 1.8% for the eu in 2016.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on the european semester for economic policy coordination: implementation of the priorities for 2016. in its 2016 country specific recommendations, the commission paid particular attention to the three priorities to further strengthen economic growth: supporting investment for innovation, development and job creation, achieving socially balanced structural reforms and encouraging the responsible management of public finances. a number of country-specific recommendations support a functioning and integrated single market, including the creation of financing and investment opportunities that foster the development of enterprises and in particular smes, contributing to job creation, the smooth functioning of e-government, public procurement and mutual recognition, including the mutual recognition of qualifications. however, more efforts are needed from the commission to support the sustainability of public finances in line with the stability and growth pact, making full use of its flexibility clauses. we call on the commission to prioritise measures that reduce the obstacles to larger investment flows, obstacles which at eu level are caused by a lack of clarity on the strategies to be pursued, in particular in the following areas: energy, transport, communications and the digital economy.
in writing. ‒ i am in support of the report as it addresses the challenges facing europe in the context of the global economic slowdown. firstly, it recognises the importance of coherence between european union’s framework on economic governance and policy instruments to strengthen cohesion among member states in the eu by reducing regional development disparities of the member states. secondly, the report stresses that the lack of sustainable investment and the shortcomings in completing the single market are depriving the eu of its full growth potential which is imperative given the deteriorating international environment, the failure to implement sustainable reforms and the divergences in the economic and social performance in different parts of the union. thirdly, i am in full support of the report’s confirmation and welcome of the agreement of the paris climate conference (cop21) in december 2015 and its call on the member states and the commission to implement it.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the own-initiative report on the european semester for economic policy coordination: implementation of the priorities for 2016. it also includes the opinion of the regional development committee, which recommends the use of the european fund for strategic investments (efsi) in a complementary and additional way to the esi funds, so that the full potential of public and private investment can be exploited and a fairer geographical balance ensured.
in writing. ‒ trans fatty acids (trans fats) are a type of unsaturated fatty acids that have been widely used in the food industry since the 1950s. they are added to foods because they enhance the texture of processed foods and increases their shelf life, or as a cheap alternative to other fats. there is now broad scientific consensus that high consumption of trans fats significantly increases the risk of coronary heart disease, and may also be associated with other diseases. industrial trans fats are the single most dangerous nutrient for heart health, and adding them to processed foods isn’t necessary. therefore they should be banned eu-wide, just as they already have been in denmark, austria, latvia and hungary. the commission must come forward with legal limits as soon as possible, because it has the potential to save tens of thousands of lives annually.
in writing. ‒ trans-fatty acids (tfas) are a type of unsaturated fats that are uncommon in nature but became commonly produced on an industrial scale from vegetable fats to be used for producing margarine, snack food, packaged baked goods and frying fast food. i have voted for this motion for a resolution that reiterates the concern of the risks posed by tfas to human health.
in writing. ‒ industrially produced fatty acids are most often used in cheap food, directly affecting people with low incomes, who are much more at risk of developing cardiovascular disease, infertility, alzheimer's, diabetes and obesity. i believe that the imposition of mandatory limits on industrially produced fatty acids, linked in particular to the consumption of industrially produced partially hydrogenated oils, means more attention to the health of citizens.
in writing. ‒ trans fats cause heart disease, and heart disease is one of europe’s biggest killers. that’s why in this resolution the european parliament is calling for eu-wide legal limits on industrial trans fats in foods. this policy has already been tested elsewhere. we know it works, and we know it saves lives. the solid medical evidence for the harmful effects of trans fats is in stark contrast to the low public awareness about the dangers of this macronutrient. so we need to act now, with legislation, to improve public health across europe and especially to protect those vulnerable sub groups of the population who have greater exposure to industrial trans fats in processed food and fast food. i call on the european commission to act as quickly as possible and to make the necessary legislative proposals to protect public health.
in writing. ‒ protecting the health of its citizens is one of the european union's priorities. in these circumstances, the regulation of the content of food marketed in the union is of paramount importance. one compound that has raised concerns in recent years is fatty acids used in the food industry to alter the texture of foods, to extend shelf life or as a more convenient alternative to other fats. studies by international experts have found that high consumption of fatty acids increases the risk of coronary heart disease and may cause other conditions. since four member states (denmark, austria, hungary and latvia) have decided to limit the fatty acid content of food by law, which has resulted in the saving of lives, it is necessary to adopt limitation measures at european level. even the world health organization has recommended the elimination of partially hydrogenated vegetable oils, which are part of the fatty acid category, and in the united states, they will be banned starting in july 2018. in this context, it is necessary to restrict the use of these compounds at an early stage, with a view to their eventual prohibition. i support this resolution.
