in writing. ‒ the security environment surrounding the eu is volatile, complex and uncertain. in this context, security and defence should remain at the heart of the european agenda. europe must be stronger, faster and more reactive in real threat situations. he must take his share of the responsibility and act on his ambitions. i support the ep's motion for a resolution on the european defence union. a new european security strategy has long been needed. we need a fresh approach, taking into account the radically changed security environment, to define the eu's political ambitions, but also to make the eu a stronger actor in the field of security. we need to make full use of the treaty provisions in the area of the common security and defence policy (csdp) and to operationalize the provisions laid down in the lisbon treaty. in order to put an end to isolated and uncoordinated islands of military cooperation, priority should be given to the launch of permanent structured cooperation (pesco).
in writing. ‒ in recent years, the security situation in and around europe has deteriorated significantly, generating difficult and unprecedented problems that no country or organisation can solve alone. the european union is facing a security crisis on its territory more than ever, with these threats becoming increasingly complex. i voted for a common union defence policy which must strengthen europe's capacity to promote security within and beyond its borders. the european defence union must be based on regular joint assessments of security threats by member states, but it must also be flexible enough to meet the security challenges faced by each member state and to respond to their individual security needs. the eu must remain a guarantor of respect for human rights, the promotion of democracy and the rule of law.
in writing. ‒ the report backs the idea of progressing in the direction of a european defence union and for such a structure to represent an ‘umbrella’ for military capabilities at the disposal of the european union. it proposes the activation of permanent structured cooperation, it proposes setting up an eu operational headquarters, it encourages fostering the eu defence industries. i strongly support the developments in the field of csdp and encourage the steps towards a substantial autonomous defence capacity for the eu, aiming at protecting its citizens and promoting its values and interests, with full respect for the treaties, international law and human rights. therefore, i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ as an alternative rapporteur in the imco committee for the opinion on the european defence union, i consider this report to be very important for the common security and defence policy provided for by the lisbon treaty, according to which the eu must promote peace and security globally. enhanced european cooperation in defence would lead to greater effectiveness, enhanced eu assets and capabilities, and possible positive effects on defence research and industrial aspects. the development of eu capabilities through joint procurement could provide a boost to europe's defence industry, including smes, which stimulate economic growth and job creation. it is important to foster a functional, accessible and transparent european defence market that supports smes and aims to empower member states to maximise their defence and security budgets.
in writing. ‒ i fully support the development and fostering of the eu’s autonomous defence capacity. the european defence union should be supported in order for the eu to have its own common military capability.
in writing. ‒ due to the latest developments, europe’s security environment is facing new challenges thus calling for the revival of european security cooperation and integration. i voted for this report that stresses the need for a broad set of relevant policy instruments as well as strong and modern military capabilities in order to ensure long-term security in europe.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the report on the european defence union because there is a need to promote wider and more systematic european cooperation in defence to ensure the availability of key capabilities. a common union defence policy should enhance europe's capacity to promote security within and beyond its borders, as well as strengthen the nato partnership and transatlantic relations, and will therefore make possible a stronger nato, thus further promoting more effective security and defence at the territorial, regional and global levels. we encourage the commission to work in collaboration with the european defence agency to strengthen the industrial and technological base of the defence sector, which is essential for european strategic autonomy. research carried out in collaboration with the european defence industry in all member states can help reduce fragmentation in the sector and increase its competitiveness.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report because it proposes a framework of realistic measures in terms of the actions to be taken to establish a european defence union. the document underlines the importance of the continuous development of the european cyber defence policy with a view to increasing the cyber defence capabilities of the member states, as well as operational cooperation and information exchange. as regards the legislative component, the report calls on the european parliament to set up an independent security and defence committee with the objective of monitoring and implementing permanent and structured cooperation in the field of european defence. at institutional level, i also share the rapporteur's vision of reform by asking the council of the european union to establish, as a first step, a permanent format for meetings bringing together the defence ministers of the member states in a decision-making and consultative forum.
in writing. ‒ i believe that the establishment of a european defence union in the current political context in which the eu finds itself is not an effective security solution. on the contrary, it involves huge logistical costs. at the same time, the objectives it proposes do not coincide with the reality facing the eu. the only political-military concept that can offer real guarantees in terms of security is the north atlantic treaty.
in writing. ‒ in the context of certain negative phenomena, such as terrorism and illegal immigration, which increasingly threaten the security of the european union and whose sources are to be found in conflicts close to the community's borders, there is a need to strengthen the common security and defence policy (csdp). this is all the more so as the new administration in washington could change the support it currently gives to european defence, which would constitute a critical vulnerability for member states. in these circumstances, coordinated measures to strengthen security, including military security, would be required at union level. one of these measures could be the activation of permanent structured cooperation, including through the establishment of an independent security and defence committee within parliament. an eu operational centre could also be created and the european defence industry could be encouraged. this would allow existing eu missions to be better coordinated and the necessary measures to be taken more quickly and efficiently. however, all this must take account of the european treaties as well as the rules of international law and human rights. i support the adoption of this report.
in writing. ‒ passenger shipping plays a key role in ensuring the sustainability of the european transport sector, and the potential of innovative technologies needs to be harnessed to make ships greener and more energy efficient. at present, there are a high number of people commuting to europe by road, leading to congestion and blockages on europe's main arteries. given that europe's geography benefits from a number of waterways, their use would be appropriate both to reduce congestion and co2 emissions and to ensure better and faster transport services. i voted in favour of this initiative because i believe that shipping is one of the most sustainable modes of transport and that it is necessary to exploit the potential of this type of transport in accordance with environmental standards.
in writing. ‒ transport is the foundation of any economy. market integration, economic growth and transport activity are closely linked activities. in the eu, effective transport links have facilitated the creation and integration of the internal market. however, efforts are still needed to exploit the potential of passenger shipping to achieve a more sustainable and efficient european transport sector. i support the ep's motion for a resolution on the report on the exploitation of the potential of passenger shipping. waterways are the only mode of transport that offers a large available capacity. accidents are very rare, making this mode of transport an ideal environment for passenger shipping. to this end, we need a review of legislation at european level to improve the way existing rules are enforced. the current regulatory framework may also be further simplified to remove requirements that are obsolete or overlapping.
in writing. ‒ passenger shipping plays a crucial role in achieving a more sustainable and efficient european transport sector, in synergy with policies on safety, environmental standards, cross-border cooperation and competitiveness. due to the large number of people transiting europe daily, road traffic is faced with numerous bottlenecks and congestion. if the available capacity of passenger shipping were used more efficiently, we would not only reduce carbon dioxide emissions and traffic congestion, but also improve the transport system across the union. the geography of europe offers extraordinary opportunities for the development of shipping. i voted for the development of this enormous potential offered by passenger shipping. every year, some 400 million people pass through eu ports. eu legislation on passenger ship safety has led to an improvement in passenger safety.
in writing. ‒ i support the rapporteur's position on the need to integrate passenger shipping into urban, regional and cross-border public transport networks, which allows for more efficient mobility and better environmental protection, in conjunction with the increased decongestion of land transport networks and comfort in cities. on the other hand, it is beneficial for member states to promote and support local initiatives to activate inland waterway transport as a means of supplying crowded areas, including through the development of distribution centres in river ports and the development of passenger transport, in particular to make the areas concerned more attractive to tourists, as well as to move towards the increased use of greener, more energy efficient, lower emission vessels.
in writing. ‒ this ini report makes recommendations to improve ferry, barge and cruise services for passengers, including proper integration of waterborne passenger transport into existing public transport networks and improving integrated ticketing. the use of existing eu funding should be fully exploited to develop further the inland and coastal waterborne transport routes. waterborne passenger transport can be an environmentally and consumer friendly transport mode, as well as a vital service for tourists and commuters in remote/coastal areas. further measures can be taken to promote this mode of transport which can have a positive effect on economic development along coastal areas and relieve congestion on land. i supported the report in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report, given the importance of passenger shipping. this sector has great potential to use the available excess capacity in both infrastructure and ships and plays a key role in connecting the different regions of the european union, thus constituting an important factor in the development of cohesion. this report underlines the importance of encouraging the development of maritime highways, including by third countries, which promote efficient multimodal transport, facilitate its integration with other networks and modes of transport, remove bottlenecks in key network infrastructures and ensure territorial continuity. blockages at the level of links between the extended inland navigation system in western europe and the existing system in eastern europe should be removed. i believe it should be the responsibility of the european commission to fully support investments in quality infrastructure in the hinterland, which can help reduce local traffic congestion, and to ensure that local people are not affected.
in writing. ‒ this type of transport can be an environmentally and consumer friendly as well as a vital service for tourists and commuters in remote or coastal areas. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ a crucial role in achieving a more sustainable and efficient european transport sector is played by waterborne passenger transport, which includes ferries, inland ferries, barges and cruises. i have voted for this report that will enhance efficiency, environmental performance, quality of life and will provide lifeline services to remote communities.
in writing. ‒ passenger transport in the context of coastal transport (short sea shipping), ferries running on inland and maritime waterways, urban and peripheral mobility, cruises and tourism, has a great potential to use the available excess capacity, both in terms of infrastructure and in terms of ships, and plays a key role in connecting the different regions of the european union. we invite member states to promote and support local initiatives to activate inland waterway transport as a means of supplying crowded areas, including through the development of distribution centres in river ports and the development of passenger transport, primarily to make the areas concerned more attractive to tourists. we welcome the efforts of the passenger shipping sector to transition to greener, more energy-efficient, lower-emission ships, developed as part of a european framework aimed at greening shipping. this would lead to cheaper, sustainable, more attractive and thus more economically competitive solutions.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report because, firstly, it proposes to remove the existing bottlenecks between the large inland navigation system in western europe and the existing system in eastern europe, the links between which are currently in a high state of degradation. secondly, the report calls on the european commission to integrate the npt into its eu-wide mobility strategy and to take action to reduce co2 emissions in line with the cop 21 agreement. last but not least, i support this report because it reiterates the commitment of the ec and the member states to respect environmental standards to reduce air pollution, to monitor the quality of fuels and engines, with a view to using especially fuel-efficient ones.
in writing. ‒ harnessing the potential of passenger shipping contributes to the eu's objective of becoming the world leader in maritime research and innovation, set out in its maritime transport policy strategy by 2018. the development of maritime passenger transport, boosted by the exponential pace of technological developments, as an alternative to road transport, is an environmentally friendly mode of transport with beneficial effects on the environment and on the quality of life of citizens. in addition, exploiting the potential of the npt, based on adequate infrastructure, including through the development of projects co-financed by eu funds, generates the development not only of tourism but also of other sectors of the european economy. i agree that an analysis of all npt projects co-financed by eu funds and a synthesis of the implementation of eu npt strategies, coupled with an appropriate dissemination of all such statistical information, is necessary in order to take an integrated approach to exploiting the potential of maritime passenger transport, as this sector represents an important added value for the european economy.
in writing. ‒ the success of european transport policies will depend to a large extent on how well the european union can redirect transport flows across all existing modes, and on the quality of the services provided. in the context of growing demand and a growing concern for reducing emissions, water transport can be the solution to sustainable and safe transport, giving a new impetus to economic development in riparian and coastal areas. this report recommends that member states and the commission pay greater attention to passenger transport by water, starting with the rehabilitation of the necessary infrastructure and ending with rigorous training of staff in this sector. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's policy on the environment and climate change, and will continue to monitor the implementation of the union's policy on climate change and its impact on the environment. parliament also called on the european executive to step up cooperation with the member states to attract european funds, especially those for smes and cohesion policies, in order to develop a transport strategy that meets the needs of each region, but also in relation to the priorities of the ten-t network.
in writing. ‒ the eu has long been committed to improving aid and development effectiveness through development cooperation. december 2016 will mark the fifth anniversary of the adoption of the busan partnership for effective development cooperation, a political commitment also undertaken by the european union, which aims to improve the quality of the implementation, management and use of official development assistance in order to maximise its impact. in this regard, the commission and the member states should develop new initiatives to strengthen flagship south-south and tripartite cooperation projects involving new emerging donors and other middle-income countries, based on addressing global challenges of mutual interest, without losing sight of the perspective of poverty eradication. i support this report because it is absolutely necessary to fully exploit the potential of decentralised cooperation in order to promote the development effectiveness agenda, while respecting all guarantees with regard to transparency, effectiveness and coherence and avoiding further fragmentation of the international aid architecture.
in writing. ‒ the commitments made in busan to effective development cooperation have helped to define an international standard on aid effectiveness applicable to all development actors. the busan partnership agreement has been endorsed by 161 countries and territories and 54 international organizations. the european union plays an important role both in the development of current aid effectiveness standards and in the adoption of the 2030 agenda. joint programming is currently applied in more than half of the partner countries receiving eu development assistance. we voted to continue along this path, but also to step up efforts on aid effectiveness and development cooperation. the commission shall, by means of implementing acts, lay down the rules on the participation of the union in the development of the union's macro-financial assistance.
in writing. ‒ i support the rapporteur's view that the european parliament needs to be regularly and timely informed of the position adopted by the commission within the gpedc steering committee in order to fulfil its essential role of democratic control of european union policies. the progress made is also welcome and supports the need to ensure access to information for all partners on funding mechanisms and programming transparency, as well as possible projects and aid flows targeting development cooperation, in particular in the context of the international aid transparency initiative and the establishment of the eu aid explorer website. proper monitoring, analysis and exchange of information and experience on development progress in beneficiary countries are also needed.
in writing. ‒ i believe the eu should ensure a more effective development cooperation aid if it wants to have a real impact in alleviating poverty in a context of increasing humanitarian and development crises and scarcity of resources. the eu, as world’s biggest development aid donor, has a special responsibility to improve the effectiveness of and bring more accountability to eu assistance. the eu should lead global efforts in advancing the development effectiveness agenda. in the previous mandate, parliament took a stance on the issue of improving aid effectiveness by providing its input in view of the fourth high level forum on aid effectiveness. five years later, it is important to take stock of the implementation of the global commitments achieved then. the report is thus a good occasion to analyse how aid and development effectiveness could contribute to implementing the sdgs and the addis ababa agenda on financing for development. our amendments achieved to defend a stronger global partnership for effective development cooperation (gpedc), more inclusive of civil society organisations and with a larger mandate, mainly by ensuring a better south-south and triangular cooperation and more transparency in access to information.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report which aims to have a real impact on poverty reduction and ensure more effective development cooperation aid in the context of growing humanitarian crises. the eu is the leading development donor, responsible for improving the efficiency of cooperation.
in writing. ‒ in 2011 the busan partnership was agreed upon in south korea by a wide range of governments and organisations for effective development cooperation. i voted for this report that will advance development effectiveness by increasing aid transparency, improving joint programming and addressing the issues of conflict and fragility.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which ambitiously proposes that all development actors coordinate in line with the commitments made in paris and busan to achieve the objectives of the 2030 agenda in terms of the optimal use of public and private resources for development. the report also highlights the key role of oda (official development assistance) in eradicating poverty, reducing inequalities, providing essential public services and supporting good governance. another factor that led me to support this report is that it calls into question the longstanding commitment of eu member states to allocate 0.7% of gni to aid and to strengthen their development assistance, including through the eu budget and the edf. this report recalls the important role that citizens, local communities, elected representatives, faith-based organisations, trade unions and academia play in the development of the society in which we live.
in writing. ‒ a common approach, in the sense of a global partnership, to making development cooperation more effective is necessary if we are to truly transform the world we live in, i.e. implement the 2030 agenda. it is time to hold accountable (obviously differentiated) even those who receive aid. the shift in focus from 'aid effectiveness' to 'development cooperation effectiveness' is salutary in this context, but only to the extent that it is grounded in concrete results in terms of contributing to the achievement of sustainable and inclusive development. the principle of 'leaving no one behind', which is the general philosophy and core commitment of the 2030 agenda, is at the heart of making cooperation for societal development more effective at global level. however, the process of applying this principle efficiently and effectively requires operationalization and monitoring indicators, exchange of good practices and substantial evaluations, dissemination of results and progress, so that the accountability and impact of development cooperation is increased, not only at member state level. it also requires properly reasoned national policies on development aid adequacy to increase the accountability of all development stakeholders.
in writing. ‒ as the world's main source of development aid, the european union also has a great responsibility for regulating this sector properly. the main problems in this respect are the effectiveness of aid and the transparency of funds provided by the union to developing countries. following the fourth high level forum on aid effectiveness in 2011, it was agreed to establish an institutional mechanism to monitor this area in the form of the global partnership for effective development cooperation (gpedc). it is intended to be a platform for dialogue at international level and to ensure the fulfilment of commitments made by the participating states. the final objective is to achieve the sustainable development goals (sdgs) adopted by the un general assembly and to implement the addis ababa action agenda adopted in 2015. to achieve these objectives, the eu is supporting a number of innovative approaches to make each of the relevant actors achieve their goals, as well as new mechanisms such as triangular cooperation projects involving national parliaments, local authorities, civil society and the private sector. it is a laudable initiative and i therefore support the adoption of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the own-initiative report by mr cristian preda on increasing the effectiveness of development cooperation. the report calls on all development actors to build on commitments made and to renew and step up their efforts to make development cooperation as effective as possible in order to achieve the ambitious goals and targets set out in the 2030 agenda and to make the best use of public and private resources for development. it also calls for the use of all development policy instruments to eradicate poverty. as rapporteur for the eu regulation on conflict minerals, i am an advocate for more effective development cooperation, because only by stepping up efforts to eradicate poverty and the exploitation of people and communities in conflict zones can we truly exercise the eu's mandate to promote democracy and human rights across the globe.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, honourable members, thank you all for keeping a constant focus on syria in your plenary debates. i am really sorry i could not be with you in person last month, but i believe this is the fourth or fifth time this year that we have had a plenary debate on our work on syria. last month i was in brussels for the afghanistan conference, another important file in which the european union has a very important part to play, but the slovak presidency briefed me on your october exchanges, and they also provided a very important input for the discussions we had at the foreign affairs council both in october and last week. we have discussed syria again, as i mentioned, in the foreign affairs council both in october and last week, on monday to be precise, and i have engaged in a number of meetings with both syrian, regional and international actors, so for me this debate is a very precious opportunity to update you with the most recent initiatives and contacts and work we are carrying on, starting from the work on the humanitarian side that, together with christos stylianides, we have carried out relentlessly, i would say, in these last months. over the last few days, there has been a new escalation of violence against the eastern neighbourhoods of aleppo. the resumption of airstrikes has worsened the humanitarian situation even further, particularly because it has left hundreds of thousands of besieged civilians without access to functioning hospitals. together with christos and his team, whom i would like to praise, and together with the united nations, we are working literally day and night to create the conditions to let the humanitarian aid in, and to let the wounded out, of east aleppo, as as well as to other besieged areas all across the syrian territory. to reach this goal, we are engaging both internationally with all relevant actors, and on the ground. we are in constant contact with the city council of eastern aleppo, as well as with civilian administrations in several parts of syria. we are helping them provide services to the local population in the areas where this is possible. our activity on the ground is increasingly recognised, first of all by the local players, by the syrians themselves, and this is for me – and i can speak also on behalf of christos and all the people who are working with us on this – the number one priority, that our work reaches the syrians on the ground. believe me when i tell you of our frustration at not managing to do more, but all the humanitarian work that is done is basically thanks also, i cannot say all, but almost all, to the funding, the work, the support, the logistics, the commitment of the european union. here again, i would like to thank our team, both on the ground and in brussels, which has been working really at an incredible rhythm on this, in full coordination always, with the united nations. our work, as i said, is increasingly recognised inside syria but also internationally. the contacts and the channels we have developed in this field will be crucial also to any settlement and to the transition. as you all know, the delivery of humanitarian aid is proving to be a very difficult exercise, given the lack of a broader political agreement on the cessation of hostilities, and we have realised very clearly in these last couple of months that the military-to-military work on the cessation of hostilities is more and more difficult in the absence of a wider political understanding on the future of syria. so what we risk is a vicious circle. this is why, after having discussed this with the foreign ministers and with the heads of state and governments in the foreign affairs council and in the european council, i have started to reach out to the key regional actors on the future of syria. this means that in the last weeks i met and had talks with the foreign ministers or leaders, presidents, of different countries of the region on a clear agenda. in the name of transparency, and also in sharing with you this work, let me go into a rather detailed list again. i know this is not the politics we need to talk – we would also need to talk politics, but i think it is also important for you to know exactly what this regional outreach is meaning by now. meetings with foreign minister al thani of qatar in brussels. then i headed to tehran where i met president rouhani and foreign minister zarif, and two days later to saudi arabia to see king salman. last week i discussed this in brussels with foreign minister bassil of lebanon. over the weekend i met with emirates foreign minister sheikh abdullah and foreign minister of jordan nasser judeh. contacts with others, notably turkish foreign minister çavuşoğlu and egyptian foreign minister shoukry will also follow. and on friday, just a few days ago, we hosted a meeting with the syrian opposition groups, the leaders of different groups that i met at length in brussels to share this process with them, to listen to their views to ensure full ownership and an active participation on their side. and obviously all of this is done in constant contact with staffan de mistura and his team, both in geneva and in the united nations headquarters in new york. so now to content. the focus of this outreach is on the future of syria, looking in particular at the post-conflict end state. what i am trying to do is identify areas of common ground and possible elements of a positive agenda with all the key actors. the issues that we are discussing in the framework of this outreach include political accountability, decentralisation or devolution, participation and protection of all components of the very diverse syrian society. i know that this chamber is particularly attentive to the situation of christians in the region; this is also part of our outreach. reconciliation, especially the local exercises of reconciliation, and economic reconstruction. on the latter let me be extremely clear: the european union is and will be ready to engage in the economic reconstruction of the country, together with other partners. but, let me stress as i stress it to our partners in the region, this will only happen once a political transition has begun under the framework of un security council resolution 2254. this work aims at improving the chances for the success of the un mandate and the un special envoy for the intra-syrian talks. our regional outreach can help create some space and some confidence for the talks to start because of course it is, as i said, for the syrians to decide the future of the country in direct talks under un auspices, but in the meantime, if as the european union we can provide some space regionally to accompany this process, it could only be useful. in six years of war we should have learned something about the conflict in syria. at times, an agreement between global powers could not hold, even if it was found, because the situation was out of control on the ground. in other cases, local ceasefires did not hold even if they were reached, because there was no agreement on a broader political level, either in the region or internationally. as i said, sometimes it is a vicious circle. things locally do not hold because the international regional framework is not accompanying; at some other times you find an agreement on regional and international level and you do not have the local actors on your side. so peace in syria will require at the same time an agreement among world powers, the un framework, among regional actors, the work we are trying to do, and all local players. i understand that it might sound strange to talk and to work on post-conflict at exactly the moment when war still rages on, and yet, talking about reconstruction, reconciliation, post-conflict, the system of governance, that could ensure syria future a way, is a way of maybe opening the door for a process of peace. because only if we start putting all the pieces together and to create some kind of consensus among the regional actors and among the citizens will we contribute to building peace in syria. now as you know very well, and as i repeated many times, the european union is not militarily involved in this war. this is the result of a political decision, one that was taken years ago, that i fully share and that unites us all in europe. we are not a party to the conflict. but this is not a constraint on our diplomatic action. on the contrary, this puts us in a privileged position as we work for peace. from our position, we understand better than others that there is no military solution to the war. we see that every escalation leads us further away, and not closer, to peace. we are in a privileged position as we can talk to everybody, we do talk to everybody, we are trusted by everybody, and i am convinced that the european union will be, and is becoming, an indispensable force to make peace in syria possible and to achieve it concretely on the ground. i can only ask you, this parliament, to keep supporting, as you have done constantly this year, our work on humanitarian grounds for creating the political space for peace in syria and for all the people of syria, to benefit from a brighter future in their country.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, let me at the outset, and in order to properly frame this exchange, recall that the european union has a clear position, set out in our council conclusions, to pursue the two-state solution. the same two-state solution that since oslo has been identified as the objective of all israeli governments, of the palestinian leadership and of the international community. this to us is a clear position and also a clear objective not only of ours, but also that we share with the rest of the international community and of the parties. as the july report of the quartet points out, action is needed to preserve the possibility of achieving this goal that is commonly shared, at least formally. stopping the expansion of settlements is an integral part of the efforts to keep the solution of two viable and contiguous states on the table. the so-called regularisation bill, which passed a preliminary reading in the knesset would allow for the ex-post legalisation of israeli outposts in the occupied west bank. it would enable essentially the confiscation of the private property rights of palestinian land owners in the west bank for the benefit of settlers. this would mean crossing a new threshold, even under israeli law, for the settlement enterprise in the west bank. it would also mean the exact opposite of what the quartet that has called for, namely preserving the two-state solution. the debate in israel on the regularisation bill has not concluded, but the choices are clear: either to uphold the principle of the two-state solution, or to go down the path of a one-state reality which will only lead to further conflict and instability at a time when the middle east needs all the stability it can get. the choice belongs to israel, but i believe it is only normal that we express our own views as any friend would do. the quartet report on which the european union has worked very much has identified the process to retroactively legalise outposts as a threat against a two-state solution. there is an international consensus on this because the report is the result of common work we have done. it is true there has been a strong eu involvement and leadership in this, but we’ve done this together with the un, the us and the russian federation. so these statements that we have in the report of the quartet that we presented in july is a statement that we share with our friends in the international community. we have a very detailed description in the report of the situation on the ground, and a shared assessment of the risk it poses to peace. but is also important to keep in mind that the debate on the regularisation bill is controversial inside the israeli leadership and inside the israeli society, and that the process is still open. the israeli attorney general himself has been very explicit that this bill is unconstitutional under israeli law, against previous rulings by israel’s supreme court and in breach of international law. a final decision, as i said, has not been taken yet and i hope that the israeli government and legislators will do the right thing. we are in contact with the authorities in israel and we’ve made the position of the european union very clear to the government of israel. we will continue to follow developments on this issue very closely together with member states. let me stress here the european union is fully united on this issue. as we also reflected in the quartet report, our goal remains to help find a new path to successful final status negotiations. we need to rebuild the conditions for a peace process that can bring results – as i said several times in this house, not a process for the sake of a process – actually today even more than before we need to preserve, recreate political conditions and i would say that today even more than yesterday, it is crucial that the european union builds and preserves international unity on this issue. today is more important than yesterday, both on the fundamental coordinates of the two-state solution and on the way to get there. our role is more important than ever today. our regional partners can also play a major role in promoting and supporting a solution. the arab peace initiative in particular, with its vision for a comprehensive arab-israeli peace, remains a key basis and offers significant opportunities, including with regard to regional security that i believe would be extremely beneficial for israel itself. at the same time, we know that real peace requires a real commitment from the israeli and palestinian leaderships and this is why the internal israeli debate is so important to us. we’ve talked about settlement policy, where we sometimes differ – i would say often differ – from the israeli government, but there has also recently been some positive steps such as plans and pyramids for palestinian construction inside area c and this was also not uncontroversial at all within the israeli government and opinions. so i believe we should not only criticise when we do not agree, but also acknowledge what we see as positive steps and encourage more of this and also more ambitious steps that lead to real progress on the ground. so let me conclude on a more personal note. two months ago i was in jerusalem for the funeral of a great israeli man and a great man of peace, shimon peres. it was a very sad moment also for me personally, i had known him for many years, and yet it showed that hope is still alive. an important gesture came that day from president abbas – his presence at the funeral in jerusalem and the handshake with prime minister netanyahu were little steps in the right direction, a little moment of hope. and the night before the funeral i had the opportunity to have a long meeting with prime minister netanyahu, in which he recognised, as peres did, that only peace can bring security to israel. so in difficult times for the middle east we need to keep our eyes wide open, not only for the extremely worrying developments but also for any glimpses of hope and seize every opportunity that comes our way to make it grow. i know this parliament will keep its attention high both on the worrying developments, but also on the opportunities for peace, and encourage and accompany our work for making them grow.

rapporteur. – madam president, before i begin i would like to welcome the presence of the high representative at this debate as usual, which reflects the fulfilment of her obligation of consultation with parliament according to article 36 of the lisbon treaty, which should have governed our debate in the first place. if in 2003 the eu leaders were announcing to the world that europe has never been so prosperous, so secure nor so free, now, 13 years later, they are forced to recognise that we live in times of existential crisis within and beyond the european union. naturally, we should ask why is that. how did we get there? what have we done wrong? but primarily, we should ask what should we do to respond successfully to these times of existential crisis, and strengthening csdp is a major component of that answer. that is why the report is of the opinion that a thorough and substantial revision of the csdp is needed in order to enable the un, its member states to contribute in a decisive way to the security of the union, to the management of international crisis and to asserting the eu strategic autonomy, recalling that no country can face the current security challenges on its own. in the relative benign security environment prevalent until now, the eu and its member states could allow themselves to actuate csdp mainly with crisis management performed in relative distant places. now the conflicts around us have multiplied and have become intertwined, spilling through terrorism and refugees into the eu area. security and defence is no longer only a cry for help coming from a proud defence industry confronted with increasing difficulties like it was the eu council on defence in december 2013. now security and defence is a major, if not even the main concern of european citizens which was finally heard by the eu leaders. consequently things started to move, and only last week the implementation plan on security and defence has been approved by the member countries. and that, let me tell you, that surprised us, and we had to introduce a number of amendments in order to synch the report with the realities in the field. the commission in turn has advanced a number of defence-related initiatives, for instance the defence action plan and the defence industrial policy, getting involved in a support of a pilot plan on defence research run by eda, the only institution we have for that kind of activity whose role would have to be strengthened in consequence, and instilling more flexibility in the instrument for peace and stability. naturally, this is a big step compared to the current practices. the eu money was not used for defence and is already resisted in this parliament. however, if we really want to defend our union we should be prepared to make this step because otherwise we would continue to linger on in this complacency which brought us where we are today. in the end, i would mention the relationship with nato, guided now by the joint declaration signed in warsaw last summer. the relationship should be one of cooperation and not competition. the eu needs to acquire a degree of strategic autonomy, particularly for situations where it might have to rely mainly on herself. let us not forget that nato is a collective defence alliance and not a company whose unprofitable branches could be shut down. born from the lessons of two world wars, built with sacrifice by all the member states, and meant to defend and promote the values which brought us together in the eu too.
and for the first time, we're seeing soft power surpass hard power in actual influence. in the face of this new reality, both the union and the member states are unprepared and vulnerable. this report, together with the commission's efforts, will increase the union's capacity to act in this regard. member states must engage in a thorough and rapid rethinking of the common security and defence policy. this includes the commitment to allocate 2% of gdp to defence. at this point in time, the union cannot ensure the protection of citizens and institutions against manipulation or cyber attacks. we still need cooperation and complementarity with nato. the same register should take advantage of the transatlantic partnership, especially in the context of limited resources. more than ever, the union needs to support the strengthening of the defence industry and research, and this needs to be reflected in the financial allocation for the remainder of the current multiannual financial framework. i would like to congratulate mr pascu and support a positive vote and hope that the directions indicated will become institutional practice as soon as possible.
mr president, the increase in the security of the eu member states will certainly require a diversification of the forms of european defence cooperation in the future. this is true even if nato's defence capabilities and resources as a military alliance are irreplaceable. at the same time, defence cooperation could also contribute to the further development of european integration as a whole, since it would require cooperation and openness between member states in one of the most sensitive areas. the development of defence industry, cyber defence cooperation, joint defence research opens up a whole new area of integration, and may be just what europe needs today, with so many fault lines. building greater trust between member states in this important area can benefit the eu as a whole. it is important to emphasise that defence cooperation is for peace, as a continent that cannot respond to the challenges of the times will be weak and vulnerable, and this could lead to internal tensions.

in writing. the deterioration of the european security environment, generated by the increase in the number of threats, whether conventional or hybrid, has led to an increase in the sense of insecurity among european citizens. according to the 2016 eurobarometer 85.1 survey, around two thirds of them want the eu to become more involved in security and defence policy issues. in this context, i believe that measures should be taken to enable both the more efficient use of existing csdp instruments and the creation of new, relevant instruments that make it possible for the european union to intervene in any type of crisis management action, from prevention to resolution. the european foreign and security policy must also be unified and there must be better cooperation and coordination between member states. only in this way, together with effective funding, will the effectiveness of the psac be increased and a strong collective defence be achieved. last but not least, i think it's unfair to rely on the investment coming from the us alone. the united states of america must be seen as a partner, and not just as the sole provider of security and stability in various parts of the world, including europe. these are the reasons why i welcome this initiative.
vice-president of the commission. – thank you, madam president. last week, the oxford dictionary named ‘post-truth’ the word of the year 2016. ‘post-truth’ describes a situation – and i quote from the dictionary – ‘where objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief’. this phenomenon has always existed, for sure, but it has become even more relevant in the age of internet. we know that the quality of the information is not always what makes content go viral. social media and search engines tend to promote contents that confirm the user’s views instead of challenging them, and we all understand how relevant this can be in political terms, including for our european union. so i am glad that the report we discussed today has given this parliament the opportunity to reflect on such a delicate and crucial issue, where not only security has to be taken into account, but also everyone’s freedom of expression. as the report states, exposing this information is an important task and i am glad that the report commends the work carried out by our east stratcom task force. it is clear from the task force’s work that the challenge coming from this information is not receding. let me thank the parliament for its close interest and support for the work we have been doing with the task force over the past year, as well the member states who have contributed to the team. i can only welcome the proposal that this parliament this advanced to strengthen both our east and south task forces on strategic communication. as i mentioned, both of them – stratcom east and south. let me stress that our work on this information is very different and depends on a case-by-case scenario. this information can be contrasted with fact-checking and rational arguments. the propaganda of terrorist groups, like daesh, needs instead to be confronted first and foremost by taking down illegal content from the internet. to address the issue of the accessibility of terrorist materials, the commission has established an internet referral unit at europol that actively scans for terrorist content online and refers it to the internet companies. so far we are still in the initial phase; we have referred over 15 000 pages, and in 90% of cases the material has been removed. yet we know that this part of our work, however crucial, cannot be enough. what matters even more is to explain what the european union is doing and how it is making a real and positive difference to the lives of so many people inside and outside the european union. now the report tackles with the issue of propaganda by third parties, but let me say that this is an issue that would be interesting to see inside the european union, starting maybe from this very hemicycle. we need to give voice to the people who have benefited from our policies, amplify the positive stories, simplify the messages and talk about real life. the truth – to the east, to the south and inside our union – is that this positive added value of the european union has to be more visible. this is why we have put public diplomacy among the key areas of implementation of our global strategy. so the east stratcom task force is doing this, providing expert guidance to our delegations; working closely with governments in the eastern partnership region and with the commission; reaching out to a russian-speaking audience that want better access to information about the european union in real time in russia and from a source they can trust. similarly, the task force south is addressing arabic-speaking communities in north africa and in the middle east together with our delegations. in particular, it is engaging with young people, working closely with the on behalf of the alde group. – madam president, the european labour market faces challenges like never before. in a digitalised world, the skills demand is constantly shifting towards new jobs, making low skilled jobs as well as traditional jobs obsolete, outlining the flaws of the educational system and leaving a big segment of the workforce unemployed. the commission proposal considers that something must be done for those with low proficiency in basic skills, literacy and numeracy and digital skills and recommends a set of policies and initiatives to support them. the proposal limits itself, however, to addressing only the effects of a wider problem without questioning why these individuals lack basic skills. is school drop—out one of the reasons? is poverty a possible answer? i would welcome more commission research into the causes of this lack of skills, be they poverty, unsustainability of educational systems or the need for mentality change, rather than seeing that the eu is once again focusing on patching up only the damaging effects of a problem. if this phenomenon is not tackled appropriately, the number of people without basic skills will simply repeat itself. therefore, i urge the commission to have a holistic vision towards the labour market and address its issues with strategies aimed at repairing its faults.

in writing. ‒ once ceta enters into force, the eu and canada will immediately and completely abandon some tariff lines for industrial and fishery products, and the rest after transitional periods of up to seven years. the same applies to agricultural products. secondly, in the area of public procurement - an area that is sometimes underestimated but has the potential to be worth hundreds of billions of dollars - ceta brings significant liberalisation, meaning that european firms will be able to bid for public contracts in canada at all levels of government (with some limitations in the provinces of quebec and ontario). all of this will bring more business opportunities, a bigger market, increased exports and more jobs. experts estimate that the eu will have an annual gain of €12 billion. romania will benefit from the reduction in areas such as the production of leather and footwear products, agriculture, automotive components, ceramics, textiles. in addition, as part of this agreement, romanian citizens will no longer need a visa from 1 december 2017. the 28 member states have agreed unanimously, and as such support the implementation of ceta as soon as possible.

in writing. ‒ the european security environment has deteriorated considerably, becoming increasingly volatile, complex, dangerous and unpredictable. member states are highly interdependent in terms of security and react in an uncoordinated and fragmented way to common threats and dangers, complicating and often preventing a common approach. the european union is obliged to respond to the emergence of increasingly complex crises, it must step up dialogue and cooperation with third countries in the region and it must be prepared to deal with structural changes in the international security landscape. i voted for the integration of cyber security and defence as core elements of the common security and defence policy, given that conflicts and crises in europe and its neighbourhood take place both in the physical and cyber space. legislative reform is needed to allow defence industries to benefit from the same state aid as us industries.
in writing. ‒ i strongly support the call for an eu white book on security and defence and a stronger defence industry, and i welcome the european defence action plan. i believe it is time to reform the athena mechanism for financing the missions and operations of the eu. i think it is the right moment for us to push for a bolder approach to eu defence, towards a full military alliance. the european union and nato must divide their tasks to avoid duplication of efforts. we must reach a common position and encourage steps towards a substantial autonomous defence capacity for the eu, aiming at protecting its citizens and promoting its values and interests, with full respect for the treaties, international law and human rights.
in writing. ‒ i believe the csdp should have a strong cooperation with nato. however, the eu must have an autonomous defence capacity. as such, i fully support this project.
in writing. ‒ due to developments in the last years, the security in the european union has deteriorated thus becoming a more complex and dangerous and less predictable issue. i have voted for this report. i have voted for this report that will enable a revision of the csdp in order to enable the eu and its member states to better contribute to the security of the union.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the report on the implementation of the common security and defence policy because member states should coordinate their security and defence investments and improve their financial support for defence research at eu level. strong commitment, adherence and support from member states and national parliaments, in close cooperation with all relevant eu bodies, are needed to ensure the swift and effective implementation of the global strategy for the european union's foreign and security policy. a future eu defence research programme should fund research projects in priority areas agreed by member states.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report because it recalls the strong interdependence of member states in terms of security and raises the alarm about the fact that they are reacting in an uncoordinated and fragmented way to common threats and dangers. the report also finds that europe lacks the resilience to respond effectively to hybrid threats, which are often cross-border in nature. another element that led me to vote for this report is that it highlights the negative impact of the military occupation on the security of europe as a whole and reiterates the idea that any change to the borders of ukraine is a departure from the principles of the un charter and the helsinki final act.
in writing. ‒ the deterioration of the european security environment in recent years, manifested by the multiplication of conventional, unconventional and hybrid threats, calls for the strengthening of the union's common security and defence policy (csdp). the rise of the terrorist phenomenon generated by radical islamic organisations and the emergence of complex crises near the union's external borders require a stronger response from the member states within the common framework established by the csdp. in this respect, there is a need for better coordination of the defence capabilities of the member states, while intensifying cooperation with existing structures within nato. it would also be useful to support the european defence industry and reform the athena system for financing eu military missions and operations. the adoption of an eu white paper on security and defence would be an important aid to the mapping of the main priorities in this area. the adoption of the european defence action plan (edap) and the european defence research programme (edrp), together with the strengthening of the role of the european defence agency (eda), are likely to strengthen the cfsp and enhance the security of european citizens. for these reasons, i support the adoption of this resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the own-initiative report by mr ioan mircea pașcu on the implementation of the eu's common security and defence policy. the report proposes a detailed and in-depth review of the csdp, taking into account the fact that the european security environment has deteriorated considerably, becoming increasingly volatile, complex, dangerous and unpredictable. i agree that a successful revision of the cfsp will need to fully involve eu member states from the outset of the process, to avoid the risk of future deadlock.

in writing. ‒ european citizens all have full rights, whether we are talking about people with disabilities, especially women and children, and especially deaf and hard of hearing people. these persons use sign language as a means of communication with other persons, and therefore have equal rights and are entitled to inalienable dignity, equal treatment, independent living, autonomy and full participation in society. sadly, this is made difficult by the use of sign language. i therefore support the need to ensure the training of qualified and professional sign language interpreters, and the necessary measures are the official recognition of national and regional sign languages in the member states and in the eu institutions, formal training (at university level or similar, equivalent to three years of full-time studies, corresponding to the necessary training of spoken language interpreters), and registration (official accreditation and quality control system, such as continuing professional development).

in writing. ‒ i have voted against the motion for resolution on the draft commission implementing regulation renewing approval of the active substance bentazone because bentazone is controlling volunteers of herbicide-tolerant crops and is safe when used appropriately. bentazone is important for european farmers, being one of few ingredients which controls broad-leaf weeds in post-emergence of those crops. the active ingredient has a different mode of action which make it a key tool in resistance management in controlling difficult weeds like ambrosia, datura, matricaria etc. furthermore, bentazone has not been identified as an endocrine disruptor under the current interim criteria. moreover, this motion neglects the significant impact such measures can have on european farmers, regarding their productivity, competitiveness, and sustainability.
in writing. – the objection does not focus on the characterisation of the substance and whether bentazone itself should be banned or re-authorised, but it is based on the authorisation process itself as the commission (once again) proposes to re-authorise an active substance for the maximum period possible (15 years) while at the same requesting confirmatory data to evaluate its safety. this is against the eu ombudsman’s ruling from february 2016 (case: 12/2013/mdc), against the provisions in the regulation 2009/1107 and against any logic of evaluating safety of pesticides. the severity of this objection might be not as high compared to the objection on active substance glyphosate but the principle of respecting the existing law is crucial. otherwise we would find ourselves in a position where approved substances in the eu are, in some instances, unsafe and/or not in accordance with relevant legislation. the commission should take into account all necessary data confirming safety of a given substance before issuing the authorisations. the approval period should be proportionate to the possible risks inherent in the use of such substances. the precautionary principle should be the guiding principle in the authorisation process of plant protection products.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this objection to the use of bentazone, which expires on 30 june 2017, but whose draft measure approves the renewal of the authorisation of the substance for another 15 years (until 31 january 2032). the commission shall take into account all necessary data confirming the safety of the substance before issuing authorisations. the period of approval shall be proportionate to the risks, if any, inherent in the use of such substances. the precautionary principle should be the guiding principle in the product authorisation process.
in writing. ‒ bentazone is used as a herbicide against broadleaved weeds in a broad range of crops in agriculture. i have voted for this motion for a resolution that requests the commission to assess and complete all relevant information before taking a decision regarding the approval of use for this substance.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution calling on the commission to withdraw its draft regulation renewing the approval of the active substance bentazone and to submit a new draft. the active substance bentazone is the most commonly detected authorised pesticide in water, as it has a high potential for direct infiltration into groundwater. we invite the commission and the member states to fund research and innovation in the field of sustainable and cost-effective alternative solutions for pest control products, with the aim of ensuring a high level of protection of human and animal health and the environment.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this resolution because of doubts about the process for approving active substances and the possible implications for health and the environment. there is great concern that the commission is using the confirmatory data procedure too readily, which can mean the approval of substances which have not been fully analysed. the european ombudsman has raised concerns about the fact that substances can be approved without understanding the extent of their potentially harmful effects. in this case, the risks relate to mammalian toxicology, ecotoxicology, and the environment. these are important data gaps which should be addressed before authorisation, not years afterwards.
in writing. ‒ the health of european citizens is one of the priorities of the union and its institutions. the presence of harmful chemical compounds in agricultural products used in the food supply to consumers as a result of the use of weedkillers is unacceptable. one of those compounds is the active substance bentazone and is currently used in the agriculture of the member states against broadleaf weeds in a wide range of crops. at european level, it is the commission that authorises the use of these products, usually for a period of 15 years. however, in this case, the commission extended the approval period until 30 june 2017 as a number of adverse effects on pregnancy and foetal development were identified following tests on mice and in view of the completion of tests on surface water. if these indications are confirmed, the compound should be included among the endocrine disruptors and prohibited. in these circumstances, the draft implementing regulation drawn up by the commission cannot be approved, as it represents a risk to the health of european citizens. i support the adoption of this resolution.

in writing. the current european vat system was introduced 23 years ago as a temporary system. this system has encouraged tax fraud in trade between member states within the single market. finally, the european commission has recognised that a switch to a vat system based on the payment of vat in the country of origin is not possible. the european commission is therefore proposing to maintain the vat system based on the payment of vat in the countries of destination of exported goods and services. this is the right solution. however, we need to find the best solutions to stop vat fraud, namely for importers to declare, on their own initiative, their vat obligations for imported goods and services. unfortunately, the european commission's proposals in this direction are still not convincing.

in writing. ‒ the sector of institutions for occupational pension provision is developing in many member states where occupational pensions have until now played a limited role, including through the establishment of regulatory frameworks. higher governance standards, reflecting best practices at national level in the wake of the economic and financial crisis, are needed to protect scheme members and beneficiaries and to facilitate the provision of safe cross-border pensions. regulatory divergences, overlapping requirements and overly burdensome cross-border procedures need to be reduced. these elements constitute barriers to the development of cross-border occupational pension markets. reducing these barriers will help businesses, including smes and multinational firms, to organise their pension provision activities at european level in a more efficient way. i voted in favour of this report, taking into account that the existence of more secure and efficient occupational pensions will contribute to the adequacy and sustainability of pensions by increasing the contribution of supplementary pension savings to pension income.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the proposal that member states grant prior authorisations to those institutions that decide to operate a scheme in another member state on the basis of authorisations allowing institutions to collect contributions from undertakings established in any member state. the management of pension schemes with members from more than one member state should be carried out in full compliance with the provisions in force of the host member state's social and labour law relating to occupational pension schemes, such as: the establishment and payment of pension benefits and the conditions for the transferability of pension rights. in order to ensure legal certainty of the cross-border activities of institutions, the scope of the prudential rules should be clarified.
in writing. ‒ i support the report, as it will improve the protection of members of occupational retirement schemes and will encourage the development of stable cross-border schemes. member states should take into account the objective for all institutions of ensuring the intergenerational balance of occupational pension schemes, by aiming to have an equitable spread of risks and benefits between generations. i support, especially, the national social and labour provisions that focus on the protection of scheme members and introduce, at the same time, the concept of duty of care in order to avoid a regulatory race to the bottom through cross-border schemes. for the first time in eu legislation, environmental, social and governance factors have been introduced concerning investment decision, by also avoiding stranded assets due to social and environmental risks through an ex-ante risk assessment. last, but not least, taking into account that the gender pension gap in the union is 39% on average, i am of the opinion that an extensive study is needed on the impact of different pillars, pensions systems and their structures on both women and men; to ensure equal levels of pensions for both women and men across the member states.

in writing. ‒ we voted in favour of this report which proposes to create a european legal framework to develop savings for occupational pensions. the economic and demographic crisis we are facing directly affects the future income of people who are out of work. i consider very important the principle that member states will have sufficient flexibility to apply and regulate the requirements of the directive in a way that can reflect the wide variety of pension systems in europe.
in writing. ‒ in order to ensure a balance between generations and as social security systems are under increasing pressure, it is necessary to develop secure and stable occupational pensions in all member states to complement existing pension sources, bearing in mind that a viable pension system includes diversification of products and institutions as well as efficient and effective practices. this will enable member states to protect their citizens from poverty when they are old and helpless, which is not the case in some member states today. as such, this initiative to encourage member states to create adequate, sustainable and secure occupational pension schemes, provided through institutions for the provision of occupational pensions, is welcome. iorps, as long-term investors, should operate in accordance with european law and under the full responsibility of the member states in relation to their role and functions, thus ensuring a high level of protection and safety for members and beneficiaries of occupational pension schemes. in order to achieve this, iorps should implement their corporate governance systems, taking responsibility towards all stakeholders.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the legislative resolution on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the activities and supervision of institutions for occupational retirement provision (recast). in the internal market, institutions for occupational retirement provision (iorps) should have the possibility to operate in other member states while ensuring a high level of protection and security for members and beneficiaries of occupational pension schemes. thus, iorps play an important role in the long-term financing of the union’s economy and in the provision of secure retirement benefits. they are a vital part of the union economy, holding assets worth eur 2.5 trillion on behalf of around 75 million members and beneficiaries. in line with the eu law, i welcome the provisions in order to protect members and beneficiaries of occupational pension schemes, provided that such provisions are consistent with member states’ obligations under union law.
