in writing. ‒ the free movement of people and goods within the eu also entails transfrontier illegalities committed by european citizens. vat fraud alone is estimated to cost eur 60 billion annually. cross-border transactions entail high administrative costs, which are difficult for smes to bear. to avoid this, simplified rules are required through cross-border cooperation between authorities, which reduces the administrative burden by using a common digital reporting base. in view of the rapid evolution of electronic commerce, it is necessary to identify measures aimed at increasing cooperation between member states in the field of digital transactions in order to implement an integrated and comprehensive strategy to combat electronic fraud. to meet the new challenges, tax authorities are forced to adopt new technologies so that the monitoring of the flow of transactions takes place in real time. the linking of all payment terminals to an online system is a safe and effective way of combating vat fraud. i voted in favour of this report, taking into account that late submission of reports is another obstacle in the fight against fraud and that national tax authorities should give priority to facilitating the exchange of information with judicial authorities as well as with europol and olaf.
in writing. ‒ the current vat system of the european union, established in 1993, was conceived as a transitional regulation, which generates an important and increasingly valuable source of revenue in the eu. it represents about 7% of the eu's gross domestic product and is also a source of the european union's own revenue. the commission estimates that the total vat losses due to fraud amount to approximately eur 170 billion per year. a major obstacle to the implementation of vat reform has been the unanimity to be achieved among member states. i voted to initiate a reform that would give member states more freedom and create a definitive model for the vat system. in this way, the financial and bureaucratic burden on businesses would be considerably reduced and fraud would be gradually eliminated.
in writing. ‒ vat is a major and growing source of tax revenue in the eu, but however, the current vat system is too vulnerable to fraud, too burdensome and complex for businesses that wish to expand beyond the member state in which they are established. therefore, i support the outcome of the report, which puts forward proposals to improve the vat collection system, eradicate vat fraud and reduce red tape, supporting the need to reform the vat system with the aim of achieving a single eu vat area that helps promoting employment, growth, investment and competitiveness.
in writing. ‒ in 1993 the european union vat system was put in place as a provisional arrangement stating that the taxation of trade between member states should be based on the principle of taxing goods and services in the country of origin. i have voted for this report that proposes to modernise vat for cross-border e—commerce in order to try and eliminate competitive disadvantages of eu companies against third-country suppliers that can supply vat—free goods to consumers in the eu under the exemption for imports of small consignments.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i consider the fight against tax fraud to be one of the main challenges we have to face in the context of this single market which we all want to be as fairly regulated as possible. the report adopted today calls on the european commission to create a definitive vat system by extending the reverse taxation procedure to all commercial transactions across europe. the current procedure for pre-taxation and refund of excess amounts would no longer be necessary, thus reducing the risk of fraud. at the same time, by facilitating and improving the exchange of information between member states and competent judicial authorities (olaf, europol), fraud in transactions between countries with different vat regimes can be prevented and combated more effectively.
in writing. ‒ the need for a definitive, easy and efficient vat system that helps to combat vat fraud is evident, given that vat is an important source of revenue, valuable for member states, but vulnerable. the business world, developing some of the most unexpected tax avoidance strategies and models, and the digital age have facilitated this world's demise, negatively affecting citizens and responsible actors in european markets. in this context, member states are called upon to develop integrated strategies to combat fraud, with simplified collection measures, using easy and transparent reporting tools, effective tax models, appropriate databases and facilitating the flow of information between tax and customs authorities on imports, harmonised at european level. this approach at the level of each member state should be monitored in terms of the performance achieved by the national tax authorities and coordinated at european level. i voted in favour of facilitating the rationale and operationalisation of integrated strategies to combat fraud by establishing a portal accessible to the general public and to stakeholders with viable, detailed information on all vat-related issues, agreeing that member states should set up such public information systems as are necessary to inform final consumers.
in writing. ‒ value added tax (vat) is an important source of revenue for the member states of the european union, representing no less than 7% of eu gdp in 2014. unfortunately, separate national regulations lead to annual losses of eur 170 million, of which eur 50 million is due to cross-border fraud. the eu has set itself the medium- and long-term objective of harmonising vat rates at union level, with a view to making collection procedures more efficient and to eradicating fraud and combating corruption in this area. this will be beneficial for simplifying the operations of smes at european level and for generating sustainable economic growth. however, despite numerous initiatives to remedy the situation, reform proposals are consistently blocked by some member states. the document sets out concrete proposals from the commission to tax goods and services in the country of destination, introduce a one-stop shop for online sales, apply the reverse taxation procedure widely, develop the eurofisc network and improve cooperation between the member states' specialised structures. i believe that this is a necessary regulation and i support the adoption of this report.
in writing. ‒ wildlife trafficking is a form of international organised crime estimated to be worth around eur 20 billion annually and has grown worldwide in recent years to become one of the largest and most profitable forms of cross-border organised crime. it also poses a growing threat to global security, political stability, economic development, local livelihoods and the rule of law and therefore requires a strategic, coordinated approach at eu level with the participation of all actors involved. in this regard, i welcome the commission's action plan against wildlife trafficking, highlighting the need for coordinated action to address the causes of wildlife trafficking in order to implement and ensure effective enforcement of existing rules and to strengthen global cooperation between countries of origin, transit and destination. i voted in favour of this report, taking into account the need to act, given that the european union is both a transit and destination point for trade and a source of illegal wildlife products protected under eu law.
in writing. ‒ the wildlife trade has become a multi-billion euro criminal activity dominated by organised crime groups. the european union is both an important player in the fight against wildlife crime and a transit point. we voted for the action plan until 2020, which aims to combat wildlife trafficking globally through a set of priorities: prevention, enforcement, cooperation. it is the common responsibility of eu member states to respond to this challenge and halt the rapid decline of some of the world's most prized species. in this way, we will not only preserve biodiversity for future generations, but also improve and strengthen the eu's security framework.
in writing. ‒ the european union is and must remain an important actor in the fight against wildlife crime. the main reason is that europe is an important destination for illegal wildlife products, but also a transit and often origin point for wildlife trafficking, especially between africa, asia and latin america, but also within the eu. i therefore support the european union action plan which is part of the eu's response to the un 2030 agenda for sustainable development. it calls for urgent action to end poaching and trafficking of protected species and to combat the demand and supply of illegal wildlife products. i also support the organisation of information and awareness raising campaigns for citizens on the prevention of wildlife trafficking, addressing its root causes in order to reduce the global demand and supply of illegal wildlife products using the tools available.
in writing. ‒ the need to protect our planet’s flora and fauna from the predation of transnational organised crime has become a major priority for the international community in recent years. i believe the eu has the duty to continue to lead the fight against wildlife trafficking, to take strong action to prevent these illegal activities and to better cooperate with third countries to face the dramatic surge we have seen in the last years. wildlife trafficking has devastating consequences for the sustainable development and for the well-being of the local populations which are affected by it. wildlife trafficking and poaching damage ecosystems and present great risks for rural communities, which are often threatened by heavily armed criminal groups, often acting on a transnational level. moreover, its negative consequences for ecotourism harm local economies.
in writing. ‒ wildlife crimes poses a real threat to biodiversity and is currently being regarded as a security issue in some source countries. i have voted in favour of this report that will put in place an eu action plan aiming to prevent wildlife trafficking and address its root causes.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the problem of wildlife trafficking is a very big one worldwide, with major implications and ramifications in all types of illegal activities. the cartels that ensure the flow of wildlife to markets around the world are the same or closely linked to those that traffic in people, drugs, firearms and ultimately support, through direct or indirect action, instability in certain states or regions and even terrorist organisations. i welcome the fact that all eu member states have committed themselves to fighting wildlife trafficking, as i believe that it must follow the same path and determination already shown in the fight against iuu fishing. the eu action plan on wildlife trafficking proposed by the commission shows the scale of the problems we are facing at the global and european level. they also support this report because it sets out objectives and actions that will complement existing strategies in specific sectors.
in writing. ‒ wildlife trafficking is one of the main causes of the increase in the number of endangered species worldwide. the european union is the main market for this type of harmful trade, with revenues of billions of euros, including in hunting trophies. in this context, it is necessary to regulate this practice, which is considered a threat to biodiversity at european level and to international peace and security, with the involvement of organised crime groups, appropriately. the eu action plan for 2016-2020 has been drawn up in response to the un 2030 agenda for sustainable development, which calls for urgent action to eradicate poaching and trafficking of protected species. this document will strengthen the eu's role in combating wildlife trafficking globally by preventing the root causes of the practice and by implementing existing rules against organised wildlife crime. a strong emphasis is also placed on strengthening the global partnership between countries of origin, consuming countries and transit countries. the eu and its member states are responsible for preserving biodiversity for future generations. i support the adoption of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the own-initiative report which welcomes the commission's action plan against wildlife trafficking. wildlife trafficking is a form of international organised crime estimated to be worth around eur 20 billion annually and has increased worldwide in recent years to become one of the largest and most profitable forms of cross-border organised crime. this type of trafficking is closely linked to other forms of serious and organised crime which it finances. trafficking in wildlife has a major negative impact on biodiversity, existing ecosystems, the natural heritage of the countries of origin, natural resources and species conservation.
in writing. ‒ small and medium-sized enterprises (smes) are the main engine of the european economy, accounting for 99,8% of all non-financial enterprises in 2014. in recent years, job-creating smes have been found mainly in the services sector, playing a key role in the smooth functioning of mobility in europe. unfortunately, they often face difficulties in accessing and maintaining their market, in particular due to the presence of monopolies. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that a regulatory and administrative framework is needed to encourage investment and access to finance, while ensuring sustainable growth and quality jobs in small transport enterprises.
in writing. ‒ small transport enterprises bring together all those enterprises which provide passenger or freight transport services. all of these play a decisive role in the transport of passengers and goods, facilitating mobility. the importance of information and communication in transport has naturally made this sector a fertile ground for the digital economy, and the first challenge for these businesses is the digital transition. whether they're active participants or not, they have to adapt to avoid decline. at present, due to differences in the application of the legislation and its non-compliant use, economic and social market distortions remain widespread, while small enterprises are severely affected by the absence of a single european transport area. i voted to accelerate efforts to complete the single european transport area, thus putting an end to irregularities stemming from legislative gaps.
in writing. ‒ small and medium-sized enterprises play a decisive role in passenger and freight transport, facilitating mobility, traditionally structured by the 'big players'. they have the advantage of better knowledge of local markets, are closer to customers and bring important benefits in densely populated areas, but also in remote areas where the construction of rail infrastructure or the organisation of public transport would be too costly and where the private car is often the only means of transport possible for certain categories of population. i therefore support supporting these enterprises - family businesses, smes, micro-enterprises, craft enterprises or start-ups - because they operate in a well-defined market segment and are often dependent on large enterprises, without necessarily aiming for exponential growth. in addition, they make an important contribution to ensuring the mobility of citizens at european level.
in writing. – the report criticises anti-competitive practices which can lead to serious distortions such as social dumping. it notes the importance of flexible working models as negotiated with social partners, while also emphasising the opportunities in increased digitalisation in monitoring driving time and rest time. it warns of the dangers of a concentration of data by a limited number of platforms. it also notes the importance of decarbonisation in the sector, and the role of public transport in rural and remote areas which should be maintained. the transport sector faces many challenges and possibilities in the emergence of the collaborative economy. a coherent european approach is needed to support the emergence of new business models and smes and to provide services with and alongside existing operators on the market.
in writing. ‒ as an alternative rapporteur for the committee on transport and tourism, i voted for this report because of the concrete proposals to improve the situation of small transport enterprises by creating new opportunities. smes in the transport sector face many challenges to survive in the market. the european and national institutions must support them. in the report, i proposed that member states and the commission take appropriate measures to combat anti-competitive practices by large integrated groups of large carriers. i also requested the publication of a roadmap on the release of publicly funded transport data to ensure transparency. in addition, the report calls for the establishment of cooperation structures between small transport companies, research institutes and local and regional authorities to organise urban and inter-urban mobility.
in writing. ‒ small transport undertakings in europe are strongly represented in road, river and marine transport, and less so in railways and aviation. i have voted for this report that will identify new opportunities for small transport businesses and how they can better take advantage of the digitalisation transition.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that smes are the main drivers of job creation in the services sector, and also the main engine of the european economy. in this context, the report adopted today calls on member states to put an end to the phenomenon of over-regulation, which increases inequalities. at the same time, i welcome the idea of inviting member states and the european commission to consider pooling small transport companies, which would facilitate the development of partnerships between them.
in writing. ‒ the european economy is driven by smes, which create jobs and, in growing numbers, generate innovation and creativity, and an effective expression of entrepreneurship, which promote social inclusion and respect the principles of equal opportunities and gender equality. smes are favourable contexts for the implementation of effective management methods and tools. it is known that the service sector is the one that attracts smes, especially due to the low costs of market entry, generating socio-economic development. i certainly agree that smes in the transport sector contribute to making mobility in the eu more efficient, but they need to create contexts that generate new opportunities for sustainable development, precisely because of the complexity of the sector (e.g. inconsistent definition of service providers, use and marketing of transport services, safety and security, etc.) and its governance system. in particular, the digital economy has created challenges in all aspects for all businesses, regardless of their size and field of activity. sharing economy models can be successfully applied in the development of smes in the transport sector if member states respect european rules on social and working conditions (wages and social security systems) and eu fundamental freedoms.
in writing. ‒ the dramatic growth of the digital economy and the emergence of platforms will radically change the transport market, especially for small businesses. they come with new services and a degree of flexibility that is hard to match for traditional players. they also raise the issue of maintaining a balance between innovation and the protection of social rights. the european parliament proposes a realistic approach, anchored in the certainty that technology is advancing and things are changing. we need to mobilize to act before we are overwhelmed by the complexity of the new conditions. we need a modern transport system as well as new services to meet the growing demands of our citizens. this report is a good opportunity to start the discussion on how the european institutions can create a legislative framework that propels europe to the forefront of innovation and quality in transport services.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the own-initiative report on new opportunities for small businesses in the transport sector, including sharing economy models. smes in the transport sector play a key role in the smooth functioning of mobility in europe, but often face difficulties in accessing and maintaining their market position, in particular due to the presence of monopolies in this market. by transport undertakings the rapporteur means those undertakings which provide services for the transport of passengers or goods.
in writing. ‒ the progress made by belarus over the past two years has contributed to the improvement of eu-belarus relations. in particular, this concerns belarus' proactive participation in the eastern partnership and the mid-term consultations on modernisation issues, the resumption of the eu-belarus human rights dialogue, as well as the start of negotiations on visa facilitation and readmission agreements and on a mobility partnership. unfortunately, however, the well-being of belarusian citizens is endangered by certain policies that do not serve society as a whole, but only certain groups. in this context, we are talking about the violation of freedom of expression and the media, the limitation of civil and political rights, but also the stagnation of the economy for over 20 years, with important sectors still in state ownership. it should also be noted that belarus is the only european country that still applies the death penalty, an inhuman and degrading treatment. i voted in favour of this resolution in the hope of a better treatment of citizens, of a state that respects democratic values, but also of a dynamic civil society that can contribute to the social and economic well-being of this country.
in writing. ‒ the continuing use of the death penalty in belarus, the only country on the european continent that still applies the death penalty, is to be deplored. i strongly support the call on the authorities of belarus to commute the remaining death sentences and establish without delay a formal moratorium on executions as a first step towards abolition of the death penalty. the introduction of the moratorium would be a decisive step in bringing belarus closer to the pan-european legal standards. it is important to increase cooperation in the areas of legal and labour migration; asylum and the protection of refugees; prevention and combating of irregular migration and on maximising the development impact of migration and mobility. however, we cannot forget that the situation in belarus is not improving from a political rights and social freedoms point of view. the repression of democratic opposition and of independent civil society activity has to be condemned by all means.

in writing. ‒ i have voted for this motion for a resolution that stresses the shortcomings observed during the 2015 presidential elections and the 2016 parliamentary elections, calling on belarusian authorities to begin work on a comprehensive electoral reform as part of a broader democratisation process.
in writing. ‒ the situation in belarus has evolved significantly in recent years, although it is still far from meeting the union's standards on democracy and the rule of law. following the release of the last political prisoners by the minsk regime at the end of 2015, the eu lifted sanctions against the belarusian state and began a critical dialogue with it. the legislative elections of 11 september 2016 marked the election of two independent opposition deputies to the lower house of the parliament of belarus. it is a step forward, although the democratic opposition forces in belarus have condemned these elections as unfair. from an economic point of view, the minsk regime needs financial resources to overcome the current difficult situation. the eu can provide these resources, but only in exchange for the continued democratisation of the belarusian state structures and the abandonment of dictatorial and authoritarian methods of governance. the union's main objective must be to promote its values in belarus, an important state in its eastern neighbourhood, and a better economic situation for the belarusian citizens. i support the adoption of this resolution.

in writing. – the european parliament called for an agreement that would provide data protection safeguards for personal information transferred between the eu and us. on 3 december 2010 the council authorised the commission to open negotiations on such an agreement that would provide the right to privacy with respect to the processing of personal data when this information is transferred to the competent authorities. on 8 september 2015 eu and us officials concluded the agreement, guaranteeing a high level of protection for all personal data that will be transferred between the law enforcement authorities of the two parts. the personal data will only be exchanged and processed with the scope of investigating, detecting or prosecuting criminal offences and acts of terrorism in the framework of police cooperation and judicial cooperation in criminal matters. any citizen from the two parts that considers that his data has been misused will have access to several accessible and affordable dispute resolution mechanisms. this is the first time that personal data information is exchanged in a secured way with strong obligations on companies handling the data, clear safeguards and transparency obligations on us government access and an effective protection of individual rights.

in writing. the european union solidarity fund (eusf), established in 2002, is a non-reimbursable financial instrument needed for emergency and rescue actions by authorities following natural disasters that have a direct impact on people's lives, the natural environment or the economy in a specific affected region. over time, the eusf has undergone several revisions, with a view to its development, at least in terms of process, procedures, time period, content, notions with which it operates, indicators for assessing the effectiveness of aid, scope/sphere. this is because the evidence shows that, as a result of climate change, natural disasters within the eu are continuously increasing in number, severity and intensity. the impact and importance of the eusf in promoting sustainable solutions is enhanced if, in this context, other european structural and investment funds (esi funds) are also used appropriately and synergistically by national, local and regional authorities, in particular for the purpose of preventing natural disasters, underpinned by effective specific strategies. it is clear that the authorities must disseminate to the general public, by modern means, information on both the aid that may be granted through the eusf (including monitoring its progress) and the results of the aid already granted from 2002 to the present.

as a member of the committee on legal affairs of the european parliament, i welcome the initiative of our colleagues to change the legal framework on the incompatibility regime for commissioners and the declaration of interests. the changes introduced by this new document are a step forward in combating abuse, in promoting transparency and - why not? - in increasing trust in the european institutions. i take this opportunity to mention an example that has been widely reported in the press and in the debates that have taken place on this subject in the european parliament. i am referring to the former commissioner for agriculture, dacian ciolos, who now has two incomes. he receives a daily allowance as a former commissioner of around €8,300 per month, while he collects the salary of the prime minister from romanian taxpayers' money. i don't know if we can refer to this as an incompatibility, but it certainly took advantage of the lack of clear legal provisions. i am saddened that such possible abuses can be committed by an experienced politician, but i am glad that we have succeeded in this final draft on the incompatibilities regime and the declaration of interests to combat such immoral solutions by introducing precise measures on such situations. thank you. thank you.
thank you, madam president. the main concern of farmers today is to get their products to a price that is acceptable and that will enable them to survive in the market. the big grocery chains, especially in western europe, have a close partnership with local farmers, which is a very good thing. the commission notes that the measure is not intended to provide a guarantee to the beneficiary of the aid. this implies a limited number of economic operators engaged in economic development activity, as well as close relationships between producers, processors and consumers. the european commission has, however, shown an excessive zeal in this case, initiating preliminary infringement proceedings, which i regard as being limited to the legality of the treaties. i would point out that the law adopted does not restrict the presence of european agri-food products on the shelves of traders in romania, so it is not an obstacle to intra-community trade, and this law must certainly be applied in romania. thank you. thank you.
madam president, commissioner, i would like to draw your attention to the ex ante conditionalities imposed on the member states. these requirements are a tool used to enforce the policy of the european commission and another case of overstepping the powers conferred by the treaties. under the pretext of setting conditions for the effective implementation of the funds, the european commission actually obliges the states to implement certain structural reforms and strategies at national level. the need for them is determined unilaterally by the european commission, without being able to be discussed or modified according to specific national particularities. for example, romania was imposed 36 conditionalities to be met by the end of this year, including for areas that are the exclusive competence of member states, such as health and education. member states have noted the high complexity and the lack of clarity of those cross-compliance. if we add to this the danger of suspending funds, then national institutions will tend to adopt formal measures just to avoid sanctions. in the current context, when more and more voices are calling for simplicity and clarity in regulations, i believe it is absolutely necessary that these conditionalities be revised and that the allocation of funds is not affected by the stage of their implementation. thank you. thank you.
december 1 is the national day of romania and all romanians, marking a moment of great historical significance, 98 years since the great union at alba iulia. it is a moment that honors the sacrifices made by hundreds of thousands of romanians over the centuries for the realization of national unity. over 300,000 romanian soldiers died in world war i for this goal. of these, over 22,000 died and were buried outside the country's borders. because this day belongs to all romanians, wherever they may be, i decided to take a moment to recall the graves of the eight romanian soldiers killed in world war i here in belgium, in mons. and the most important place in my soul and in the romanian people is alba iulia, the place where modern romania was born. that is why i hope that in 2018, when the centenary of romania will be celebrated, alba iulia will benefit from more recognition from the romanian state and become a landmark for everything that the future of romania means. i invite all our european partners to join us in supporting this country project. happy birthday to romania, happy birthday to alba iulia, happy birthday to all the romanians!

mr president, i have to say that i am very pleased. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteurs and all the political groups who understood the urgency of amending article 136 of the customs code, which applies from 1 may 2016. that is why i hope that today this amendment to the simplified procedure, this report, will be voted on. as the commission has also argued, under the current form of article 136, the relevant authorities in the member states have no legal basis to apply the provisions relating to the notification of the arrival of a seagoing vessel or aircraft, the carriage and the presentation of goods to customs when unloaded or transported. for this reason, the absence of legal regulation, of a legal basis, could lead to insecurity, to non-taxation and non-application of fiscal measures, to the absence of sanitary controls and, obviously, to risks related to goods arriving in ports. thank you and i wish my country happy birthday too because i cannot be with the romanians, i am here in parliament. i thank you and hope that the report will be voted on.
in writing. following the entry into force of the provisions of the regulation establishing the union customs code, certain irregularities and shortcomings have been identified which prevent the correct application of this code. the initiative therefore aims to correct these errors in order to ensure equal treatment of goods. the main problem identified relates to the lack of a legal basis for the competent authorities in the member states to apply the provisions on the carriage and presentation of goods to customs when unloaded, notification of the arrival of a seagoing vessel or aircraft, provisions on temporary storage. in the absence of a legal basis, the fulfilment of customs supervision tasks becomes difficult to achieve within optimal parameters. as a result, the authorities will be unable to correctly collect import duties and properly apply non-fiscal measures, as well as to identify risks related to goods arriving at their ports or airports. i voted in favour of this report because i consider it necessary to remedy these deficiencies in order to properly carry out customs supervision tasks.
in writing. ‒ this proposal changes one article of the union customs code, which has proved to be problematic in practice and concerns goods which have temporarily left the union territory by sea or air. in committee, the proposal was dealt with under simplified procedure (rule 50) and the com proposal was adopted without amendments. i supported the report in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ as rapporteur for the imco commission, i voted for this report because the union customs code sets clear rules and fair conditions for all operators in the field and clarifies the regulated procedures. the amendment of the customs code will ensure an increase in security regarding products entering the territory of romania and a correct taxation. this report is important as the relevant authorities in the member states currently have no legal basis under the current article 136 to apply provisions on lodging of entry summary declaration; notification of arrival of a seagoing vessel or aircraft; transport and presentation of goods to customs when unloaded or transhipped; waiting for authorisation before unloading or transhipping of goods; provisions on temporary storage. these provisions apply to the specific case of goods which have temporarily left the customs territory of the union while travelling on a direct route between two points in that territory by sea or air, without any stop outside the union. the absence of a clear legal basis makes it difficult for the customs authorities to effectively carry out their customs supervision tasks.
in writing. ‒ the union customs code (ucc) is the new framework regulation on the rules and procedures for the customs throughout the eu. i voted for this report that will put in place provisions for the case of goods that have temporarily left the eu’s customs territory while moving by direct route by air or by sea, between two points of that territory without a stop outside the eu.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report which identifies the shortcomings of regulation (eu) no 952/2013 and proposes the necessary amendments to the regulations on the carriage of goods by sea or air. in accordance with article 136, at this stage the relevant authorities in the member states do not have a legal basis to apply the provisions on lodging the entry summary declaration, the carriage and presentation of goods to customs when unloaded or transhipped, or the provisions on temporary storage of goods. they should apply to the specific case of goods which have temporarily left the customs territory of the european union while travelling on a direct route between two points by sea or air, without any stop outside the european union. in the absence of a clear legal basis requiring the presentation of goods to the customs authorities of the country of transit, the effective performance of customs supervision tasks is hampered. i consider that the proposal to amend article 136, which clearly specifies this obligation, removes this shortcoming and provides once again the legal basis for control, as it was established in the old customs code.
in writing. ‒ in order to facilitate trade flows, the amendment of the union customs code with regard to goods temporarily leaving the customs territory of the union by sea or air is salutary as it brings the necessary clarifications to the proper and adequate application of fiscal and non-fiscal measures (such as veterinary and phytosanitary controls), thus addressing the shortcomings identified in the implementation of the customs code, applicable from 1 may 2016. for example, logically, temporary leaving the customs territory of the union does not change the status of goods, that of union goods, as confirmed by the amendments made to the union customs code. in the light of the findings of the member states with regard to the use of the union customs code, the need for legal regulations is evident, mainly concerning the arrival of a seagoing ship or aircraft, the carriage and the presentation of goods to customs when unloaded or transported. moreover, the amendments to the union customs code ensure consistency with existing policies and objectives relevant to trade in goods brought into or taken out of the customs territory of the union permanently or temporarily.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the ep report on the eu regulation on goods temporarily leaving the customs territory of the union by sea or air. the provisions apply to the specific case of goods which have temporarily left the customs territory of the union while travelling on a direct route between two points in that territory by sea or air, without any stop outside the eu. the amendment to the regulation aims to ensure equal treatment of goods and to provide again the legal basis which was already established in the old customs code.
in writing. regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 aims to improve the protection of retail investors investing in insurance-based structured individual investment products (priips) and to restore consumer confidence in financial services, given the effects of the financial crisis. in order to achieve these objectives, both the obligation for the creators of these products to comply with the disclosure requirements and the obligation for retail investors to receive key information documents (kids) are provided. in view of certain delays in the adoption of the delegated regulation, it was proposed to postpone the date of application of the regulation by 12 months in order to ensure compliance with all standards and to ensure the achievement of the objectives of the regulation. i consider this 12-month delay to be appropriate in order to remove all legal uncertainties, which is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the priips proposal introduces a series of measures aimed at enhancing investor protection and rebuilding consumer trust in the financial services industry by increasing transparency in the retail investment market. it requires manufacturers of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products to produce a key information document (‘kid’). the regulation was adopted in 2014 and was supposed to come into force on 1 january 2017. the commission came forward with a regulatory technical standard (rts) on the exact content of the kid. in order to allow the commission to come forward with a revised rts, as the previous one was rejected in september 2016, and avoid uncertainty in the market, in agreement with parliament and the council, the commission postponed the date of implementation by one year. therefore, i support the technical proposal to postpone the date of implementation to 1 january 2018 in order to allow a level 2 legislation on the key information document to be adopted with stronger protection clauses for investors.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report on documents for packaged retail and insurance-based investment products with regard to the requirement to provide presentation, content, review and revision of key information documents.
in writing. ‒ in the current context, consumers of insurance products need transparency in the financial services sector, responsible behaviour by financial service providers (creators of insurance-based and structured individual investment products) and, above all, the proactive involvement of competent authorities in the member states and at european level. this is because, on the one hand, the range of individual structured and insurance-based investment products is increasing, some of these products are combined with insurance, and are in any case complex and difficult for investors to understand, and, on the other hand, member states are taking divergent and uncoordinated action to ensure investor protection. communication and transparency thus contribute to creating the conditions for the development of constructive competitiveness in the market for individual investments, irrespective of the type of financial intermediary (who produces or markets them) and those relating to investor protection. in this context, the delay of 12 months in the application of regulation (eu) no 1286/2014 is timely and justified, providing the necessary time for member states to adhere to measures designed to increase investor protection and consumer confidence in individual structured and insurance-based investments.

in writing. the cotonou agreement establishes partnership relations between the african, caribbean and pacific group of states, of the one part, and the european union and its member states, of the other part, and also governs relations between the republic of kiribati and the european union. the eu-kiribati agreement on the short-stay visa waiver provides for the abolition of the visa requirement for citizens of the union and of the republic of kiribati travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a stay of no more than 90 days in any 180-day period. this visa waiver benefits all categories of persons, thus encouraging tourism and investment. i have spoken in favour of this agreement because i believe it is a powerful instrument for strengthening economic and cultural relations and for intensifying political dialogue between the european union and the republic of kiribati.
in writing. ‒ the agreement provides for visa-free travel for the citizens of the european union and for the citizens of kiribati when travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. the visa waiver may act to boost economic investment in the area, and facilitate travel for business and tourism, which may be very limited in some areas. the signing of short-stay waivers steps up europe’s economic and cultural relations and intensifies political dialogue.
in writing. ‒ the cotonou agreement was signed in june 2000 by eu member states and the african, caribbean and pacific group of states and was concluded for a 20-year period, until 2020, making it the most comprehensive partnership agreement between developing countries and the eu. i have voted for this report on the waiver of short-stay visas for citizens of the eu and the republic of kiribati when travelling to each other’s territory for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. this will step up economic and cultural relations and intensify the political dialogue on a wide range of issues like fundamental freedoms and human rights.

in writing. ‒ i welcome this agreement, which aims to establish a framework of data protection principles and safeguards for when personal data is transferred for criminal law enforcement purposes between the eu or the member states and the us and supplements, where necessary, data protection safeguards in existing and future data transfer agreements or national provisions authorising such transfers. therefore, it will bring a significant improvement to the current situation. however, i believe that there is a need to solve its main problem, the absence of sufficient rights to judicial redress for permanent residents who are non-eu citizens, as they are excluded from the protections of the judicial redress act. moreover, we must ensure that the european data protection authorities keep their rights to independently assess the data protection environment, as the current wording would solidify the status for the us, regardless of what changes they would make to their internal legislation on data protection.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this recommendation because i believe that human rights and freedoms must form the basis of any agreements and understandings that the european union signs with its partners to combat crime of all kinds. i strongly believe, as this document proposes, that we can strike a balance between the protection of our citizens' right to privacy and the processing and transfer of personal data between the competent authorities of the european union and the united states. the european parliament reiterates in its recommendation that the transfer of data of citizens and their processing must be done only for the purpose for which these data were collected and cannot be used for any other action unrelated to this purpose. the exchange of data under this agreement should therefore only be for the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences, and this listing is of utmost importance. the agreement is new in that it will allow citizens to have the legal possibility to seek judicial redress if they believe their rights to access personal information have been violated by both european and us authorities.

in writing. the offshore safety directive aims to establish requirements for the prevention of major accidents in offshore oil and gas operations within the eu and for limiting the consequences of such accidents. although the provisions of that directive establish that the holders of offshore licences are strictly responsible for preventing and repairing all environmental damage caused by their oil and gas operations, the directive does not regulate liability for civil damage to natural or legal persons or matters relating to criminal liability for offshore accidents. the initiative thus proposes to establish third-party compensation mechanisms for traditional damage caused by offshore oil and gas operations and to create an effective compensation system for the management of relevant payments. i voted in favour of this report because i believe it is essential to provide for systems of compensation and financial guarantee for offshore oil and gas operations in the eu.
in writing. ‒ in september 2015 the commission presented a report to the ep and the council on liability, compensation and financial security for offshore oil and gas operations pursuant to article 39 of directive 2013/30/eu (the offshore safety directive or osd). the osd defines the elements of such a comprehensive eu-wide framework for preventing major accidents and limiting their consequences. the report deals with what kinds of damage are being paid, financial capacity of liable parties, disbursement of compensation and liability regimes. in his report the rapporteur has focused on the importance of updating existing liability systems in the member states to ensure the application of the polluter-pays principle not only to environmental but also to traditional damages (bodily injuries/ property damages/ pure and consequential economic losses). incidents in european waters should not adversely affect the future of the offshore oil and gas operations of the state in question, nor that of the entire eu, were the incident to occur in an area that was largely dependent on tourism for revenue. as a result, compensation and financial security systems for offshore oil and gas operations in the eu should be brought up to speed. i supported the report in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ over 90% of oil and 60% of gas produced in europe comes from offshore operations with ongoing operations planned to take place in the territorial waters of 18 member states. i have voted for this report that will bring together eu member states and the commission to work and ensure that compensation and financial security systems for offshore oil and gas operations in the eu are up to date, providing for compensation of third party claims amongst others.
in writing. ‒ it is well known that offshore oil and gas exploration, production and production activities require a high level of protection due to the major impact on all stakeholders and, in particular, on the environment. eu action in this area must, as a matter of urgency, be based on the principles of precaution, prevention and sustainability and be internationally harmonised. clearly, the polluter pays for the social and economic damage, as incidents in the eu oil and gas sector have serious and lasting, direct and indirect repercussions not only on the environment, but also on various sectors of activity, especially the 'blue economy' sectors (coastal tourism, fishing, etc.) and the community. as such, it is essential to implement a legislative mechanism, based on the assessment of the transposition and application of drm and dso, which is necessary not only for adequate and effective compensation/compensation, but also for the remediation of traditional damage, applicable throughout the eu, for all categories of damage to the environment, to persons (natural and legal), to the community, to the economy, to society in general. member states shall include in that mechanism the guarantee of the existence and/or maintenance, the provision of adequate financial means (including financial guarantee instruments) at the level of operators in the field or responsible persons, necessary to cover the damage and the restoration of ecosystems.
in writing. ‒ the scope of this report is to underline the importance of updating existing liability systems in the european union, such as the offshore safety directive, to ensure the application of the polluter-pays principle not only to environmental but also to traditional damages (bodily injuries/property damage/pure and consequential economic losses). it is crucial to have effective and adequate compensation mechanisms and claims handling mechanisms for such damage, especially in areas largely dependent on tourism for revenue. such damage would limit the arrival of tourists and reduce the total revenue in those particular areas of the european union. therefore, there is an urgent need for compensation and financial security systems to be brought to speed and to make up for the lost money. as an advocate of the tourism industry in the european parliament, i support this report.

in writing. ‒ regulation (ec) no 1896/2006 of 12 december 2006 creates a european order for payment procedure for claims not contested by the defendant. this simplifies, speeds up and reduces the costs of litigation in cases involving more than one eu country. it also permits the free circulation of european orders for payment which are recognised and enforced in all eu countries. it applies to all civil and commercial matters in cases where at least one of the parties lives in an eu country different from the one where the application for an order is made. it applies to all eu countries except denmark. the report on the application of the european order for payment procedure is meant to give feedback on the almost 10 years of experience in applying this procedure throughout europe. the main conclusions of the report were positive towards the successful operation of the procedure in all the member states, but making the point that it should be made sure that it is more known and widely used, by informing and assisting citizens. the report also asks the commission to produce an impact assessment and a future revision should focus on ensuring more harmonisation in the application of the procedure and on removing certain exceptions.
in writing. the european order for payment procedure makes it easier to recover amounts in cross-border procedures. it is an optional procedure that can be an alternative to internal payment orders. statistics show that the european order for payment is cheaper and faster than national procedures. however, this instrument is used below its potential as it is mainly used in member states with similar national legislation. i am in favour of this procedure because it has great potential for the economic environment. late payment is one of the main causes of insolvency, threatening the survival of enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises. the benefits of the procedure should be better understood by ordinary citizens, businesses and legal professionals. the procedure can be made more efficient if it can be done online. updated impact studies are needed. consumption varies widely from one member state to another. citizens are not informed, and this risks diminishing trust in eu legislation.
in writing. ‒ the european payment order is a procedure that can be used in cross-border cases as an alternative to domestic payment orders. i have voted for this report that will provide easier recovery of sums in cross-border proceedings.
in writing. ‒ the european order for payment procedure allows creditors to easily obtain an order to recover uncontested civil and commercial claims. it can be applied for by correspondence or electronically, does not require the assistance of a lawyer, and is enforceable in other member states without any need for additional formalities. this system simplifies, speeds up and reduces the costs of litigation in cases involving more than one eu country. it also permits the free circulation of european orders for payment that are recognised and enforced in all eu countries. this report gives feedback on the almost 10 years of experience in applying this procedure throughout europe and provides some recommendations for the future. i support this report.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, we are all aware that these are challenging times for free societies, for europe and for fundamental rights. almost daily, we see challenges to our values and our way of life on things that we hold dear, that are fundamental, that enable us to live freely and in harmony with our fellow human beings. the way some people, some politicians included, talk about the terrorist threat, the refugee crisis and the economic situation, all tends to feed these worrying developments. such discourse polarises societies and fuels division, hatred and intolerance. it also nourishes fake news, a reality seen through the spectacles of emotions and not facts. this only leads to a constant erosion of the values and principles that are at the foundation of the democratic societies and the european union. allow me to congratulate the rapporteur on wide support for this resolution and to comment on some key aspects. let me start with accession to the european convention on human rights. as you know, the commission remains fully committed to eu accession to the european convention on human rights. the commission, in its capacity as eu negotiator, is currently consulting with the relevant council working party on solutions for addressing the various objections raised by the court. this work is making good progress. on the rule of law, the commission fully agrees that our common values as enshrined in article 2 of the treaty on european union must be respected and enforced. as first vice-president timmermans underlined at the plenary session in october, the key issue is to identify the best means to achieve this objective. in that respect, the commission is examining the european parliament’s resolution on a union pact on democracy, the rule of law and fundamental rights very carefully, in line with article 225 of the treaty and will give this resolution the serious response it deserves. on mainstreaming the eu charter of fundamental rights, systematic fundamental rights checks during the legislative process are carried out to ensure compliance of draft eu legislation with the eu charter of fundamental rights. the commission’s better regulation agenda includes a fundamental rights checklist that the commission is to use when conducting assessments. the commission also trains specific departments to ensure application of a fundamental rights-based approach to policy and law-making. in accordance with the interinstitutional agreement, the commission also committed to systematically introducing a summary of its fundamental rights assessment in explanatory memoranda. furthermore, when mainstreaming the rights in the charter in relation to disabled persons, the obligations enshrined in the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities should be observed. now let me say a few words on the topic of migration and refugees. full respect of the charter and the safeguarding of individuals’ fundamental rights and freedoms have also been a stated priority for the commission in the design of eu policies and measures in the areas of migration, asylum and integration. in particular, the further harmonisation of the common european asylum system will contribute to swifter access to international protection for those in need of it, safeguarding protection against refoulement and the right to an effective remedy. it will reinforce the guarantees for vulnerable asylum applicants such as unaccompanied minors and women, in terms of their reception conditions and procedural rights. at the same time, it will counter the misuse and abuse of the fundamental right to asylum, including by reducing secondary movements. in parallel to reforming the common european asylum system to adapt it to changing circumstances and better ensure the principle of solidarity between member states, the commission is closely monitoring the transposition and implementation of existing legislation by member states. the action plan on the integration of third country nationals recalls the importance of fundamental values for a successful two-way integration process. understanding and subscribing to the fundamental values on which the european union is built is an essential element of living and participating in the host society. at the same time, these rights also protect the third country national and foster his or her inclusion into our society. the eu agency for fundamental rights is currently working on monitoring the social inclusion and participation of migrants and their descendants in society from a fundamental rights perspective. it will publish in 2017 the results of the second wave of the largest eu-wide survey on experiences of discrimination, hate crime, victimisation and societal participation of migrants and minorities. the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities stipulates the obligation of states parties to ensure the protection and safety of persons with disabilities. it requires protecting their integrity and ensuring that they are free from exploitation, violence and abuse. the european commission implements the convention through the european disability strategy for the years 2010-2020 and will soon adopt a progress report. the report also takes into account the un committee’s concluding observations for the eu. trafficking in human beings is prohibited in the eu charter of fundamental rights and constitutes a serious form of organised crime. as required by the 2011 directive in this field, on 2 december, the commission published two reports, one assessing the transposition of the directive by member states, and one assessing the impact of existing national law establishing as a criminal offence the use of services which are the objects of exploitation of trafficking in human beings. the recommendations in your report are very timely since the commission is working now on the post-2016 policy framework and therefore will assess them carefully. on freedom and security, as regards surveillance measures by the state it needs to be kept in mind that such activities by police and intelligence agencies of member states may be based on national legislation pertaining to the protection of national security, an area within the sole competence of the member states. where measures of surveillance are applied by the member states in the context of implementing eu law these states are, however, bound by the charter. on the european arrest warrant, it should be noted that it is operating correctly and successfully in general. every year it helps in bringing thousands of suspects and convicts of dangerous offences to justice. let me inform you shortly about what the commission does against radicalisation, discrimination, xenophobia, hate speech and hate crime. following the approach elaborated in the commission communication on radicalisation, the commission, together with the radicalisation awareness network, supports member states’ efforts in countering radicalisation, in full compliance with fundamental rights, promoting social inclusion and avoiding stigmatisation of any group. the network centre of excellence pools relevant expertise. it identifies best practices and issues policy recommendations and practical guidance that provide member states and stakeholders with the skills and tools to implement more effective preventive measures at national, regional and also local level. the commission’s contribution is focused on the internet, research, inclusive education, common values, rehabilitation and reintegration, and prisons, where it can provide a real added value, mainly by enabling first line practitioners to exchange practices and develop counter-narratives. the prevention of and fight against racism, xenophobia and all other forms of intolerance are a clear priority for the commission. the commission therefore assists member state authorities to improve their responses to hate speech and hate crime. an important area of focus is countering illegal hate speech on the internet. the commission agreed with facebook, twitter, microsoft and youtube in may 2016 a code of conduct on countering illegal hate speech online, including clear commitments by the companies to review and, if necessary, take down illegal hate speech more speedily and efficiently. we have just finalised a first monitoring of the code of conduct, which i discussed last week with it providers and ministers of justice. the monitoring showed progress, but also confirmed the need to continue improving the timing of the takedowns of illegal hate speech and also transparency towards the notifying persons. also geographic coverage in the eu is not yet balanced. i got strong support from justice ministers at the council last week to continue on this path and to come back with a further assessment in spring 2017. the fight against discrimination remains a high priority for the commission, notably through awareness-raising activities and the monitoring of the various directives in place in this area. let me say a few words about women’s rights and children and roma rights and citizenship - just to reassure you that i plan to conclude soon. on women’s rights the commission is committed to priorities of its strategic engagement for gender equality for the years 2016 to 2019, which includes actions in response to challenges highlighted by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe). substantial progress in implementation of the strategic engagement can already be reported. the commission has also made many efforts towards increasing female labour market participation and the equal economic independence of women and men. the commission monitored and assessed the progress of member states in achieving equality between women and men, and provided input to the june 2016 country-specific recommendations on female labour market participation addressed to 10 member states. the commission will continue to promote child-friendly justice and the council of europe guidelines on child-friendly justice, including through its rights of the child funding. detention conditions are so far, however, primarily a responsibility of member states, which agreed to respect the existing council of europe standards on the matter, such as the european prison rules adopted in 2006. children growing up in poverty or social exclusion are less likely than their better-off peers to do well in school, enjoy good health and realise their full potential later in life. the efforts to implement the recommendations should be stepped up in particular for children with special needs, children in street situations, children in alternative care and so on. in the context of the refugee crisis, unaccompanied minors face particular integration challenges. tailored education and training programmes, together with substantial long-term commitment from local hosting and integration systems, are needed to overcome the extremely vulnerable situation of these children. under eu law, all asylum-seeking children should have access to education within three months of filing for asylum. the eu action plan on the integration of third country nationals refers to the importance of early childhood education and care for the integration of migrant children. having an inclusive setting so that children with disabilities have equal access to training, care and facilities, remains also a challenge. the recent forum of the child identified concrete actions such as the situation in the reception facilities, effective guardianship, which we will pursue further and i will discuss this with ministers at the informal justice ministers meeting at the end of january in malta. the commission has no plans to present a specific european strategy on the rights of the child, since we believe that rather than new announcements, it is more useful to continue to focus on mainstreaming these issues right across all our policy work. on roma rights, the commission in its 2016 report on the implementation of the eu framework and the council recommendation on effective roma integration measures in the member states identified a number of most burning challenges. to address them and bring positive changes in the lives of roma, the commission called on member states to address urgently the enforcement of anti-discrimination legislation, eliminate segregation in education and housing and so on. the commission is strongly committed to support member states, ensure the necessary commitment to roma inclusion at the european level, and use all available means to promote dialogue and cooperation. let me conclude with several words on citizenship. the eu charter of fundamental rights has become a powerful safeguard, as demonstrated by its prominence in the rulings of the court of justice, as well as national courts. that being said, general awareness of the charter can still be improved among national judges, as well as citizens in general. to this effect, the commission is funding several projects accessible through the e-justice portal, enabling individuals to know who to turn to in case of breach of a fundamental right. in particular, in october 2016 the e-justice portal integrated the clarity online tool developed by the fundamental rights agency, which helps individuals to identify the competent national non-judicial bodies with a human rights remit. the scope of the tool will be further extended in the upcoming months. we are now more than ever called upon to defend fundamental rights, democracy and the rule of law with strong determination. the draft resolution of the european parliament is an important contribution. in writing. the cultural and creative industries must become a central element in the european union's development and economic policy. the potential of these sectors, their attractiveness to young people and their added value are arguments for investing more at european level. i therefore believe that this report can be a first step towards a common, coherent and constructive policy. to do this, we need to start with a single piece of legislation that defines the opportunities, but is not restrictive, in order to maintain the innovative nature of these industries. we need to create an ecosystem for creativity and innovation, and this involves investing in education and training, in local development and in supporting entrepreneurship or supporting the commercialisation of the products and services offered by these sectors. i come from a country, romania, where these industries are booming, and i would like to be able to say that in the future, the young creative people in my country will be able to turn their ideas into reality, thanks to the european union. in fact, we need to take it on ambitiously that we are willing to take a constructive role in supporting these industries now, when the european union is still competitive and our human resources have not yet left.

in writing. the clean energy proposal promises to increase gdp by 1% over the next ten years and create 900 000 jobs. the commission must, however, put the necessary legislation on the table to ensure the necessary transition to sustainable energy. this transition should focus on energy efficiency, renewable energy, smart infrastructure and on finding european-level solutions for interconnections, lng terminals and energy storage capacities. however, it should not be overlooked that the production of energy from renewable sources requires the continuity of conventional energy production. the exploitation of hydropower in the case of romania, of high-efficiency gas and coal-fired power plants, benefiting from the latest technologies, can make a key contribution to unlocking the european energy market. the development of renewable energy implies the creation of a new energy market design, which ensures a level playing field for all market participants. legislative proposals should enable consumers to control energy costs and have access to the full real costs of electricity supplied, including those associated with transmission and distribution.

in writing. ‒ deep-sea fishing in the north-east atlantic has developed at an accelerated pace, against the backdrop of unsustainable practices and overfishing on the continental shelf. this rapid development has occurred without reliance on comprehensive information on the state of deep-sea fish stocks, the level of discards or the effects on marine ecosystems of this fishing activity. the commission has also proposed to amend the fishing opportunities for bluefin tuna set out in the annex to regulation (ec) no 1224/2009 in order to allow the member states to limit the fishing opportunities available to bluefin tuna. this is to collect comprehensive data on the state of fish stocks and to protect vulnerable marine ecosystems on the seabed. i voted in favour of this proposal because i believe it is essential to promote sustainable development in marine ecosystems, precisely to protect marine diversity and deep-sea species.
in writing. ‒ i strongly support this compromise text on deep-sea fishing in the north-east atlantic. it is in line with the principles of the new basic regulation/cfp reform and it ensures conditions for preventing significant adverse impacts on vulnerable marine ecosystems. targeted deep-sea fishing will be limited to the area where it occurred in 2009-2011 (freezing the ‘footprint area’); fishing with bottom trawls below 800 metres will be prohibited; vessels will be obliged to report encounters with vulnerable marine ecosystems below a depth of 400 metres and to immediately stop operations and move to an area at least five nautical miles away from the area of encounter. furthermore, it includes an increased scientific observer coverage of 20%, establishes specific sanctions, better conditions for improving data collection and stronger transparency rules. member states will finally be required to provide information on the location of vulnerable ecosystems and the commission will assess this data annually and adapt the allowed fishing area accordingly.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report. it ensures conditions for preventing significant adverse impacts on vulnerable marine ecosystems and establishes better conditions for improving data collection and stronger transparency rules.
in writing. ‒ i have voted against this report on deep-sea stocks and fishing in international waters.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this recommendation because i believe that the final agreement negotiated with the council representatives is a good one, which brings improvements to the legislation on the protection of the deep sea environment. given the fragility of this type of marine environment and the fact that the diversity and quantity of deep-sea fish stocks are at risk due to their slow regeneration, i believe it was extremely important for the eu to adopt a comprehensive and firm regulation in this regard. i appreciate that this agreement imposes high standards of environmental protection, protects deep-sea biodiversity and respects the common fisheries policy and its objectives.
in writing. ‒ in general, promoting sustainable development means including environmental protection requirements in the definition and implementation of eu policies and actions. as regards deep-sea fishing, the need for regulation (in accordance with the precautionary principle) derives from the need for long-term sustainable exploitation of these stocks, not only to prevent significant harmful effects on vulnerable marine ecosystems, but also to ensure the conservation of those fisheries resources. in this respect, scientific advice is indispensable. thus, fishing activities should be made subject to a prior environmental impact assessment, adopting, where appropriate, measures to close areas with vulnerable systems, specific measures to prevent significant effects on vulnerable marine ecosystems, conservation measures to protect vulnerable marine ecosystems. impact assessments of the application of the provisions shall be based on actual and relevant data and information collections. in the interest of environmental protection, it is beneficial to phase out fishing methods that are highly damaging to vulnerable marine ecosystems, while presenting high levels of unwanted deep-sea species catches.
in writing. ‒ fishing is one of the main economic activities for a large part of the eu member states. a significant proportion of this activity is covered by fishing for deep-sea stocks in the north-east atlantic area. in order to protect the vulnerable marine ecosystem on the seabed, the european institutions have been engaged in a stricter regulatory process since january 2014. the agreement currently reached provides for a freeze on the fishing footprint, defining the area in which fishing activities are allowed. that area includes a region in european waters of the north-east atlantic where directed fisheries were conducted during the period 2009-2011 and where catches of deep-sea species are no longer allowed to represent more than 8% of the total annual catches. the depth limit below which this provision applies is 400 m and vessels that fail to respect a distance of at least 5 miles from the area concerned will suffer specific penalties. it also provides for strict rules on the reporting of all catches, the provision of information by member states and the presence of scientific observers on 20% of vessels entering the area. i support the adoption of this recommendation.
